the committee on petitions has also tabled a number of amendments. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, european citizens have denounced, in hundreds of petitions, the difficulties and obstacles which are holding back the spread of renewable energies. they have been calling loudly for a stable, clear and transparent regulatory framework, not retroactive, to concretely promote the use, self-production and self-consumption of renewable energy. the opinion of the committee on petitions put these demands in black and white, called for an increase from 27 to 35% for the union's target for the share of renewable energy consumption by 2030 and called for the reintroduction of binding national targets, which are crucial if we want to be credible in the union's energy transition. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft budget for the financial year. but it requires more courage, more ambition, more consistency and less hypocrisy. the five star movement needs an ambitious but achievable 45% target to quickly project ourselves into the future of energy, which we want to be renewable, for the benefit of the climate, the environment, employment, and conceived as a common good and as a right for all.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there are many points which are very important to us in this energy package. one concerns the eu's anti-pollution regulations, which exist for all sectors but not for geothermal energy. in italy, for example, mercury emissions from the 34 geothermal power stations, according to the only official data available for the tuscany region, are equal to 1.5 tonnes of mercury per year. the union has banned conventional thermometers containing as little as two grams each; so it's as if around the geothermal plants in italy, in a small area, 750,000 thermometers break down every year. in the same year, 16 000 tonnes of hydrogen sulphide and 6 000 tonnes of ammonia are released into the atmosphere. these quantities are not even included in the eu's inventories of polluting emissions. in addition, some types of geothermal power plants emit more climate-altering gases over their life cycle than fossil-fuel power plants of equal capacity, but receive incentives for union climate targets. for the union, geothermal energy with a high environmental impact is as if it did not exist: i am not going to go into the details of the commission's proposals, but i will say that the commission has already made a number of proposals. we have tabled amendments (357 and 358) to the report on the renewable energy directive to the effect that the european commission should study the problem of geothermal emissions in order to assess whether or not an ad hoc legislative proposal on geothermal energy is necessary for a truly sustainable, emission-free geothermal energy.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, investing in renewables is not just about the planet, it is also about saving european industry, jobs and our growth prospects. alongside the astonishing advances in technology, the paradigm of policy has finally changed - as some of the speakers have already said - from environmentalism to economic competitiveness. renewables, which were seen as a loss-making investment years ago, are now a very real challenge for world powers such as the united states, china and japan. we in europe have a lot of technological and industrial excellence, we have one of the richest markets on the planet to absorb and develop this excellence. we just have to be careful not to throw this heritage away to pursue false neoliberal myths. the technological revolutions are made possible by massive and courageous public investment, by ambitious choices, as we in our group here in parliament want, and by careful public policies, made up of incentives and trade protections. just look at the chinese solar power exploit to see what's happening. protesting against chinese anti-dumping practices is right but not enough: we must also have a globally competitive industrial policy in europe, and to do that we must create an ecosystem which will foster a genuine industrial revolution towards this transition.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the debate we are having is very complicated because it crosses a huge number of objectives in order to find a synthesis, and the work of the political side is immense. we sometimes compare ourselves by taking technical analyses apart, and often these technical analyses document different positions even within the technical discussion. fortunately, there is a place for political synthesis, and this is that place. the work done so far is excellent and is faithful to the balance achieved within the paris agreement. we do not turn the paris agreement into a weapon of mass destruction; we are keeping the best part of these agreements, which is the attempt to ensure a fair balance between environmental and developmental considerations. there are examples, such as renewables and biofuels, where we have sinned by being overzealous: the transition from first-generation to second-generation biofuels must take account of the social reasons for sustainable development.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur, my colleague mr mato, his team and the committee on fisheries (pech) for the work done to achieve the report on our proposal for a new technical measures framework. regulating technical measures is about setting out how fishermen can go about their work at sea – what gears to use, what specifications to meet and which standards to strive for. it is therefore a key element of how our common fisheries policy operates on the ground. the current legal framework is quite old and no longer in line with the ambitious objectives of our reform policy in terms of greater sustainability, as mr mato said. i welcome parliament’s position, which embraces key elements of the commission’s proposal, including a firm rejection of reinstating the existing complex array of technical rules and support for the commission’s proposal on measures to protect sensitive species and habitats. we also welcome the pech committee’s approach on how regionalisation would work in the context of technical measures. however, i would like to take this opportunity to discuss several areas of concern. this is the third attempt to reform technical measures legislation, and our proposal was based on the concept of results—based management and accountability by the operators. this was proposed to deliver simplification and flexibility to amend technical regulations at a regional level, while retaining oversight and minimum standards by setting quantitative objectives. i have to express my disappointment in the fact that the clear and measurable eu targets included in the commission’s proposals have been deleted in the draft ep’s report. these targets would introduce accountability and be the basic measuring stick for results—based management. it is a fundamental element of the commission’s proposal, and its deletion risks emptying the proposal of much of its intended purpose. for example, the draft report introduces compromise amendments to regionalise the rules governing the use of different mesh sizes. with no eu quantitative objectives and targets, there is no way to ensure that regional rules will deliver greater sustainability and selectivity in line with the cfp goals. the deletion of eu targets therefore represents a major concern about how regionalisation may work in practice. we no longer have common objectives across union waters. we therefore run an unacceptable risk of having an uneven application of a common policy between different areas, and of having different level playing fields between our fishermen. this is of significant concern, as it undermines the core principle of the cfp. my second concern relates to the eu landing obligation. the reform of the cfp aims at gradually eliminating the wasteful practice of discards through the introduction of the landing obligation. this radical change in fisheries management aims to improve fishing behaviour through improvements in selectivity. amendment 136 essentially introduces a derogation from the landing obligation on the condition that all catches are fully documented. here i would like to point out that the obligation to fully document catches is already a legal requirement. in effect, this amendment would provide an exemption from a key element of the cfp. if this amendment is passed, it will significantly undermine the incentive for fishermen to improve selectivity. i am also aware of the discussions surrounding the issue of electro-pulse fishing, and i would like to remind you that the current technical regulations permit the use of electro-pulse fishing on a limited basis. in our proposal we have proposed to remove the five-percent limit, but to retain the geographical restrictions to the southern north sea. this is based on advice from both the scientific, technical and economic committee for fisheries (stecf) in 2012 and ices in 2016. ices, for instance, considers that the conventional way of fishing by beam trawling has a negative impact on ecosystems, while electric pulse stimulation, if properly controlled and applied, may offer a more ecologically benign alternative way of fishing by reducing unwanted by-catch, reducing seabed damage and lowering co2 emissions. there are other elements in the report that are problematic, such as amendments that weaken existing provisions – to protect sensitive habitats in the mediterranean, for example – or amendments that dilute measures to protect vulnerable deep—water sharks and other vulnerable species of marine mammals and reptiles, but the specific issues i raised earlier – that is the removal of union—wide quantitative targets and the blanket derogation from the landing obligation – would seriously undermine the commission’s original proposal and key elements of the cfp. therefore, i have to be very clear that amendments 52—60, 68 and 171 are unacceptable for the commission, as these would remove common targets. equally unacceptable are amendments 130, 131 and 136, as these would undermine the landing obligation. we therefore count on your support to ensure that the cfp delivers on its key objectives through a meaningful revision of the technical measures guiding fishing activities.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in european waters an alarming amount of fish stocks continue to be overexploited and levels of bycatch of non-target species often remain high. it is therefore clear that the current regulatory framework for technical measures has not achieved optimal results. in order to assess the effectiveness of technical measures, specific targets should be established as regards levels of unwanted catches, the level of by-catches of sensitive species and the extent of the sea bed significantly affected by fishing activities, which should be consistent with the objectives of the cfp and, in particular, should be established on a sound scientific basis. regionalization may make it possible to develop technical measures in the framework of multiannual regional plans which are better suited to the specific characteristics of the various types of fisheries. finally, i believe that electrical pulse fishing, as a form of unfair competition for small-scale fishermen and as a non-selective technique which is likely to cause enormous damage to the marine environment, should be banned at least until more economically and socially sustainable conditions are established.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing industry is not affected by the current crisis. they are currently contained in over 30 different regulations and this complexity and fragmentation is a burden on fishermen, who have been calling for radical simplification for years. i have always said that technical measures are an opportunity to put the principle of regionalization into practice, and we have tried to work on this because, unfortunately, until now regionalization has been more on paper than in the real common fisheries policy. all too often fishermen have perceived european rules as distant and administrativeally burdensome, and that is why, commissioner, we have included this solution on the regionalisation of the targets, which does not mean reducing the objectives but means making them consistent with the characteristics of the various territories. the complexity of the matter, it is true, required long negotiations in the pech committee, and today we have achieved a good result. we need to ... on behalf of the green group in the european parliament. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the number of amendments tabled here in the chamber - and there are many - shows how critical this dossier is. we hope they'll help us, that we need them to improve this file. we also understood this from the speech by commissioner vella, who made a specific, numerous list of amendments which weaken this proposal and make it somewhat ineffective, something which does not allow us to fully implement the common fisheries policy. regionalization was the time when we had to apply the true regionalization, but by telling us what regionalization is. regionalization means leaving it to the individual states and regions to choose a path, a trajectory for the application of technical measures, but aiming at common, precise, clear and numerical objectives to be set for the whole union. they have to be numerical because over time we have a need to monitor whether we are getting closer to those goals or not. this regionalisation, as it is now in the dossier, is anarchy and not regionalisation.
in writing. the reform of the common fisheries policy in 2013 introduced the technical measures as we know them today. it is appropriate and consistent with the path that has been taken that they be re-examined, on the basis of the results achieved and with particular attention to the sector as a whole. the commission should perhaps have taken account of the complexities faced by the operators who live off the fisheries industry on a daily basis and acted accordingly on the existing legislation, which has been kept virtually unchanged and thus led to regulatory confusion during the adjustment process. on the other hand, the elimination of the rigidity of the current legislation and the promotion of legislation which is more evolutionary and adapted to the territory is certainly an objective which has been desired for some time. however, this progress must be accompanied by a parallel respect for the balance between the institutions of the union, so that delegated acts do not become a tool to circumvent general rules, or the role of parliament. the multiannual plans therefore remain the most appropriate instrument for promoting the efficient development of the regionalization process we are discussing. in summary, increasing its flexibility by means of an approach tailored to the specificities of each eu sea basin will prove all the more essential as we are able to adapt the union's role to the needs of the sector.
member of the commission. – mr president, i would again like to thank the rapporteur for the general support for the proposal and for the amendments, which clarify and improve the original commission proposal. in fact, only a few amendments were not acceptable from the commission perspective. the sprfmo transposition regulation will, as has already been said by most of the members, allow a faster and more efficient implementation of new conservation measures in union law, thanks to the delegation of certain well-framed powers to the commission. this practical approach will allow the union to deliver on its international obligations vis-à-vis rfmos in a timely manner. there was one comment that i would like to comment on. mr mato mentioned the need to transpose in good time. however, we have to keep in mind that the sprfmo is a very young rfmo, and its first annual meeting was held in 2013. after this meeting, the sprfmo had envisaged a medium-term plan to adopt a comprehensive system of conservation and management measures by 2016. therefore, it was decided to delay the transposition until the new measures were adopted in order to avoid having to repeat a lengthy and complex transposition exercise twice within a limited time. the transposition is a complex and time-consuming process. it requires an article-by-article analysis of every sprfmo conservation and management measure in order to incorporate it into eu law. in most cases, the original provision does not allow for a simple replication. that means we cannot simply copy and paste the text. it is therefore necessary to adapt the provisions to the eu language specificities and actors. my thanks again to the european parliament for its opinion. we look forward to our discussions in the upcoming trilogues and to the quick adoption of this regulation.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, let me first of all thank the commissioner who is here to listen to us and to discuss with us and with all the colleagues who have contributed to this work and to produce a text which i believe represents a suitable starting point for the european commission itself. an implementation report such as the one we are discussing today is a tool at our disposal to analyse where we have come and, above all, to understand together what the best ways are of increasing and improving the tools that the union puts at the disposal of its citizens. i believe that we have succeeded in this objective and that is why i ask the commission and the commissioner to continue to work together to give a positive follow-up to the work done so far. in coming to the report, we have been able to understand how, although relatively young, macro-regional strategies have become a well-established tool and as such need to be treated, moving beyond the experimental phase, using best practices to improve governance mechanisms and, above all, to establish forms of direct funding for strategies on both the european and national sides. that is why we ask two fundamental things in this report. the first request is addressed to the member states: we are asking for specific commitments, especially in the early stages, at the very moment when the strategies are being drawn up, in terms of financial and human resources. we also ask that, with the support of the commission, incentives or facilities be provided for actions implementing the strategies. secondly, we ask the commission to use the forthcoming reforms of the financial framework and cohesion policy both to redefine and better calibrate the targets and objectives of the macro-regions, and to define in future regulations a new role, areas of intervention, also in the light of the new priorities that the union is giving itself, and forms of implementation work, to identify specific measures and projects and to define sources of certain financing to achieve them. in general, the mechanism whereby strategies must, from time to time, request funding from different programmes must be progressively overcome, in effect strengthening from the outset the direct link between the actions of the strategies themselves and the sources of eu funding. as regards the rule of the three no's (no to new structures, no to new rules and no to new financing), i think it is time to start thinking about it, that is to say, to understand how and in what way it should be abandoned, ten years after the first strategies, so that it can continue to have a meaning that we understand and not just become a hindrance. we therefore ask the commission to provide us with an analysis of the impact of the three no's on the implementation of the strategies and the implementation of the projects in the next report. finally, governance, which is probably the most sensitive point. we agree that the implementation of strategies can no longer be left to national governments alone but must be shared and implemented with the consensus and close cooperation of local, regional and, above all, civil society levels. in fact, too often - and i would like to conclude on this point - strategies sin by lack of ownership and suffer from this lack. the national level is too distant and probably too inattentive. it is therefore essential to bring the ownership of strategies closer to the citizens, giving local authorities and regions an active and decisive role in the planning and implementation phases. i think that is where we have reached a broad consensus in the report and i hope that the debate will confirm this.
i would like to thank mr cozzolino for his very precise and timely report, which contains some very interesting proposals. i think we all need to remember that the european union is very large and, moreover, cooperates with many countries around it, and the logic of macro-regional strategies is that in international competition with large countries it is useful to coordinate european strategies for large coherent areas, which have a common history, economy and culture. however, these strategies often do not work as they should. i agree with the rapporteur that the first thing - and i say this to the commissioner - is to give greater power to the regions and local authorities, because they are the ones who can bring the strategy to life. the second point is a push to really pool the funds. the third is calls for proposals specific to the individual areas, which does not mean ad hoc money but calls for proposals specific to their specificities.

abandoned. the discussion has not been concluded yet, but there is nothing that indicates a consensus emerging on a policy shift towards introducing trade sanctions. the key issue here is that sanctions are supposed to counterbalance specific trade costs, demonstrating that the trade costs of a country not respecting certain basic social and environmental standards has concrete effects on trade. with regard to civil society, it is indeed a very important ally in ensuring that labour and environmental standards are promoted. civil society is also an important partner that is able to member of the commission. – mr president, 2018 is the european year of cultural heritage. as you will remember, it was launched at the european culture forum in milan on 7 december 2017, in the presence of a vibrant crowd of 800 participants from a wide range of cultural organisations: unesco, the council of europe, the member states and the european institutions. we were joined by the estonian presidency, the committee of the regions and the european parliament. we were honoured by the presence and active participation of the european parliament’s president, mr antonio tajani, the chair of the committee on culture and education, ms petra kammevert, and ms sylvia costa, who led the european parliament’s negotiating team on the decision for the year. i would like to warmly express my thanks to all of them, including the european parliament’s rapporteur, mr mircea diaconu, for the decisive role they played in making this european year of cultural heritage happen. the european year of cultural heritage comes at a particularly decisive moment in the history of our union. it comes at a time when the european union is grappling with issues that go to the very heart of the values it stands for, and that will have a bearing on how the union will evolve. the european year of cultural heritage also comes at a time when culture is high on the european union’s agenda. in gothenburg last november, the european heads of state and government discussed the important role of education and culture in strengthening people’s sense of belonging to a cultural community. as a contribution to this debate, the commission issued a communication on strengthening european identity through education and culture, which proposed, among other things, to strengthen the european agenda for culture. in december, the european council followed up, recognising the importance of the 2018 european year of cultural heritage. indeed, the european year of cultural heritage offers us a unique opportunity. by engaging with our cultural memory, we can better understand and raise awareness of the many cultural influences on which our identities are based and we can develop our vision for the future. we can reconnect our citizens with their roots as europeans, while respecting and cherishing the values created by different communities. this is the message we want to pass on, with the motto of the year: ‘our heritage: where the past meets the future’. so, what have we done so far to put this year in motion? first, we have mobilised a wide network of civil society and heritage operators who are helping us to implement the year on the ground. we have also mobilised member states. we each have a dedicated national coordinator for the year and have national and regional programmes of activities. we have been working very closely with the european parliament, listening to you and involving you in all our stakeholder meetings. we have launched a specific call for proposals under the creative europe programme, to fund transnational cooperation projects in the field of cultural heritage. we have developed synergies with existing initiatives in the field of cultural heritage, in particular the european heritage days, the eu prize for cultural heritage and the european heritage label. all these are fully involved in the european year, and we have established a committee of stakeholders involving 35 heritage, cultural and youth networks, selected through the voices of a structured dialogue framework on culture. furthermore, commission departments have joined forces to top up the year’s dedicated budget with additional projects funded through regular funds. in the case of research, for example, this has led to over eur 100 million of investment in cultural heritage. finally, we have launched a communication campaign to give high visibility to our actions. the website is up and running in 24 languages, in addition to a video, leaflets, a very active social media strategy and a newsletter which goes to 4 000 stakeholders. but the year has only just started. a wide array of activities and events lie ahead. we are now putting the final touches to ten major initiatives at european level, organised around four pillars: engagement, protection, sustainability and innovation. we have an ambitious programme, comprising over 100 european-level events and around 2 000 national and regional events during the year. these are designed to resonate far beyond the year itself. it is only in the light of its long-term impact that we will be able to judge the year’s success. a successful year will help us to better protect and manage tangible and intangible testimonies from our past and ensure that our fellow europeans become increasingly aware of the value of cultural heritage for our identity and for our future. i know the commission can count on this house’s support and active participation to turn this vision into reality. cultural heritage makes us europeans. our heritage makes europe meaningful, so i believe that this is a project we all endorse and uphold, because in these difficult times, in this existential moment for europe, culture is one of the pillars of our existence.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, there are now more than 5 500 regulated professions in europe, to which must be added many other professions which are not regulated. this varies widely from country to country ranging from the 76 regulated professions in lithuania to the 543 in hungary and covering 22% of the european workforce. with the report we are putting before you today for debate and vote in this house, parliament intends to respond to the european commission's communication on recommendations for reform of professional services. this initiative is to be welcomed as it has the merit of providing an overall assessment of the state of implementation of this directive and an overview of the rules that apply in the different member states to architects, civil engineers, accountants, lawyers, industrial property consultants, real estate agents and tourist guides. the communication first of all stresses the need to implement the provisions of the directive fully. the need for greater mobility and competition in the professions is clear, and the commission document undeniably shows that there is considerable room for manoeuvre in the legislation of the member states. i also believe that any assessment of the effectiveness and proportionality of national legislation must be made taking into account not only economic and quantitative factors, as is too often the case and as can be seen from reading the documents of the european commission. the direct link identified between reforms and economic growth, between deregulation and job creation, cannot and must not be the sole guiding light for policy makers. it is important to stress that the quality of professional services is one of the key factors in preserving our social and economic model and in ensuring the competitiveness of our economy. this is why we need to promote rules that support young people's access to employment, growth and innovation, while at the same time protecting the quality of services provided, public interest objectives and consumers. in order to assess the regulation of professions, therefore, a combination of economic considerations and political assessments is necessary in order to defend general public objectives, while respecting the non-discrimination and proportionality provided for in the treaties. to preserve a high quality of professional services, however, we need not only an effective and proportionate regulatory framework at the level of the european union but also active policies to support the professions, especially in relation to the challenges posed by globalisation and digitalisation. the freelancer must be considered in two dimensions: the first is that of a professional in the strict sense and the second is that of a small entrepreneur. this requires lifelong training, services to promote greater intra-european mobility and a greater propensity for internationalisation, a reduction in bureaucratic burdens and easier access to finance. in particular, strong attention should be paid to the impact of digitalisation on professional services. on the one hand, the opportunities can certainly be highlighted, but on the other hand, the implications in terms of employment and the quality of the services provided will have to be carefully assessed. ladies and gentlemen, europe's competitiveness and the preservation of our social, economic and cultural model also require the protection of the quality of professional services for the benefit of citizens, businesses and authorities.
member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank the members for this interesting debate. it is clear that we share the common aim of creating an effective legal environment so that we can ensure high—quality professional services. the mutual evaluation exercise was an important first step, but it also showed that much work remains to be done. analytical tools like the restrictiveness indicator can support us in this effort by pointing out possible instances of inadequate regulation or over-regulation. it is then for the member states to examine the justification for these restrictions and to check whether there are alternative, less harmful measures. the proposed proportionality test will also be a key instrument for preventing the adoption of disproportionate professional rules. the commission thanks the house once again for your support for its policy initiative and looks forward to working with you to create competitive and high-quality professional services.
the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in closing this debate, let me thank all the shadow rapporteurs for their cooperation and all those who took part in the debate this morning. in conclusion, i would like to stress one word: the balance between the two has been underlined by several interventions. we are dealing with a market which has very often been perhaps the most closed of all european markets, sometimes not only at national but also at local level. the professional has often been identified as one who operates on the ground, on a local basis, and we need - and this is what the european directives call for, and the work we are doing we reaffirm in this report - to expand the intra-european mobility of professions, to give more opportunities for inter-european mobility to young people, to improve the quality of services, to increase supply within the eu and competition. but at the same time we also need to ensure that national regulations guarantee proportionality, are proportionate in terms of access to these professions, protect citizens, protect public authorities and protect consumers. however, i would like to stress one point at this final stage. i believe, madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, that the competition will not be between european professionals. the digital market is opening up our market to the world: now that you can find online platforms offering professional services from anywhere in the world, the barriers have been broken down. and so i think that the qualifying point we want to work on and which we have included in this report is that we need stronger, more capable professionals, more able to be on the international market, and this is done through training, through digitisation, through collaboration between the national professional system and within a european system. this is what we're looking at. the challenge is difficult, it is a challenge we will continue to work on, and i believe that with the cooperation of the commission and the adoption of the next directive on the proportionality test, we will have the elements to ensure that european professionals have the characteristics and the capacity to compete in the global world.

in writing. geoblocking is a discriminatory commercial practice used to artificially segregate markets in order to maximise profits. in other words, what happens in practice is that online sellers either prevent consumers from accessing a website because their ip address points to a specific geographical location, or they redirect them to a local online sales site that offers different prices. in this context, and with a view to the completion of the digital single market, geoblocking practices should be prohibited, especially in those sectors such as audiovisual where such a practice is obvious and unjustifiable in the eyes of the ordinary citizen. the regulation in question is therefore a relevant piece of legislation, but its effectiveness has been drastically reduced by the exclusion of audiovisual content, streaming music, video games and e-books from its scope. who are you? certainly not to the citizens of europe who will continue to suffer from the practice of geographical blocking, with a negative impact both on the circulation of content and on the promotion and safeguarding of cultural diversity. the economic interests of a few have, once again, prevailed over the interests of the collective.

the first item on the agenda is the early termination of the office of a vice-president of the european parliament. please be careful. we shall now vote on the proposal from the conference of presidents concerning the removal from office of a vice-president of the european parliament, mr ryszard czarnecki. in accordance with rule 21 of the rules of procedure, in order to be adopted, the proposal must be approved by a two-thirds majority of the votes cast, in favour and against, representing the majority of members of parliament, i.e. 376. in accordance with rule 178 (3), only the votes cast for and against the proposal shall be taken into account for the purpose of obtaining the necessary two-thirds majority. please note that the total displayed at the top of the screen will include abstentions, but only those marked with a "+" and a "-" will be counted. in accordance with rule 180a (2), the political groups which reached the high threshold requested that the vote be held by secret ballot. we can now move on to the vote.
as regards the interpretation of the rules of procedure, since this is the first time that a vote has been taken under rule 21, account must be taken of the general interpretation of the vote in all matters similar to this. abstentions shall not count in the election of the president, the vice-presidents and the quaestors. as regards the approval of the rejection of any text, and therefore of any proposal, only the votes cast in favour and against are counted, says article 178, except in cases where the treaties provide for a specific majority. there is no provision in the treaty for this, and i therefore intend to give a broad interpretation of article 178 and all the other rules which have always governed the election of persons. so, since this is the revocation of an election, i intend to interpret the regulation in this way. so i confirm that the votes counted will be those for and those against.

informal committee of permanent representatives (coreper) meeting. since then, discussions took place in the relevant working party and five successive presidencies conducted intensive technical work on this file. in november 2016 and december 2017, coreper was involved and held an in—depth discussion on these very sensitive issues. after these two meetings the presidencies met with the two co—rapporteurs in order to give them a comprehensive overview and a clear state of play of the discussions. the first meeting took place in january 2017 and the last one in december 2017. minister the necessary domestic measures in time for the 2019 elections. to sum up: despite these difficulties, we are determined to continue the hard work on this important file in the council. we are also happy to continue working closely with the european parliament in a very constructive spirit to try to overcome the difficulties and seek solutions that are acceptable to all.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, honourable members, madam commissioner, you have invited the presidency to intervene in this debate. first, let me say that common values such as democracy, equality, the rule of law and human rights are the cornerstone of the european union. each member state must therefore respect, protect and promote them. let me assure you that the rule of law and the separation of powers have always been at the heart of the council’s attention. we believe that dialogue and cooperation are necessary to ensure the best standards and conditions for our citizens in all our member states. the council addressed the situation in romania in its conclusions on the cooperation and verification mechanism adopted on 12 december 2017. the council welcomed the fact that romania has taken a number of positive steps and encouraged the country to renew momentum on the reforms, in particular those related to the independence of the judiciary and to the fight against corruption at all levels. the council reiterated the importance for romania to focus on further consolidating progress and to fully address the concerns and all the recommendations set out by the commission in its report on progress achieved under the cooperation and verification mechanism. we hope that the ongoing communication between the romanian authorities and the commission will continue to prove efficient in assisting romania to remedy some shortcomings.
member of the commission. – mr president, the discussion in romania over the last year about its justice laws has led to concerns being expressed by a wide range of stakeholders, both inside and outside the country, across the eu and beyond. romanian citizens have taken to the streets to state their opposition to the proposed changes to romanian law. they are concerned that this may undermine the long—standing efforts in the fight against corruption and the independence of the judiciary. the commission has made no secret of the fact that it shares these concerns. so too does the council of europe’s anti—corruption watchdog, the group of states against corruption, which for the first time has decided to launch its own inquiry – with a report due in march. the independence of the romanian judiciary and its capacity to fight corruption are directly relevant to the progress made under the cooperation and verification mechanism, which, as you know, was set up in 2007 to assist romania and bulgaria in the fields of judicial reform and corruption and (for bulgaria) the fight against organised crime. after ten years of continued efforts, romania has one of the best judiciaries in the region. back in january 2017, the commission proposed a limited set of remaining recommendations which, if implemented fully and provided that there is no backtracking, would bring romania out of the cooperation and verification mechanism. one of the recommendations called on the romanian leadership to ensure a consensual legislative process, to finalise reforms of the justice laws and the criminal codes, and also to respect judicial independence and court decisions. on 15 november 2017, in our latest cooperation and verification mechanism report, the commission voiced concerns on the process and the content of the draft justice laws. as the debate on justice laws was evolving in the course of 2017, the superior council of the magistracy – the constitutional guarantor of the independence of the judiciary – continued to voice concerns and issued a negative opinion citing detrimental impacts on judicial independence and on the effective functioning of the judicial system. these concerns need to be taken seriously in the legislative process. therefore the question we put to the romanian authorities in the november report remains valid, namely whether the process would take into account the legitimate interests of the judiciary and respect judicial independence. unfortunately, we have continued to see open criticism of the judiciary and defiance of judicial decisions or integrity rules, which do not inspire a feeling of confidence in the process. events since have done nothing to address these concerns. on 21 december 2017, the parliament adopted amendments to the justice laws in a fast—track procedure and the laws were immediately challenged in the constitutional court through three referrals. the constitutional court proceedings are ongoing but, in its first hearings, it declared the unconstitutionality of some of the provisions. these are issues to be looked at carefully in relation to judicial independence and on which there are european standards. the council of europe’s principle is that you cannot reform the judicial system against the judiciary. this common sense advice underpins the commission’s recommendation to the romanian authorities that they consult the venice commission before the justice laws are promulgated. the commission considers that it is still possible for the justice laws to be improved and become good laws which will strengthen the independence and professionalisation of the romanian judicial system to serve all romanian citizens. this is a crucial moment, given that the first two draft laws are back in the romanian parliament following the rulings of the constitutional court. the debate on how to address the concerns expressed by the constitutional court should be used as an opportunity to have a good, frank dialogue and build a better shared understanding and trust among all parties concerned. therefore, i reiterate the call made by president juncker and first vice—president timmermans to the romanian parliament to rethink the course of actions proposed, to open up debate in line with the commission’s recommendations, to build consensus on the way forward, to safeguard the independence of the judicial system and further step up the fight against corruption. the president of romania also has a key role in the process and, from his meeting with the college last week, i know he takes that very seriously. the commission stands ready to continue its ongoing dialogue with the romanian authorities and will contribute as best it can to help ensure that this process is taken forward constructively and in a way that builds trust. we will look thoroughly at the final amendments to the justice law, the criminal codes and laws on conflicts of interest and corruption. as always, when dealing with these and similar matters, the commission will remain objective, facts—based and law—based, politically colour—blind and clinical in our approach. romania and romanians have been running a marathon. the finish line is in sight. to step backwards now would be a major disappointment to romania’s many friends, but most of all to romanian citizens. the speed with which romania will reach the finish line is up to romania, but the commission stands by to help romania get there.

madam president, it is sad that nowadays we are still witnessing not just slavery but its most heinous and awful form, child slavery. in haiti poor parents from rural areas send their children away under the illusion that they will be educated and well kept and will have brighter opportunities in life. restaveks are, in fact, exploited physically and verbally abused, whipped, humiliated and sometimes sexually exploited. moreover, children live in precarious conditions of health and nourishment. often prevented from going to school, they are forced to work 18—20 hours per day. every time a restavek implores to be sent back home, he or she is likely to receive a beating in return. at the end of this nightmare these undefended children will end up on the street. the two major factors that perpetuate the restavek system are widespread poverty and a social acceptance of the practice. therefore, i wish to invite the european union and the member states to increase their financial support to the haitian government on condition that it complies with the obligation to respect the united nations convention on the rights of the child.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in the disturbing panorama of human rights violations there is a specific category, which is perhaps the most insidious and disturbing of all, and i am referring to violations affecting the lives of children. they are certainly the worst of all, for they have a devastating impact on the person the child will become, thus condemning not only his present but also his future and thus the future of the entire country in which they occur. in haiti, the term restavek is used to describe the condition of a child who is born into a poor family and is literally sold to a different family, often in the city. this condition, which affects as many as 40,000 haitian children, is becoming a form of modern slavery. 95% of these child slaves are subjected to physical and psychological abuse and 25% of girls are sexually abused before the age of 18, all in the corrupt silence of the ruling class. we must put an end to this abhorrent practice. the haitian authorities must ratify and respect the un convention on the rights of the child and the european union must provide maximum support to the very poor caribbean island, supporting the fight against poverty and for literacy. a society's moral sense is measured by what it does for its children.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report by mrs gardiazabal rubial on the annual report of the european investment bank has the merit of being comprehensive. i agree in principle with the eib's potential to improve the economic situation within the european union, and i am referring to the soft loans it provides to small and mediumsized enterprises, to its potential in our neighbourhood. i have already pointed out in the committee on regional development the problems of the eib's high-risk operations, the so-called special operations. in essence, part of our budget guarantees, by means of financial engineering, the eib's riskiest operations, protecting private investors. once again, privatization of profits and publicity of losses in the midst of the crisis. i recognize that great importance is attached to mechanisms to avoid financing to companies that commit tax fraud, but i would have liked the report to address more boldly the lack of transparency regarding access to data on projects financed by the eib. finally, we tabled a number of amendments condemning the involvement of the eib in the financing of large infrastructure projects with a high environmental impact, such as tap. i would like to stress here, mr president, that our position is based on the same principles that the eib is proud of, but which it then denies. the tap project is not only in breach of the precautionary principle, which everyone in this house seems to share only in words, but above all of the bank's aspirations, which i would remind you are to be socially and environmentally responsible investments. i do not see the creation of another monstrous building with disastrous environmental and social impacts as a choice, let alone a responsible investment. for this reason, we voted to abstain.

author. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european investment bank is allocating 1.5 billion for the trans adriatic pipeline, or tap. a useless, harmful project that goes against the principles, the standards that the european union professes. the european union itself, even through the structural funds, has financed this work. the citizens have been denouncing this for years, but europe has been blind to it. europe is not only blind, it is complicit. it is complicit in a fraud against the citizens, because tap costs tens of billions and is of no use to the european union, it is of no use to italy. building tap is not going to help the economy, get out of the crisis. tap has a useful life of at least 30 years and, given the energy transition underway, will we still need this much gas in 10 or 20 years? the data says no, it tells us that the pipeline is to emancipating the european union and italy from supplies from other countries, some of them high-risk countries like libya. it is a pity that the tap, which will land in puglia, will also pass through countries that could give some concern: the eu has already made progress in this area. as regards azerbaijan, have we forgotten the investigation into what happened at the council of europe with the buying and selling of votes to stop the motion of condemnation of azerbaijan, which would have prevented eib financing? remember the accident in austria? the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. we want clear answers from the european union on this too. tap also violates citizens' rights and the rule of law. the tap shipyard in melendugno is a wild west, where the law of the strongest prevails, to the detriment of the rights of citizens and public authorities. even the city police had to wait almost an hour before they could enter the construction site, where they only wanted to verify the regularity and legitimacy of the work in progress. we are facing the militarization of san foca. peaceful protests by citizens and neighbouring municipalities were silenced by the police. in conclusion, we ask brussels to carry out an assessment study on the environmental, economic and social consequences of the gas pipeline, to give its opinion on the protests of the inhabitants of melendugno and the municipalities concerned, because the rule of law must be respected, because in the european union we want, the law of multinationals cannot apply at the expense of the rights of citizens, because our sea must be respected, because tap must be stopped.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, on behalf of the commission i’d like to express my appreciation to the members of parliament who have worked hard in recent months to examine and to improve the commission proposal on the alignment of the spirit drinks regulation. in particular i wish to thank ms ayuso, as rapporteur, and the shadow rapporteurs for their work. the current regulation (ec) no 110/2008 was the last cap regulation still left to be aligned to the lisbon treaty. the spirit drinks sector is strategic for eu geographical indications (gis) and is a top gi export category. it brings a significant value added to the eu agricultural sector. given its importance and successful application, the commission proposal did not seek to change the rules but merely to improve the legislative text and to simplify current lengthy and burdensome gi procedures in the spirit of simplification. the commission notes that most of the amendments voted by the committee on environment, public health and food safety committee last month go in this direction and provide real improvements to the text. however we do regret the position of the environment committee in favour of withdrawing many of the empowerments that in the past years have allowed the commission to maintain the current regulation in line with the actual needs of the market. in its proposal, the commission has used these empowerments only when necessary to supplement provisions of the basic act and adopt uniform rules for implementation that are currently dealt with by means of commission regulations or that may need to be tackled in the future. the commission has divided those empowerments into delegated and implementing acts. there is little margin of manoeuvre for the definition of these empowerments so therefore the commission considers to have proposed an appropriate balance in compliance with the requirements of the treaty. i would point out that the empowerments currently provided for in the regulation that i’ve mentioned are wider than the empowerments proposed for the alignment, as those did not need to be framed by specific conditions for their implementation as is the case under the lisbon treaty. in particular, we need to maintain a sufficiently flexible framework to allow changes in spirit drink categories. if the structure is too rigid we will not be able to respond to the needs of the sector as the commission has done by amending the regulation annually since 2012, always upon request of member states and always with the support of the sector. furthermore, amendments to definitions and categories are already subject to the scrutiny of the parliament and the council. the commission can amend them under the regulatory procedure with scrutiny which, however, no longer exists under the lisbon treaty. turning to the proposal to introduce the possibility of using ethyl alcohol from beer in the production of spirit drinks, the commission acknowledges the issues at stake. nonetheless, we would prefer not to open the door to the use of ethyl alcohol not obtained from agricultural products that are listed in annex 1 to the treaty, as is currently the case. in fact, we considered that spirit drinks, and alcoholic beverages in general, should continue to be produced on the basis of high-quality agricultural products to preserve their reputation worldwide. using a by-product of beer production to produce other alcoholic beverages may undermine the prestige of those products. as regards the chapter on geographical indications, we would prefer to maintain the current definition of spirit gi, which is in line with the trips agreement – meaning that geographical indications are all indications identifying spirit drinks linked to a geographical area, and not only the indications which are already registered. in addition we hope to conclude the validation of the established gi before the adoption of the new regulation. however, we should be allowed to continue that process in the new legal framework in cases where such an examination has not being concluded. therefore we need to maintain a legal basis for that purpose. we remain confident that these and other issues will be resolved smoothly during the forthcoming trilogue negotiations, given the collaborative spirit of all concerned in these institutions and in the common objective of reaching the most balanced and satisfactory result which allows for a modern framework for the growth of the spirit sector.
the commission has already submitted a proposal for a regulation to the council on the basis of the opinion of the committee on international trade. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the spirits sector, with €10 billion in 2016, represents 8% of european agri-food exports. the measure is therefore of particular importance not only for the internal market but also for international trade in these products. the commission's contribution focused on three points. the first is the new electronic register, which will be transparent and accessible and will be open to the registration of quality products from countries with which we have agreements. the second concerns the reintroduction on the label of the additional translation of the protected original names, which is essential to facilitate the recognition of these products in third countries. the third and final point is the strengthening of the protection of geographical indications against counterfeiting and abuse. the regulation provides for the first time for the interception and blocking of products which fraudulently use geographical indications and which transit through the territory of the union to reach third countries.

mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would like to speak briefly about the question of the mixing of alcohol from beer into spirits. of course, the ethanol that comes from the processing of nonalcoholic beer is also ethanol. just like you can make ethanol from the by-products of winemaking, from sugar beets, from corn and many other things. that's not the point. the point is that decades ago the by-products of winemaking were given this small competitive advantage, that these products can be mixed into spirits, whereas the by-product of beer-making, which has only appeared in recent years - since we have it in non-alcoholic beer - is a waste product and does not have this advantage. i think we should think very carefully about whether, without knowing what quantities we are talking about here and what we are going to get, we should just throw this waste product overboard, whether we should give this extra refinement and allow it to be mixed with spirits. i shall in any case vote tomorrow in favour of maintaining the status quo, which means that the distillation of by-products of wine production will continue to be preferred in the production of spirits.

much the collective feministe nove, whose manifesto commits me to trying to make a difference in this institution too, and the global feminist movement non una di meno, which also took to the streets on 8 march, for the strength it gives to each and every one of us, including me. when this parliament began, a report we commissioned from the committee on international trade called the eu's trade policy 'gender-blind' and gave us some guidance on how to make it 'gender-sensitive'. in the report i was rapporteur for in 2016 report on social and environmental standards, human rights and corporate responsibility and their impact on international trade policies we were already trying to call for a reversal of the union's trade policy, a reversal that made human rights clauses binding, and not subordinate to those clauses that instead protect profit and investors' rights. in that report we called for human, social and environmental rights to be defined not simply as non-tariff barriers but as central elements to be safeguarded in trade policy too. in this report we are dealing with those fundamental human rights which are the rights of women. gender equality is a universal objective enshrined in international instruments and also in the fundamental treaties of the european union, which should commit itself to promoting and ensuring gender equality in its political the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank you for your support and for the support you have shown me in the preparation of this report on the less developed regions of the european union. a report highlighting the serious impact of the economic and financial crisis which has seriously damaged the growth of these regions: the commission has already proposed a number of measures to combat fraud. the report is the continuation of a crucial initiative, launched in 2015 by commissioner crețu, which aims to bring about a better understanding of the complexity of the challenges faced by these regions, characterised by internal structural weaknesses that make them, or at least should make them, the biggest beneficiaries of cohesion policy. the path we have taken has been difficult, as the positions of the various political groups differed widely, but i think we have nevertheless managed to reach an excellent result, even if we have sacrificed some steps in the negotiations, in order to take account of everyone's interests, of course. we are starting from the awareness that the macroeconomic framework has a significant impact on regional growth and that the imbalances of the current crisis risk not only weakening the economies but also undermining the spirit of solidarity which characterizes the european context and the very principle of cohesion policy, which would thus see its efforts, especially in these regions, minimised. we have tried to bring to the commission's attention a number of good practices aimed at encouraging and increasing growth in these regions, especially as regards the specific character of the territory. this is, in my view, part of the vindication of our political role and foreshadows solutions other than those identified by the commission. if we are to be useful, then, we must overcome the ideological barriers that sometimes trap us, and that is why the report outlines three points to achieve this balance, a balance that is likely to be compromised otherwise between politics and economics, between cohesion and economic governance. the real problem we have tried to solve is the definition of the relationship between cohesion policy and european economic policy, the principle of macroeconomic conditionality which supports internal and external symmetries between various regions, and which should be reformed in a positive and constructive way to encourage and stimulate reforms, with the specific aim of investing in those territories which present the greatest structural difficulties. we are discussing the relationship between cohesion policy and the european semester, which should provide country-specific recommendations as a stimulus to growth and not, on the contrary, in the form of a constraint. we must continue to stress and emphasize the importance of cohesion policy, which is an essential tool for correcting competitive imbalances and which should continue to provide ambitious funding for these regions, as a priority for the european union. the member states must play a key role in this respect, including by adopting national strategies designed specifically for the growth of these regions, which are suffering from serious structural deficiencies. as the report states, there is therefore a need to continue investing in infrastructure and education, and to expand and improve relations between business and education. conditionalities should focus on respecting the fundamental values of coexistence and solidarity rather than on the respect of macroeconomic parameters. this is essential if we are to create real european added value for citizens through actions aimed at strengthening economic, social and territorial cohesion, which must always be our objective. in thanking you, and even before the vote in plenary, i look forward to your comments.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the macroeconomic imbalances caused by the crisis risk undermining decades of efforts to implement cohesion policy, particularly in regions with low growth and where worrying levels of public and private debt are impeding development. in the difficult relationship between cohesion policy and european economic policy, it is necessary that macroeconomic conditionality, which should bind cohesion funds to compliance with european economic governance rules, be dealt with exclusively in a positive light, in order to encourage and stimulate reforms, with the aim of investing in territories with greater structural difficulties. the need for the member states to play a key role in improving the use of cohesion policy instruments is becoming increasingly evident. this is done by adopting, in conjunction with the commission, national strategies for the growth of lagging regions, which are suffering from serious structural deficiencies, by investing heavily in infrastructure, but also in education, and by exploiting the potential of traditional activities which help to define territorial identity.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the report on the so-called backward regions contains several positive points, but also some criticisms. it is positive that the need for a truly solidarity-based approach to the migration challenge is highlighted, without which the contribution of cohesion funds, which should not be allocated to immigration in themselves, will not be effective. it is positive to underline the extremely negative effects of the economic crisis and the related cuts imposed by the stability pact, as well as the proposal to assess the impact on public investment of the exclusion of national and regional co-financing of the structural funds from the deficit calculation. but we cannot agree to a too timid approach to structural reforms, which is different from the initial draft. it cannot be said that reforms can help member states and regions to achieve better results if the commission does not first clarify their purpose and definition. because of the opposition of the majority of other groups, there is no mention of the danger of the commission's proposal to use the performance reserve of 21 billion to allocate these resources to privatisations or to measures to precariousise the labour market.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the growing opportunities for connectivity and the dissemination of information, the increasing use of digital products and services and the internet of things are having a positive impact on every aspect of our daily lives. on the other hand, they also expose public services to new risks and increase their vulnerability, because they are able to cross borders and frontiers. the theft of sensitive data, the increasing number of cases of payment fraud, the dissemination of illegal content and the large-scale cyber attacks that have filled the headlines show that our societies are still not sufficiently equipped to defend against these risks. the nis directive was the first measure on cybersecurity, with the aim of ensuring the resilience of strategic infrastructures and increasing their coordination in preventing and responding to cyber threats: the commission has already taken a step forward, and we can already see the benefits, but it cannot meet the challenges because of the reluctance of the member states. one year after the adoption of the network security directive, we have another opportunity in these months to strengthen the cybersecurity system, and to do so in a coordinated way through a new european act that we are working on, which will have to achieve two ambitious objectives. the first is to strengthen the european union's cybersecurity agency, enisa, with more resources and operational powers. the second: the creation of a new pan-european certification system to ensure the security of digital products and services, thus increasing the trust of consumers who use connected goods and services every day. only investing in resources and expertise in this area will ensure that the digital single market is able to deliver a more secure and reliable system for citizens and businesses.
in writing. there are many reasons for social alarm that can be fuelled by cybercrime. some of these issues have been raised in the various speeches by the rapporteurs during this debate, and all require attention and concrete action, starting with the implementation of the directive on measures for a high common level of security of network and information systems in the union. on the other hand, as already pointed out in this parliament's resolution on the fight against corruption and as a follow-up to the crim resolution, cybercrime is a frequently used means of money laundering and counterfeiting. this form of crime therefore constitutes a significant source of income for many criminal groups and, for these reasons too, union legislation and cooperation between member states and with union agencies in this area needs to be strengthened. we cannot ignore the fact that, through the fraudulent use of the internet for illegal purposes, such as the promotion of drug trafficking or human trafficking, criminal organizations have succeeded in greatly expanding the volume of their illicit trafficking, also endangering the security of citizens.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, i’m happy to talk tonight about corporate social responsibility. it’s an issue that is dear to my heart personally and to this commission especially, and i know that many european citizens that you represent also attach great importance to this. i’m happy to update you where we stand on this. the european union, including the member states, have a great track record on corporate social responsibility. i would say that it’s one of the best track records in the world. we have led, our member states have led and a very large number of our businesses have led, including our small and medium-sized enterprises. and this is not only about ethics and respect for others and the environment, it is about long-term sustainable growth and profits for business: shareholder value. the commission has recognised from the start that the eu has a valuable role to play here. we can facilitate the implementation of csr principles, bringing together companies from across different industries and individual sectors to find common solutions. we can incentivise it, including by setting benchmarks and other requirements, and we can also, if necessary, legislate. in 2011 we issued a communication setting out a range of actions. among others, these actions have aimed to enhance the visibility of csr and disseminate good practices; improve company disclosure of social and environmental information; further integrate csr into education, training and research; emphasise the importance of national and sub-national csr policies; and better align european and global approaches to corporate social responsibilities. we have adopted policies right across our work, from development to agriculture, to labour rights, to justice. a major step forward was the 2015 directive on non-financial disclosure. this allows shareholders to have proper disclosure and put pressure on companies to change practices if necessary, and i would say that our work has delivered results. in 2014 we carried out a major consultation on csr. it showed that over two thirds of the respondents were happy with what we have delivered, and that is not just only public sector engagement. of course there’s always more to be done, and that’s why during this mandate the work has continued. we have continued to mainstream csr across our policies. in the last year we adopted a revised shareholders’ right directive. we have been giving effect to our new public procurement legislation, paying attention to social and environmental elements, and we are working to finalise guidelines on socially-responsible public procurement. and of course, we adopted here the conflict minerals regulation – we will discuss that tomorrow; i’ll be happy to give you an update then – to ensure responsible trade in four minerals: tin tantalum, tungsten and gold. and only last week we adopt an action plan on sustainable finance. on the basis of the recommendations set out by the high-level expert group on the subject, the commission is setting out a roadmap to boost the role of finance in achieving well-performing economy that delivers on environmental and social goals. that is just the tip of the iceberg of what we have been doing. we are continuing to engage with business and stakeholders. whilst public authorities, of course, have a role to play, the final responsibility must always be with the businesses themselves. csr must be in their dna. and we are continuing to engage internationally, both through multilateral fora such as the un and oecd, and of course bilaterally. we have been developing a good dialogue with japan, for instance, on these issues, and i expect us to develop more such dialogues, because we want other countries to come up to our levels. it has been increasingly clear that there is no dividing line between csr and our wider work on implementing the united nations sustainable development goals. if you act against companies using timber that has been illegally logged, that is an issue both of the csr and the sdgs. if you act against the import of materials produced in sweatshop conditions in a third country, that is an issue of corporate social responsibility and sustainable development goals, and it’s true of our work on business and human rights as well. so under this commission, we are taking a holistic and integrated approach. we are putting our work at the heart of our implementation of the sdgs. whether you label them csr or sdg doesn’t really matter; the matter is of course that you take the most effective and proportionate action to address a situation. that can be through legislation, but it can also be through promoting industry-led standards. under our 2016 communication on sdgs we have set up a multi-stakeholder platform, made up of stakeholders from business, trade unions, ngos and others, and i expect that within this platform there will be a working group on csr. that started its work in january only, and it continues to meet. it will give us valuable input and ideas how to take this work further. we have encouraged it to look at the progress we have already achieved and give us advice on what more needs to be done. so we are looking very much forward to receive the input, carrying on also our own stocktaking exercise of what has been done and what more can be done, and the result of this work will feed into the autumn communication of the sdgs. so with this, i hope i updated you on an issue i know is very important to you as well, and i’m looking forward to the discussion.
