member of the commission. – madam president, thank you for this opportunity to discuss our action plan on alternative fuels infrastructure. the commission warmly welcomes the european parliament’s initiative. as members of this house, you have already called for a high level of ambition with the adoption of the alternative fuels infrastructure directive in 2014. the commission shares this ambition. the provision of a comprehensive, easy-to-use infrastructure for alternative fuels is a key prerequisite for the transition to low-emission mobility. our first priority was to ensure that the alternative fuels infrastructure directive is properly implemented in all member states. that is why we did not hesitate to launch immediate infringement procedures against those member states not complying with the directive. with the second mobility package, of 8 november 2017, we delivered an additional policy stimulus, particularly with our action plan on alternative fuels infrastructure. by 2030 more and broader action will be needed. we need a larger part of the existing fleet to run on alternative fuels in order to meet the eu commitments under the paris climate treaty. however, we don’t think that the directive needs to be revised at this stage. the council and parliament adopted this directive four years ago as the first ever legal instrument to ensure the promotion of a new market for alternative-fuel vehicles and vessels. since then, a lot of progress has been made. yes, the completeness, coherence and ambition of the national policy frameworks vary greatly. our analysis of the implementation of the directive shows that, on average so far, the planning under the national policy frameworks which member states had to submit pursuant to the directive would not meet the level and consistency of ambition that will be needed after 2020, when more vehicles are expected to hit the roads. however, in many places the directive has acted as a catalyst and has stimulated and broadened national planning and strategies. it is therefore time for joint and concerted action, but not for reopening negotiations. so, with the action plan on alternative fuels infrastructure, we are now providing an important and very concrete stimulus. we are making available an additional eur 800 million in the form of innovative financing instruments for the rollout of infrastructure: up to eur 350 million through the connecting europe facility (cef) ‘blending’ call and up to eur 450 million through the cef debt or innovfin instruments. we can already see how the blending of grants and loans under cef blending works in practice. several consortia will now start to roll out fast-charging infrastructure on strategic highways. this is good news for europe. but there are also less developed parts of europe where continued support action is needed. here member states can benefit from substantial cohesion policy support to accelerate such investments. in the current period of the multiannual financial framework (mff) eur 70 billion has been allocated from the cohesion fund and the european regional development fund for promoting sustainable mobility and transport, including the deployment of alternative fuels infrastructure. through the action plan we are also facilitating better collaboration among authorities and market players in relation to good practice. we have already started this process in the form of alternative fuels roadshows in member states and have received a lot of positive feedback. it is fundamental to stress the need for greater efforts to introduce alternative fuels and clean vehicles. a major lack of infrastructure is no longer a valid argument against it. the basic infrastructure is starting to be put in place in many parts of the european union. consumer buy-in depends on quality of choice. it is highly relevant that more vehicle models are being introduced into the market and this is happening quickly. with the second mobility package, we have made important proposals to further support market direction, including proposals for a new co2 emission performance standard and for the revision of the clean vehicles directive. low-emission and zero-emission vehicles will be favoured by consumers if the infrastructure is not only comprehensive but also easy to use. this is not the case at the moment, particularly not across borders. with the action plan, we have now outlined an approach for further discussion with public authorities and market players about needs and approaches for addressing the interoperability of services, including payment services, in the most effective way. we are already supporting authorities on very practical issues of data collection in order to map better the location and availability of charging and filling stations for consumers in europe. let me conclude. together, all the points of action under this action plan will help to ensure that we have in place a comprehensive, easy-to-use spec on infrastructure for the recharging and refuelling of alternative-fuel vehicles by 2025.

on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, today i would like to venture a little out of the box, a little forward and a little backward. almost 80 years ago, europe was already operating a zero-emission freight transport solution powered by renewable energy. the italians in 1938 had difficulties in supplying fuel and therefore developed a trolley that transported materials thanks to modified electric trolleys (the "trolley trucks") derived from fiat. the stelvio line reached eighty kilometers in length. it was powered by hydroelectricity. it was decommissioned in 1956. today the swedish government, siemens and volvo scania have been experimenting with this solution for years. the results are excellent, technological advances have improved the reliability of the system by making it possible to transport electrical goods over long distances, otherwise difficult with electrochemical accumulation alone. the costs per kilometre are relatively low and recoverable with exercise thanks to the efficiency of electric traction. it builds on existing infrastructure, enabling seamless flexible logistics to urban centres reachable by moving off electrified lines: for short distances with energy stored in batteries during highway journeys, with on-board electric generators or with conventional endothermic engines powered by alternative fuels. it is an innovation which does not upset the employment balance of drivers and transport companies. the european parliament already expressed its support for this solution in june 2016, but vision and coordination at eu level are needed, funds to start the infrastructure. these are the great works that we would like to leave to future generations.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that rather than promoting alternative fuels, which have very limited environmental benefits, it would be more useful to move decisively towards those which actually achieve the best environmental performance, such as electricity, which is only transient from fossil fuels, biomethane, which is only transient from methane, and hydrogen from renewable sources. the development of charging infrastructure is strategic for the spread of electric vehicles. but the deployment of the charging station network must precede and not follow the spread of electric cars, otherwise citizens and businesses will not be able to use them. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted to a company in difficulty. progress is also possible through technological innovation in support of infrastructure. two trials: smart charging and vehicle-to-grid respectively allow to control the charging volume avoiding overloading of the grid during peak hours and to reverse the energy flow of the vehicle batteries, contributing to the stability of the system. that's the direction we need to go.

member of the commission. – mr president, indeed it’s a kind of coming home to participate again in a debate about structural funds and regional policy, and everything which is related to this. it’s also good to see some well—known faces again here in the plenary. i am speaking primarily representing my successor and i don’t want to intervene too much, but there is a common commission view, of course, on this issue. i would really like to emphasise – and to begin this intervention by underlining – that the applicable provisions of the common provisions regulation as adopted by the co-legislators don’t foresee an earlier performance review, or an earlier release of the performance reserve. hence, it would be necessary to amend these provisions if the performance review was to be carried out ahead of the deadlines specified in the current legislation. the commission does not intend to propose such a change in the current provisions applicable to the date of the performance assessment and the allocation of the reserve for the following reasons: first, the rate of project selection is an important indicator of progress of programmes and of their potential final achievements, but it’s not an automatic or a sufficient guarantee that the physical and financial intermediate objectives, so—called milestones, of the programmes measured by the performance framework will be achieved. moreover, the so—called selection rate is not among the indicators included in the performance frameworks and the performance reserve may be released only when and if all indicators included in the performance framework meet the milestones in line with the applicable legal provisions. secondly, in order to avoid excessive burden on member states and regions, reporting on the achievement of milestones takes place in the framework of the annual implementation reports. any anticipated performance review would require separate reporting on the achievement of the milestones to take place before that date. moreover, the performance framework and performance reserve are included in the programmes at the level of priority axes, and anticipated performance reviews may therefore result in a situation where some priority axes in one programme receive their reserve while others have still to undergo another performance review in 2019. this would therefore add complexity to the system and increase the burden on member states and regions without bringing tangible benefits. therefore, the commission doesn’t intend to use its right of initiative to propose amendments to these rules as the potential benefits are significantly outweighed by the associated disadvantages, such as administrative burden, complexity, inconsistency across member states and programmes, and unplanned changes to the indicative budgetary profile. the additional work for the legislators to process a potential amendment comes in addition to this. having said that, the commission stands ready to listen and to discuss specific ideas to improve this instrument with the european parliament.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, each member state has an efficiency reserve from the implementation of the european structural and investment funds equal to 6% of the resources allocated. some countries have already decided on more than 70% of the expenditure relating to their allocations to the regional development fund and the social fund. however, following the resolution of this parliament adopted almost a year ago on building the pillars for a cohesion policy of the european union post 2020, no further information has been received on the unlocking of the reserve. i believe that the commission must unlock this reserve by carrying out an early assessment of the effectiveness of implementation of programmes which are ahead of schedule. among the initiatives in the package for completing economic and monetary union recently presented by the commission is the proposal to amend the general regulation on the structural funds to allow member states to leave all or part of the efficiency reserve at the disposal of the commission, with a view to implementing their own structural reform plan, which europe would pay for through a simplified procedure and without the need for national co-financing. the commission has also theorised a bipartition between low-income and low-growth regions. this is a mechanism which, although apparently simple, can create misunderstandings and confusion, especially with regard to the very notion of structural reforms, which, as the commission sees it, is completely at odds with the concept of infrastructure. my position is clear, precisely because i am aware of the infrastructure backlog that continues to penalise the regions whose development is lagging behind, such as the south of italy, which i have the privilege of representing in this house, and of the difficulties that their productive fabric encounters on a daily basis. i am convinced that cohesion policy must pursue its original aim, contrary to what the commission proposes: the commission's proposal is to reduce the gap between the territories, but between all the territories, without distinguishing between 'good' and 'bad' regions, which in the minds of some people should mean different objectives for cohesion funds. we must clear the air of the misconception that european funds, which can certainly do so much, can do everything on their own. it would be an unforgivable mistake not only to accept but even to promote the idea that they can become the reserve for all the needs and emergencies that europe is facing. on the contrary, let us all work together to relaunch cohesion policy by modernising it, rediscovering its objectives and returning to the territories the only true european policy of long-term strategic investment.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let us say without any further ado: the fact that we have diverted 21 billion - about 2.4 billion for italy - from cohesion policy, and hence from economic, social and territorial cohesion, to other objectives, such as privatisation or the jobs act, is yet another slap in the face to our territories, which are in need of investment for development as never before. the five star movement, on structural reforms, is absolutely opposed to all measures that affect the welfare state, including labour market interventions, while we are open to measures relating, for example, to improving administrative capacity or to combating tax evasion. the italian elections have shown that the citizens do not want these reforms dropped from above, that they only need the multinationals to lower the rights of the citizens. we were frankly surprised by the commission's proposal to release these resources early to be used, among other things, for structural reforms. we do not understand the hurry, especially since the current rules provide that an audit will take place only in 2019. structural reforms have nothing to do with the ratios of cohesion policy. we ask the commission to listen to the requests and appeals coming from the regional and local authorities, so as not to cut cohesion funds, not to distort the objectives of these precious resources which serve the poorer regions. we will do everything, also thanks to the strength that comes from the italian citizens, to transform this europe into a land where no one - no one - will be left behind.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after almost three years of work we have reached the end of these negotiations. in 2015, when the commission reintroduced the package after initially withdrawing it, i have to admit that the premises were not the best but significant progress has been made in recent years. the circular economy has become a priority for the european union, a priority for the co-legislators, a priority for our companies, which have seen its potential early on, but above all a priority for citizens. europe has been able to show its positive side, to bring together national interests, on paper opposed, to achieve a high degree of shared purpose in the everyday lives of its citizens and the environment in which they live. that is why i cannot deny you the satisfaction we have had with the result we have been able to bring home. with this package, europe is firmly aiming at sustainable economic and social development, which can finally integrate industrial policies and environmental protection. the circular economy is not just a waste management policy, but a way of recovering raw materials and not over-exploiting our planet's already scarce resources, even by radically innovating our production system. the package we are about to adopt certainly also contains important measures on waste management, but at the same time it goes beyond these by defining rules which take into account the entire life cycle of a product and aim to change the behaviour of businesses and consumers. for the first time, member states will be obliged to follow a single and shared legislative framework. an ambitious plan with clear and unambiguous stakes. just to sum up the main new features introduced: increasing the recycling targets for municipal and packaging waste; the introduction, for the first time, of a 10% maximum landfill leakage limit; the extension of separate collection obligations to organic, textile and household hazardous waste; but i cannot help mentioning the inclusion, here for the first time in european legislation, of mandatory measures to reduce the odious phenomenon of food waste, an environmental but also ethical problem, as well as actions to combat pollution of the seas by waste. important rules have been introduced to prevent the generation of waste: this is not only because prevention is the first level of the waste hierarchy, but because prevention means making products that are repairable and reusable by design, and it means having production cycles that use resources efficiently, that reduce waste or that reuse it for new production. and finally, prevention means introducing business models that move from selling a product to sharing a service. the circular economy is therefore a total paradigm shift that we all have to confront and is a challenge for states, which are asked to set ambitious targets to facilitate the transition to a new development model. when you get a job like this done, it means there's been a lot of input. in the few seconds i have left, i should like to thank the shadow rapporteurs and their assistants in particular for the effective cooperation they have always shown, which has been the added value in bringing the result home in a relatively short time. a special thanks to dr. marco leonardi for all the precise and meticulous work on the file. a special thanks to vice-presidents timmermans and katainen, commissioner vella and dg envi, in the person of director-general crespo, for their expertise and continued support in getting to the final result. finally, mr president, i thank the maltese and bulgarian presidencies: but a special thanks goes to the estonian presidency, without whose tenacity in wanting to conclude the negotiations, we would not be here today.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would also like to thank all my colleagues, the shadow rapporteurs and, of course, the rapporteur for the excellent work they have done. i would like to say that we will vote in favour of this package, which is a revision of the existing waste directives, because we think the compromise with the council is a good one and because, for example, it increases the recycling targets for municipal waste but also for packaging waste. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment. this is very important to us. however, it should be made clear to the public that this is only municipal waste, which represents only 10% of the total. so parliament should have been more ambitious, also to set a precedent for when it comes to changing the targets on commercial waste, industrial waste, construction waste and demolition of buildings. for example, a binding target of 30% reduction in food waste by 2025 and 50% by 2050, a target for preparing for re-use absent and a target for preparing for re-use of packaging, the mandatory return of the vacuum system. the citizens want these things. above all, we felt that there should be a total ban on the incineration of all types of waste, and that the subsidies to fossil fuels, from which all types of waste are derived, should be abolished. without these measures, unfortunately, the package we are about to adopt is only a tentative improvement on a situation which, from our point of view, needs to be greatly accelerated if we really want our economy to become circular.

member of the commission. – madam president, i would like to thank all the members who have contributed to this fine and inspiring debate and for their overall support. for me, it confirms once again that creating a circular economy is one of the big challenges of our time. but it is also offers us huge opportunities, especially in the environmental, economic and social sectors. we urgently need to make more durable and recyclable products and, at the end of the cycle, use waste as a resource and channel it back into the economy. taking a sustainable path requires multiple changes, of a technological, organisational, financial, social and also educational nature. the road ahead may seem daunting but we can make the transformation happen. embracing the circular economy offers significant opportunities as it will unleash new sources of innovation, growth, employment and well-being. it is for all these reasons that the european commission and the european union at large have made the circular economy a key political priority and that we are implementing an ambitious plan with far-reaching initiatives. a central plan of action involving taking waste legislation in the european union to the next level with ambitious, legally binding landfill reduction and recycling targets for the period up to 2035 alongside targeted waste prevention measures. it is encouraging to see that over the past two decades many member states have gradually improved their waste management in line with the eu waste hierarchy. in 1995, on average 64% of our waste was still landfilled. in 2000, the average had been reduced to 55%, while the average recycling rate stood at 25%. fifteen years later, in 2015, landfilling of household waste in the eu as a whole had dropped to 25% with recycling having increased to 45%. yet, challenges and big differences between eu countries remain. we are not closing the loop yet. in 2015, twelve member states still landfilled over 50% of their household waste and six of them incinerated 40% or more. regarding the concern expressed by ms wiśniewska, i would like to clarify that poland can get a five-year derogation for recycling and landfilling targets, so maybe she can reconsider your position and vote in favour instead of abstaining. with regards to mr pedicini’s comment that we missed a crucial chance to set legally binding targets for other waste streams like food waste, marine litter, the reuse of packaging and so on, the new waste legislation foresees a large number of review clauses asking the commission to assess the feasibility to set such targets in the next years. more and bold action is still very much needed. the new waste legislation that we hope you will approve later this week, will provide fresh impetus to this area. the commission will do all it can to make the new legislation deliver on the ground. i cannot conclude without thanking the rapporteur, ms simona bonafè. i would also like to take the opportunity to thank the shadow rapporteurs as well as all the other meps for their commitment, contribution and support to this dossier. as ms engström said, we have reason to celebrate but president of the french republic. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall try to summarize the answers to all the questions that have been raised. there was a series of questions about immigration policy. i would like to say first of all that everything that happens between france and italy is not the initiative of one or the other, but in perfect coordination. i said this while stressing the perfect understanding we have between our two countries in dealing with the flow of migration and with situations - you are right to recall this - which are always extremely difficult and worrying human situations and which call for the greatest humanity but also for this coordination. i therefore welcome the exemplary relationship between france and italy, which will continue. france adopted a reform at the beginning of the year, at the initiative of parliamentarians, to allow the application of the dublin regulation, which is currently unsatisfactory - and i agree with you on this - but not applying it at all was unsustainable for a country like france which today has thousands of people whose situation allows them to be in refugee camps, even though they have received a refusal, for example, in germany. between 50 and 60% of the people who are refugees in france, especially in the paris region, are what is called - i don't like this formula, but it is often taken up - dubliners from neighbouring countries. so if we do not make the current system work, with all its imperfections, it is unsustainable, especially for a country like france. i therefore welcome the realism we have shown in this respect, which has made it possible to resume what has been done for several years and will be continued. now the question is how to reform this system, because i am not satisfied with it and i consider that it does not allow us to respond today to the migration challenge as we know it. first, by moving towards harmonisation of the rules. that is what we want to do, particularly with germany and italy. harmonizing our rules means that we can manage reception much more coordinatedly. we should take a lot of inspiration from our german neighbours in this area, in terms of the time limits and rules on asylum and the treatment of irregular situations. it is towards this coordination that we will move in the short term through the law. finally, and more generally, there is the european stage which, as i said earlier, seems to me to be the most effective. on this point, i would like to respond to many of you by advocating greater solidarity beyond the frontiers. we need to take on a european investment to protect europe's borders and not leave the burden to the countries of entry. it is a necessary reform without which we cannot support the migration we face today and will continue to face. on the other hand, we must move towards a common asylum system. i am in favour of it; that is the best answer. today we are trying to coordinate things. i am in favour of a common asylum system where all member states would adopt the same rules. finally, we must build the rules of internal solidarity and several reflections are under way on this point. we have seen all the difficulties of a relocation policy which, in an emergency, was indispensable. if we want to build the regulations and laws that will make it possible to meet this challenge in the future, i am in favour of the idea of funding solidarity policy. that's why i'm pushing with others to have an agency that can fund the communities that will be candidates to welcome and integrate refugees. we can see the difficulty of some national debates, and we can also see cities that are ready to go in this direction. simply put, european solidarity is essential to finance reception and integration policy. on this point, as you have understood, i am in favour of much greater convergence, internal and external solidarity, and having the same common rules. in the french debate, it is often underestimated that the problem we have had for decades in france is that we do not welcome everyone, that we make everyone wait, that we have some of the highest deadlines in europe for granting asylum and that, at the same time, we do not know how to accompany those who are not eligible for asylum and who will have no title. as a result, we are in a situation where everyone is not welcomed, almost no one is integrated and no one is accompanied back to their home by persons who are not entitled to a residence permit. so i am willing to defend such a system, but i can tell you one thing: it is neither fair nor efficient. therefore, i take this passage which is unsatisfactory to everyone. some say it is unfair, because we are more harsh with those who remain in irregular situations. we are tougher to be able to welcome those who will be in a regular situation, those who are entitled to asylum. then you asked me about brexit. i have a very direct answer on the position that france will take vis-à-vis the united kingdom and the post-brexit situation. i am in favour of the most integrated relationship possible, the closest, and there is a solution: we know it well, it is eu membership. it is the one which also allows good access to the single market, which allows access to freedoms and very good integration. i know that you can't promise something to your people and then want to give them the opposite. so there will be negotiations. they are led by michel barnier under a mandate from the council. i value the friendship with britain and we have bilateral relations in terms of defence and the management of common borders, but there is no cherry-picking in the single market. it's a simple principle. i believe in europe and therefore i believe in what we have done. therefore, the freedoms in europe are solidarity-based and full access requires the recognition of all these freedoms, european jurisdiction and contribution to the budget. afterwards, we know the formulas, but we must be consistent in the choices we make. that's what democracy is, too, is explaining the what if scenario to the end. there are many people who offer to take a look at your country what if scenarios, but they do not explain it the day after: the day after is necessarily the time when you have to embrace the principle of reality. i believe one thing we respect the constitutions that our peoples have chosen. like it or not, these constitutions are not being torn down and sovereignty is not being torn down, unless the people decide to do so. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the migratory flows to the european union in recent years have made us aware of the complexity of this phenomenon and the need to provide a comprehensive response in terms of international cooperation and shared responsibility. if the european management of migration flows has proved to be rather unsuccessful in this respect, the global one, which is destined to involve the entire international community in the face of the present bleak situation, is proving to be rather problematic. the united states has long since declared its withdrawal from the global compact, considering it incompatible with its government policy. the wars, political destabilisation and economic exploitation affecting geographical areas around europe, to which the actions of the us government and other western powers are no strangers, are just one of the many obstacles to an effective international compact for refugees and safe, orderly and regular migration. if we then analyse the european situation, we find ourselves confronted by those states which, by preferring walls and fences to cooperation and by demonizing and exploiting the phenomenon of migration, making it a source of intolerance, create divisions over the negotiations of the compact and obstruct the achievement of a common position. if this agreement is to provide a comprehensive response to the human movements caused by conflict, persecution, violence, poverty and the desire to seek a better place to live, as with all international agreements, the most challenging challenge will be to move from declarations of principle to facts and commitments of individual states' responsibilities.
mr president, migration is a complex phenomenon that is not going to end, no matter how many fences we build or barriers we place. i believe that building legal avenues and stepping up pledging efforts to resettle those in need is a key aspect in order to tackle the problem. i welcome the compact on migration, and i appreciate its focus on people and the safeguard of their fundamental basic rights. this is of the utmost importance and should be the driver of any action taken. a safe, orderly and regular migration offers a wide range of opportunities to migrants, their countries of origin and the countries that host them. for instance, remittance has proved to be a tool that boosts development up to three times the total of the official development aid by contributing to the economy of the country of origin. in 2017, indeed, while migration was seriously challenging the global humanitarian aid system on the one hand, on the other hand an estimated usd 450 billion were transferred in remittances to developing countries.

on behalf of the vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, the land border incidents and subsequent detention in turkey of two greek soldiers has received attention well beyond greece and turkey, including at the highest levels of the european union. at the most recent european council in march, our heads of state and government expressed their grave concern over the continued detention of eu citizens in turkey, including the two greek soldiers. the council called for a swift and positive resolution of these issues, in cooperation with member states, and the european council is considering these matters. shortly after, president juncker and president tusk discussed this issue directly and at length with turkish president erdoğan at the leaders’ meeting in varna. the detention of the two greek soldiers is a departure from the custom, usually followed by both sides, of resolving such incidents as swiftly as possible. no charges have been brought against these two soldiers and it remains unclear when the court will examine their cases. the two soldiers have been in pre-trial detention since the beginning of march. we trust that their case will swiftly be brought to trial, in line with international detention standards. yet the situation creates unbearable uncertainty for the persons involved and for their families. on the political level, it increases strains between turkey and the european union. we still have serious concerns about the recent turkish actions in the eastern mediterranean and the aegean sea. the european council condemned these actions in march, and detentions of eu citizens also create undesirable tensions with member states. turkey is a key partner for the european union, as well as a candidate country. we do have serious disagreements with the turkish government, particularly when it comes to the negative trend of the human rights situation in the country. turkey has been moving away from the european union, in particular in the areas of the rule of law and fundamental rights, and by weakening effective checks and balances in their political system. the commission has repeatedly called on turkey to reverse this negative trend as a matter of priority. and this is again our assessment in the country report on turkey that we just adopted earlier today, after the college at noon. yet, beyond our disagreements, our dialogue with turkey is more important than ever. just think about the situation in syria. we need to engage with turkey to address a difficult and tense regional situation, and turkey needs to engage with us. in this context, good neighbourly relations would be extremely important. it is in our mutual interest to refrain from actions that only make our dialogue more difficult. this is why the european union has urged turkey to avoid any source of friction with our member states, all the more so between two countries that are also neighbours and nato allies. it is in the interest of all to avoid further irritants and instead strengthen dialogue and cooperation, as well as a peaceful resolution of any dispute that may arise. this is a message we convey to our turkish interlocutors as part of our continuous dialogue. i assure you that the services of the european union will continue to follow developments closely, and we count on the european parliament to do the same, and to work together for a swift resolution of this situation, especially for the two soldiers, for their families and for the sake of dialogue in our troubled region.

madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the financial instruments for external action are a fundamental component of european foreign policy for the promotion of our values through concrete action in the world. over the years, however, parliament has repeatedly pointed out problems of inconsistency, inefficiency and duplication which limit its effectiveness while the international landscape, particularly in regions close to us, is constantly changing. in view of the forthcoming multiannual financial framework, financial commitment should not be reduced but strengthened, despite brexit and the growing reticence of some member states, while instruments should become more flexible and transparent; the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in this respect, our guiding principle must be the principle of conditionality. the resources of the european union cannot support those who back down on human rights and the rule of law. when this happens, it must become a well-established practice of our action and direct support to civil society in the country concerned, by diverting funds to it, as is happening in turkey after strong pressure from this parliament.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank my colleagues, i thank president grässle for her words about my work and the work we have done. it is certainly a good piece of work, where we highlight a number of critical points and also give a lot of suggestions to the other institutions to work better. i am sorry that i had to remove the name but, for political reasons, i cannot accept that people should deplore the choice of the citizens in a referendum which - although i myself may not agree with the outcome - was nevertheless a popular vote and therefore we should never deplore the vote of the citizens. as regards the report on the european external action service, i remain rapporteur and would like to say that the service covers important and often urgent issues: the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the report highlighted the problems of managing delegations, especially in foreign and difficult areas, and of managing buildings and procurement procedures. both are critical and we must ensure that they do not affect the budget and the proper functioning of the institutions. as regards buildings, although some progress has been made in this area in recent years, there is still a lot of room for improvement, especially in the area of rental and purchase procedures for delegations. as regards the latter's budget, it was found that more than 40% of expenditure was related to buildings: the costs are still too high. we must therefore encourage solutions such as co-location to reduce costs and ensure that the procedures for purchasing buildings are transparent and lead to real cost optimisation. the budget of delegations should also be simplified in order to improve its management and efficiency. at the same time, a higher level of transparency can be achieved and citizens can be made aware of the expenditure incurred. the commission should also be able to assess the impact of the measures on the union's financial interests, in particular on the financial stability of the union. the european external action service therefore needs to improve its control activities and ensure that procedures are in line with the required fees, even in difficult situations. sound practices are needed to avoid errors and irregularities. i remind you that human resources must remain at the forefront: work still needs to be done to prevent harassment, to promote gender balance at all levels and to safeguard whistleblowers. finally, financial support for trainees and a merit-based admission procedure for trainees. i therefore strongly urge a transparent, rational and efficient budget. the reporting must be timely and accurate, both for the expenses incurred by the delegations and for the costs of the missions of the members of the service. in this regard, i shall include in the substance of the expenditure relating to the high representative's missions: the commission has also proposed that the council should be consulted on the draft budget for the european union. so far, only the cost of missions in the first two months of 2016 have been made public. the documentation on these missions must be easily accessible, as requested by parliament itself; it is an act owed to the citizens of the union who must continue to have confidence in the institutions. i on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the state of our planet's health shows that the 'use and throw' model has incurred costs and damage that are no longer sustainable. we have long insisted on the urgency of making a radical change from product design to product manufacture, from use to recycling, from the elimination of planned obsolescence to the recovery of raw materials. the circular economy is also a key to waste, as it significantly reduces waste production, extends the life cycle of things and reduces the amount of waste that has to be landfilled. we appreciated the effort made to set more ambitious targets to keep materials in circulation for as long as possible, including through the fight against waste, the use of by-products and new business models which already include extended producer responsibility schemes and targets for reuse and recycling of municipal waste. but we would have preferred to read about the ban on incineration, which is uneconomical and environmentally damaging. yes, because our territories, such as puglia, calabria, sicily, campania, massafra and modugno, continue to suffer the consequences of the misguided policy of being more sensitive to the interests of business than to the protection of the environment and health, and of allowing the construction of new incinerators and allegedly new oxidation plants. that is why we voted in favour.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, what has happened confirms that the business model of the multinational web companies is based on the systematic collection of user data. data that has become the oil of the 21st century, used to profile consumers/users, so that we can determine their behaviour, and then passed on to third parties. what's missing, and the cambridge analytica case has exposed that, is the lack of awareness on the part of citizens. so we have to ask ourselves: how should we react? who's making the decisions for us? what role should the states and the european union play in dealing with these phenomena? it's time to end the monopolies of a few big web giants who, by exploiting our personal data and influencing our behavior, have amassed billions of dollars. perhaps it's time to start considering our personal data as a common good, to be protected, as well as other common goods such as water, land, coastline, sea. we have a great opportunity, which is the approval of the e-privacy regulation, which is still stuck in the council. i'll close with a quote from the american economist friedman, who says, "there is no such thing as a free lunch", and so what we don't pay in monetary terms we pay with our data and our lesser privacy.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the case of cambridge analytica and facebook shows that public opinion is increasingly being influenced by the profiling of citizens and the sponsorship of more or less false news on the internet, in order to favour political parties and political tendencies and to manipulate citizens in their voting. this happened in europe. cambridge analytica was involved in the british referendum, the french election campaign and the recent italian political elections, despite us, with some success for its clients. commissioner, this is no time for timid answers: it is democracy, it is our europe. i believe that it is therefore necessary to initiate, as soon as possible, legislative measures which will lead to greater responsibility for the platforms, to verification of the authenticity of accounts and to transparency of data transactions. the next european elections are just around the corner, and we are not giving free rein to those forces which, thanks to the illicit use of data, have consolidated their support. member of the commission. – madam president, as you know, in july 2016 the commission proposed stronger rules against money laundering and terrorist financing, as a swift response to the terrible terrorist attacks which happened on european soil and the financial dealings revealed by the panama papers. tomorrow you will take the final step towards the formal adoption and entry into force of revised rules, and i believe we can be proud of the revised rules, which improve substantially the existing anti-money laundering directive. i would like to thank the two co-rapporteurs, mr kariņš and ms sargentini, and all the shadow rapporteurs, as well as the chairs, mr gualtieri and mr moraes. your commitment and expertise have hugely contributed to this result. firstly, the revised rules set a new world standard on transparency of beneficial ownership. by making beneficial ownership information available to competent authorities and to the public as regards companies, it will make sure opaque structures cannot be used to facilitate money laundering. secondly, the revised directive addresses new risks of terrorist financing. it will bring virtual currency platforms into its scope and restricts the anonymous use of prepaid cards. thirdly, the directive strengthens our approach to high-risk third countries in the area of money laundering and terrorist financing. last but not least, the directive strengthens the financial intelligence units and the national supervisory authorities, as well as the cross-border cooperation between these authorities. the result of the negotiations is a very good one: it makes the european union the world leader in fighting money laundering and financing of terrorism. with the adoption of this text, we are marking an important step in fighting against financial crime. the key aspect now is swift and effective implementation in guiding and supporting the member states’ action, and during the adaptation stage the commission will start acting immediately. i assure you of the commission’s determination to see the rules fully implemented. the commission is also taking action against those member states that have yet to transpose the fourth anti-money laundering directive, in force since june 2017. effective implementation is crucial for the credibility of our preventive anti-money laundering system. finally, i would also like to add that our legislative work does not stop here. just yesterday, the commission presented a proposal on use of financial data in the fight against serious crime. the proposed directive complements the preventive measures of the anti-money laundering directive by ensuring better use of financial information for criminal investigations and a stronger link between financial intelligence units and law enforcement authorities. i look forward to working with this house also on this new proposal, which, together with the revised anti-money laundering directive, will be a key response against financial crime and financing of terrorism in europe. let me thank again the european parliament.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it has taken two and a half years, partly because of the resistance of large interest groups and the blocking positions of some member states, to reach an agreement which will establish the most satisfactory rules which should prevent the recurrence of another volkswagen scandal. a conniving type-approval system, with clear conflicts of interest between car manufacturers and national control agencies, often privately funded by them, will eventually be replaced by a more effective system of supervision and control, with powers also of the european commission. the latter will finally have an independent role as a genuine guarantee body, with the possibility of carrying out road emission tests and periodic inspections of motor vehicles already on the market. the proposal also marks a major step forward in consumer rights: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we didn't get what we wanted. however, the fact that owners of non-compliant cars are not obliged to bear the costs of repairs or recalls is a good result. the double message from the european parliament today is clear: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in order to avoid the recurrence of scandals such as dieselgate in the future, this regulation is undoubtedly a step forward. but i think there is still a lot to be done, particularly in terms of transparency and consumer protection. the possibility of carrying out independent checks on type-approved cars is still limited and european citizens cannot benefit from a uniform system of compensation throughout the union. we cannot afford to let our guard down, and this is another area where we must act to protect the health of our citizens and the environment: we need to ensure that the co2 emissions measured in the laboratory match those in the real world. the gap between laboratory and simulated emissions is currently 40%, and it will widen if we do not solve this problem with road tests. that is why, as the five star movement, we will continue to fight for the introduction of a real driving emissions verification procedure.

the agenda includes the report by paulo rangel, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the application of the treaty provisions relating to national parliaments (2016/2149(ini)) (a8-0127/2018).
member of the commission. – mr president, i am taking this point this evening on behalf of the first vice-president, mr timmermans, who unfortunately cannot be here. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr rangel, and this house for the opportunity to discuss the implementation of the treaty provisions concerning national parliaments and for the important amount of fact finding and analysis that fed the preparation of the report. national parliaments play an essential role in bringing the union closer to the people by both scrutinising the activity of their own government at european level and engaging with the european institutions. on the specific example of the european semester, the commission shares your views that national parliaments should be more closely involved in the preparation and approval of the national reform programmes and of the stability and convergence programmes. currently only a few parliaments have the possibility to vote on these programmes, but this is a matter of national institutional organisation. as for the dialogue with the commission, i would like to stress that national parliaments have not yet taken full advantage of the rights to request direct exchanges with the commission on semester-related matters. commissioners are available for discussion with national parliaments, as with the european parliament. i also agree with the report’s assessment that national parliaments of an important role to play to curb gold-plating of eu legislation by member states. the european union is often blamed for imposing rules and burdens which do not derive from eu legislation but from national legislation and, when transposing directives, national parliaments should take responsibility and explain to the people when elements are added which go beyond the requirements of eu union law. we recognise that sometimes gold-plating can be positive, for example, to improve coherence with or the performance of national law. but it is important for people to know who did what and why. the commission believes the subsidiarity and proportionality must be important and must be at the heart of the european democratic process. in line with our better regulation agenda, the commission invests great effort in ensuring that our proposals respect the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality. while the treaties provide that national parliaments ensure compliance only with the principle of subsidiarity, the commission also checks to complaints of its initiatives with the principle of proportionality in a thorough manner. so, when replying to opinions or reasoned opinions of national parliaments, we address both subsidiarity and proportionality issues as well as all other issues, political as well as technical, that are raised by the parliaments in their opinions. the fact that the yellow-card mechanism has only been triggered three times so far may be an indicator that our efforts to check the compliance of envisaged legislative proposals with both principles well before their adoption actually are working. the commission is open to discussing these issues with national parliaments on how to improve our working arrangements on the subsidiarity-control mechanism. the task force on subsidiarity, proportionality and doing less more efficiently is currently reflecting on how to improve the practical functioning of this mechanism. i would like to stress that the commission is always happy to discuss ideas from new eu initiatives from national parliaments as part of the political dialogue. in 2015 and 2016, the commission give detailed replies to so-called green cards that it had received. these were on food waste and on corporate social responsibility. given the dynamism of the political dialogue, i do not see any need for creating a formal process that could be difficult to reconcile with the current treaties’ provisions. finally, i would like to underline that the commission is always happy to contribute to inter-parliamentary events and will be open to contributing to a european week such as is envisaged in this report. once again i would like to thank the rapporteur for member of the commission. – madam president, thank you very much for this discussion, i’m very glad to be here to discuss the bologna process. this is the right moment, in light of the upcoming bologna ministerial conference in in paris on the 24th and 25th may. i hope to be able to address most of your questions in the limited time available; i will do my best. on the current state and the evolution of the bologna process, much has been achieved in the last 20 years in its three 3 major commitments. first, the three-cycle bachelor-master-doctorate system has been introduced. a common degree structure is one of the most significant achievement of the process. second, there is a common standard for independent quality assurance in higher education, yet high education institutions should benefit even more from approaches offered by quality assurance agencies placed in other european countries, not only their own. and third, the european credit system is in use in most of the countries and has helped greatly for the contribution of diplomas and study periods abroad. these three commitments are key to build the trust which is necessary for learning mobility, cross-border academic cooperation and comparability of higher education systems. based on these achievements, it is clear that the bologna process remains highly relevant, although we know that the implementation of some of the commitments is still uneven across its 48 member countries. and this is the main challenge for now. while the structures are to a large extent in place, though unevenly, we now need genuine implementation at the level of higher education institutions, which governance structures of the bologna process find difficult to reach. this is the main factor hindering affected implementation of the bologna reforms. the yerevan communiqué in 2015 therefore called on the bologna countries to propose a method to improve the implementation of key bologna reforms. the years since then have not been a period of radical change, but more of consolidation. we must use next month’s ministerial conference in paris as an opportunity to stress the need for more even implementation of the bologna commitments and to mobilise member countries and organisations to work together more closely in other words, the commission wishes to provide support to those bologna countries which lag behind in the implementation of the key commitments. in this context, the commission supports the adoption of a new structured peer support process to ensure better implementation and monitoring of the reforms. hopefully, the bologna ministers will also commit to removing the remaining obstacles in their national legislation to cross-border quality assurance. your question also addresses the issue of social inclusion, which is also extremely important in respect of refugees. not enough bologna countries have so far introduced measures to improve the conditions for under-represented and disadvantaged groups to access and to complete higher education. the first step to foster inclusion and improve equity is to collect information on the participation of under-represented groups in higher education. only systemic monitoring can provide evidence on the effectiveness of those measures. for refugees, some countries have specific recognition procedures in place. activities built on erasmus+ funded projects for national academic recognition and information centres, which will improve the consistency of decision-making. the commission has also organised several peer learning activities for member states to share experience and good practice. the next question, on our assistance to countries in their progress towards the bologna commitments: we offer support at eu level, for instance within the erasmus+ programme where we have a targeted call for this purpose. we also assist the bologna process countries that are not part of the erasmus+ programme. they benefit from capacity-building projects, which the commission wishes to intensify in the next phase of the process. they are a key feature of the bologna process. and it is in the eu interest that a less developed system can evolve. you asked how the commission monitors the recognition of the qualification. we have to admit that this is difficult to assess, as it is usually higher education institutions which take those recognition decisions. but aside from the bologna process implementation report, the commission also carries out studies to identify obstacles, areas for improvement and best practices in recognition of qualifications and study periods. for example in 2016. there was a study on obstacles to recognition of skills and qualifications. finally, in terms of giving strategic guidance to the future bologna process, the commission’s recent initiative towards the creation of the european education area is really essential. the main purpose of the european education area is to give a strong boost to learning mobility, to create a europe in which learning, studying and doing research would not be hampered by borders so as to have a continent where spending time in another member states to study, to learn and to work, has become the standard. in addition to expanding learning mobility, this ambition requires a number of concrete policy initiatives. i will mention four of them. first, the proposed networks of european universities will act as role models for the implementation of the innovation in teaching and learning, and for the efficient implementation of the bologna instruments. they will be instrumental to further develop and consolidate the european higher education area and to build synergies with the european research area. second, the planned council’s recommendation for automatic recognition of higher and upper-secondary educational qualifications and learning periods abroad will give new impetus to the implementation of one of the three key commitments of the bologna process and will further expand learning mobility. third, the new eu student card will facilitate both mobility and the recognition process. and fourth, an upcoming recommendation will help ensure that in addition to their mother tongue, young europeans speak two other languages. language knowledge is a pre-requisite for learning mobility. thanks to the european education area, we will be able to advance faster among the european union member states, then among all of the 48 bologna countries. but at the same time, it is clear that the european education area indicates the direction to follow and will give new impetus also to the bologna process. in this context, the commission fully agrees with the european parliament’s call for synergies between those three areas: the european educational area, the european research area and european higher education area. it is expected that in paris, bologna ministers will build on this new momentum.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to begin by thanking my fellow shadow rapporteurs for their joint work and for the text they produced, and the eib, the european investment bank, for making its services available to me and my colleagues. the eib is the largest public bank in the world by volume and plays an important role, as does the cont committee, in promptly highlighting - often with harsh but constructive criticism - the aspects necessary for the improvement of institutions. the eib group's total lending in 2016 alone, the year covered by this report, amounted to eur 83,8 billion, with total investment mobilization in the same year amounting to eur 280 billion. i would like to start with investments for small and mediumsized enterprises. smes play a key role in the european economy, generating jobs and wealth and promoting innovation: they account for over 90% of all businesses in the eu and employ two thirds of the working population. supporting access to finance for smes and midcaps must therefore remain a key priority for the european investment bank and the eib must do more to support europe's small businesses. as regards the efsi, i would first of all like to stress the importance of the additionality criteria, which must be duly documented - something which did not happen in the context of efsi 1.0. this parliament has fought hard for additionality and it is a fundamental criterion. i therefore stress the importance of transparency with regard to the efsi indicator framework and therefore welcome the fact that the efsi indicator framework will be made public by regulation under efsi 2.0. we want to have parameters on social, environmental, real and actual economic interest in approving investments under this type of instrument. however, it is worrying that only 20% of efsi funding has supported projects contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation, while the eib's standard portfolio has reached the 25% threshold. these are investments which must be directed towards reducing emissions. the report then mentions some specific projects. i am particularly concerned about the eib financing of the trans adriatic pipeline project, which does not meet the minimum environmental and social standards of the equator principles, to varying degrees in the transit countries (albania, greece and italy). i would also remind you that the dieselgate scandal has raised a number of questions about volkswagen's obtaining eib loans by fraudulent and deceptive means, and it is good that the eib is implementing olaf's recommendations on taking concrete action in implementing its anti-fraud policy. on transparency and accountability, i welcome the publication of the minutes of the eib's board of directors and in this regard i urge you to publish the minutes of the management committee meetings. it is necessary to provide for stricter rules on conflicts of interest and clear, rigorous and transparent criteria to avoid any form of corruption. i also welcome the proposals of the eib's ethics and compliance committee on corporate governance and transparency, such as the introduction of ethics issues within its remit. i also stress the importance of strengthening the obligations of integrity after termination of employment and of providing for concrete sanctions for potential cases of 'revolving doors' between senior eib managers and the private sector. i call on the eib to swiftly apply relevant eu legislation and rules on tax avoidance, tax havens and other related issues and to require its clients to comply with these rules and to prevent more effectively the risks of corruption and organised crime infiltration. i leave the floor to my colleagues to open the debate and i am also prepared for further consideration in the follow-up to be given at the end.
