president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honourable members, we are grateful to have the opportunity to address this important issue today. let me start by stressing that stalking is harmful behaviour of a complex nature and most often a form of serious psychological gender-based violence that as such can go against our fundamental rights and values such as human dignity and equality. stalking is a matter of great concern and may result in serious emotional suffering and distress. it is most frequently of women, who are threatened by former or current partners and often subject to repeated victimisation. therefore, it requires appropriate attention at all levels from the european union and its member states. our challenge in this respect is both to ensure prevention and repressive measures and to guarantee appropriate protection for the victims of stalking anywhere in the european union. we should place their rights at the centre of all relevant initiatives and actions in our countries and across the union. the council shares the concerns expressed by the european parliament in its report of 14 march 2018 on the implementation of the european protection order directive, in particular as regards cross-border cases, where victims, having obtained protection measures in one member state, move to another member state. there are differences in member states’ legal systems as regards the criminalisation – or not – of stalking and in respect of the protection measures guaranteed. the council believes that, despite these differences, we should pursue the common objective of ensuring adequate and equivalent protection of victims throughout the union. the council has played a significant role both as a co-legislator and within other initiatives in respect of this sensitive issue. the european union legal framework that we have established contains a comprehensive set of rules that, if fully implemented, can contribute to broad and effective protection of victims across the european union. the european protection order may not be applicable to all cases of stalking, as it is not currently recognised as a criminal offence in all member states, but the council shares the view that the expected eu accession to the istanbul convention – and possibly its ratification by member states whih have not yet done so – should contribute to a more effective and coherent response to this form of violence. the european protection order directive has to be considered in conjunction with the victims’ rights directive. that instrument provides for additional protection measures and for procedural rights for victims of crime. however, there are also other eu legal instruments that strengthen the position of victims, namely the compensation directive and the regulation on mutual recognition of protection measures in civil matters. stalking was explicitly mentioned by the council in its conclusions from 2014 on the need to prevent and eliminate all forms of violence against women. since then, the council has – on several occasions – recalled this commitment and invited member states to sign and ratify the istanbul convention. the council has also taken non-legislative initiatives for victim protection, in particular, the establishment of the european network on victims’ rights aimed at enhancing cooperation between the competent authorities of the member states and the access of victims to their rights. as of january this year, envr has a permanent organisation. it held its kick-off meeting on 23-24 april 2018 in budapest. the presidency devotes particular attention to combatting all forms of gender-based violence. as a matter of fact, draft council conclusions on improving police co-operation in combating domestic violence and violence against women are currently being discussed, with particular focus on the protection of vulnerable victims within a multidisciplinary approach. the text of the conclusions draws on replies to a questionnaire which also covered stalking and will be submitted to the justice and home affairs council for adoption on 5 june.
member of the commission. – madam president, thank you for putting this point on the agenda of the plenary today. the definition of stalking included in the council of europe convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, in its article 34, is that it is the intentional conduct of seriously impairing a person’s psychological integrity through coercion or threats. stalking can lead to subsequent assault. in all cases, it leaves its victims extremely vulnerable. the istanbul convention obliges member states to criminalise this behaviour, and 19 member states have done so in the process of their ratification of the istanbul convention. all of us here should continue to push for the ratification of the convention by the rest of the member states. i thank all of you who have been active on this issue. i am planning to visit those member states that have not yet ratified the convention. i stand ready to discuss the proposal both with citizens and with political representatives, and i will explain and try to dismantle many myths surrounding it. two of the member states which have not ratified the convention have, however, criminalised stalking. these are the united kingdom and ireland. the commission is aware of the differences in the legal systems of the member states and of the fact that their national protection measures differ in scope, duration and nature. where stalking is classified as a crime under national law, its victims can rely on all rights under the 2012 victims’ rights directive. this means that such victims have a right to access to information, support and protection according to their individual needs. it is therefore crucial that member states treat stalking as a crime. let me underline that the right to have access to victim support services is not dependent on a formal complaint with regard to a criminal offence. this means that, even in the member states that do not criminalise stalking, the victims should receive assistance from those services. for example, they could be guided on how to deal with their situation by other measures, like applying for an injunction order or damages for anxiety and harassment. in addition, under the rules of the european protection order, any victim of stalking who has been granted protection in one eu member state should benefit from protection when she or he travels or moves to another member state. the commission is aware of the fact that the european protection order is rarely used in practice, and this needs to be addressed. national practitioners, law enforcement and judicial authorities should recommit to combating all forms of violence, including stalking. this could, for instance, be achieved by informing or offering the victim the possibility of a european protection order each time the domestic protection measure is adopted. i look forward to hearing your views on this matter.
on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank the commission and the council for the words you have used in the facts and also in your intentions. i would like to thank especially the colleagues who supported my proposal, which i am of course living in person, along with many other women. you see, the scourge of gender-based violence has continued to be the focus of international attention for several decades now. it's a problem that takes a long time to stop. certainly, much progress has been made, especially at the european union level, through the adoption of legislative provisions to prevent this dangerous conduct: prosecute perpetrators and protect victims and persons at risk by providing them with appropriate services. i am referring, for example, as you have already said, to the european protection order, the so-called 'victims' directive and the istanbul convention. the istanbul convention is the first instrument in europe to establish legally binding rules to prevent, protect and punish this criminal conduct, but it is also the first instrument to intervene and include stalking, defined as "acts of persecution", among the various crimes. stalking is a crime that is often still underestimated legally and, alas, recognized in europe in only 21 of the european countries. this is a problem because we have to make it as homogeneous as possible and we have to harmonize this aspect as much as possible, which unfortunately does not find uniformity, harmonization in all 28 member states. the behaviour we see in stalking, as sadly the daily news reports teach us, even degenerates into further and more serious crimes, such as personal injury and murder. so in the light of this - and i come to the conclusion - i would like to ask you some questions, and i would like to ask the commission what it intends to do. first of all: to intervene with a specific legislative proposal; second: the european arrest warrant is a tool for the european union to use to raise awareness and at the same time, to gain experience of a concrete analysis of the data you have verified, whether to use the european arrest warrant.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens and mutagens is a welcome step towards the creation of a european union directive on carcinogens and mutagens. persecution can take on countless forms, but they always have in common an obsessive imprint that leads the victim to fear above all for his own safety, a sense of fear that characterizes daily life, a real limitation on personal freedom. as there are many shapes, so are the executioners. statistics show that the numbers of stalking cases within the walls of the home or after the end of a relationship are high. the control that a spouse, a live-in partner, can exert is enormous and leaves the victim without any place to feel safe. and that is why we also need to pay more attention to migrant women. measures such as protection orders, removal from the family home or a prohibition on approaching places frequented by the family are protective instruments that can make a difference and significantly improve the daily lives of victims, but they cannot be the only possible means. we must provide better legal guarantees for the protection of victims of persecution, and we must take up the good practices that exist in europe - i am speaking here of my own country, italy, for example. we also need a strong investment in education, because the best long-term measure is more effective education and active cultural engagement. we can't wait any longer. we cannot allow such an important subject to be regulated in a way that is not uniform throughout the european union. i would like to conclude by saying that there are still too many countries in the european union today which have not yet ratified the istanbul convention.
we are talking about a phenomenon, the stalking of women, which affected 3.5 million european women in 2016 alone. we know that the istanbul convention, specifically article 34, requires that legislative or other measures be taken against repeated acts of psychological violence, namely stalking. we know that nine countries have not yet ratified the istanbul convention. but let us also ask ourselves what is happening in countries such as italy, which have also ratified the convention. it is for example the case that the offence of non-aggravated stalking is de facto decriminalised by the fact that the conduct can be extinguished by compensating the victim. we think this is shameful, as the italian feminist movement said, as it said "not one less". we know that violence against women is not primarily countered in the courts but through political, social and cultural intervention.
on behalf of the efdd group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission is finally going to take concrete action to combat the crime of stalking, which affects millions of european citizens, particularly women, every year. the data is impressive. 18% of women, or 9 million european citizens, have been victims of persecutory behaviour. one in ten women have been assaulted by a former partner who did not accept the end of the relationship. as we know, we have said, not all member states recognise the crime of stalking in their legislation and even in those states where there is legislation on the subject, it is difficult to enforce the law. that is why we must do more: the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. it is often the case that those who report such crimes find themselves fighting not only against those who are guilty of such crimes but also against the slowness of justice. there are several cases of chronicling, for example in italy, where, despite the various complaints of stalking by the victims to the competent authorities, they were disfigured and beaten by their partners, former partners and in some cases, alas, killed. you have to say no more! so we welcome this action by the commission, because europe has a duty to protect its citizens.
author. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam commissioner, first of all i would like to thank all the shadow rapporteurs for their cooperation in drafting this resolution. it was a great team effort, an indication of the sensitivity of all the groups to the issue. over 30 000 children arrived in europe in 2017, including many unaccompanied children, who are the most vulnerable because they are at greater risk of abuse, exploitation and violence. since the start of the migration crisis, much has been done at european level to respond to the needs of children and their families, but unfortunately some member states still do not implement the recommendations contained in the commission's communication on the protection of migrant children, presented more than a year ago. it is alarming, for example, to see that in some countries of the union, migrant children are still detained solely on the grounds of their migrant status, and we hope that on this point the council will share and support parliament's position, which has long called for the abolition of this practice and for the provision by the national authorities of community-based reception systems and suitable this parliament intends to reaffirm once again the need to ensure that these children are given the necessary protection from the moment they arrive on european territory, by ensuring that they are rights of the child. it is, however, essential for the dismantling of trafficking in human beings and the prevention of the disappearance of children that the union should work towards creating legal and safe channels of immigration with all member states sharing the principle of solidarity and responsibility, at least towards children.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, nothing can show the true soul of a society except the way it treats its children, said nelson mandela. this resolution gives clear indications of what the true soul of europe should be: the reception, care and integration of migrant children. they are young people with a past that is hard to forget, but also a present and a future project. we are asking for a series of guarantees and protections for them that go beyond the emergency management of recent years and also legal and safe pathways; we ask that no parent should entrust the fate of their children to desperate journeys. it is therefore necessary to set up humanitarian corridors, to provide for relocation, to speed up family reunification, to apply good practices such as those in my country, whose unremitting work by the institutions, local authorities, associations and civil society gives us the strength to look ahead and also helps us to rediscover the true soul of europe.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with this question we want to accelerate a genuine common european strategy to define a framework for the protection of migrant children in europe on the basis of the convention on the rights of the child: it is our duty, particularly with regard to unaccompanied minors. there are currently 15 000 in italy alone. that is why we have passed a new law in my country, which we have presented to the intergroup on children, and which takes up many of the points in our resolution tomorrow: a common system of rapid identification upon arrival, no detention, persons assigned to each hotspot, standard reception conditions, legal assistance, health care, access to education, irrespective of their status, but above all appointment of guardians and possibility of family custody, family reunification. in addition, in order to prevent trafficking, we must provide for forms of protection and monitoring in the framework of partnerships with third countries.

ladies and gentlemen, it is with great emotion that i wish to express, on behalf of the european parliament, my affectionate thoughts to nicole fontaine, who left us a few days ago after a long political life devoted to society and to the fight for the ideals that were hers. a memory full of gratitude and appreciation. first elected in 1984, she was a leading member of our assembly for 23 years, with a two-year break when she was a minister in france. during these long years, she has acquired a deep knowledge of the parliament and the political and institutional environment of the union and has worked tirelessly to strengthen our institution. as vice-president for conciliation, she worked passionately to consolidate the codecision procedure and to strengthen the role of parliament. we owe him a lot. on 20 july 1999, twenty years after another woman, simone veil, was elected president of our assembly. in varietate concordia, united in diversity that was his motto, and it has become ours, and it was adopted 18 years ago during his presidency. i recall this page of our history because beyond the symbol, there is the strength of a commitment. this motto expresses the whole of his thought and represents the guiding thread of his political action. of course, we are different, but our differences enrich us. they are merely the outgrowth of a common european culture ladies and gentlemen, as of friday our personal data and our private lives are better protected against abuse and manipulation. this is thanks to the entry into force of new data protection rules promoted by the european parliament. i thank all the colleagues who have worked on this important regulation, and in particular the rapporteur, mr jan philipp albrecht, who will be leaving us shortly to become a minister in germany, and to whom i wish all the best. the general data protection regulation is the biggest reform of privacy legislation since the birth of the internet. it is a decisive step towards ensuring that citizens can use the internet with confidence in europe, but also in the rest of the world. with this regulation, we have shown that we can set global standards on privacy and the european union is at the forefront of protecting citizens worldwide. from now on, companies and online platforms that we trust with our data will have to make their intentions known when they use it. they will have to get our explicit consent, regardless of the country in which they operate. no more tacit consensus, no more shadow zones or shortcuts that allow the rules to be circumvented. these rules will help prevent the recurrence of scandals, of millions of users' data being used to influence election results. for example, any form of unauthorized use of data will have to be notified within 72 hours. there are heavy penalties for those who do not comply with the new rules, up to 4% of total annual turnover. for the web giants, this could amount to fines of up to billions of dollars. the european parliament has played a central role in setting state-of-the-art privacy standards, but also in calling for online platforms to be accountable to european citizens. i'm glad the reporter. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in the european union only 6% of all farm managers are under 35 years old, while over 50% are over 55. generational renewal in agriculture therefore needs strong policy measures in the new cap to promote generational renewal. the text adopted by a large majority in the committee on agriculture and rural development made a number of policy recommendations aimed at improving the existing support scheme and assisting young farmers in entering the agricultural sector. access to land is, as is well known, the main obstacle preventing new farmers from starting up in the agricultural sector in europe. access to land is limited by the scarcity of land and of course also by competition from other farmers and investors. the problem of access to land has been exacerbated mainly as a consequence of the current structure of direct payments, which often leads to increases in land rents and purchase prices. too many farmers tend to stay in business as long as possible to continue receiving subsidies, using service providers to cultivate the land or working only the minimum amount of cultivated land they have. i believe that the activity levels needed to allocate payments to support the achievement of certain targets should be increased, just as i believe that a ban on the irrelevant combination of subsidies with the enjoyment of pension benefits should be applied. member states should implement new measures to grant priority access to agricultural land to new farmers and young farmers, making full use of all regulatory instruments and also drawing on best practices already successfully implemented in some member states. for example, instruments such as rural banks could be envisaged, which could further facilitate access to land, but also provide a comprehensive picture of land availability for young farmers. generational change should be facilitated through legislation, for example on inheritance and taxation, rules on access to land, land use planning and business succession strategies. the current cap does not provide incentives to encourage the transfer of farms from older to younger generations. it is a gap that must be filled, and it must be filled soon, if we are to really encourage young people. we can do this by introducing, for example, measures which can actually motivate older people to transfer land ownership, such as those on early retirement schemes or other types of retirement incentives. on the budgetary side, it is essential to continue to provide support to the young farmers programme, but by increasing the maximum level of national funding beyond 2% for the compulsory payments in the first pillar, and increasing the support rate in the second pillar to encourage generational renewal. we recommend improving measures to facilitate access to loans with preferential interest rates for new farmers, including by private financial operators, by implementing financial instruments to provide zero-interest loans for investments by young farmers. better cooperation is also needed with the eib and the european investment fund in order to promote the creation of ad hoc financial instruments for young farmers in all member states. one important point concerns simplification: the overall management of direct payments and rural development programme measures is considered to be extremely complex and difficult, in particular for new farmers who are not particularly familiar with the payment system and who therefore need a significant simplification of procedures and a reduction of the time taken in payment procedures. on training, the commission and the member states should be able to offer more training and advisory opportunities to young farmers, both potential and established, including skills for starting up an agricultural business and agricultural and technological skills related to new technologies and entrepreneurship, such as marketing, networking, communication, innovation, multi-functionality and diversification and financial skills. finally, innovation is one of the most effective tools for improving the generational change. young farmers represent a great potential for innovation and diversification, as they tend to have higher managerial skills and abilities and are more likely to access new markets, develop new production methods and make the best use of technological developments and innovations in agriculture, which can enable them to respond to the environmental challenges of agriculture. it is therefore necessary to provide strong support to young people who wish to introduce innovative production techniques and processes, such as precision and conservation farming systems, which are intended to improve the profitability and environmental sustainability of the agricultural sector. only by implementing these measures can young farmers be offered long-term prospects to prevent rural exodus. strong support for young farmers is a sine qua non for securing the future of rural areas and should therefore be identified as a top priority in the framework of the new cap for the period after 2020.

common sense is important, but it alone is not enough to solve the problems we face. the situation in libya is unfortunately still characterized by factors of great instability, not least because the continued influence of armed groups on politics and the economy is dangerous and if we do not put up some resistance now, it is likely to increase. it should be clear to everyone that without interest in libya, but also because there are quite different views on the strategies to be adopted to contribute to the stabilisation and democratisation of the country. in drawing up the recommendation we followed a number of political criteria. firstly, to ensure consistency with the european foreign policy as interpreted by the high representative. the second is to support the action of the un, represented by salamé, which today, despite a thousand difficulties, seems to be the only way forward for libya. thirdly, to ensure support for all libyan forces interested in finding a political solution for libya, with a genuine national reconciliation operation. the fourth principle is to listen to the requests and appeals from the member states bordering the mediterranean, particularly italy, which are suffering the consequences of the lack of stability in that country. and finally, to tackle the issue of migrants with realistic determination, framing it in a broader strategy, capable of involving more subjects and allowing us to respond to issues that are very important to us, concerning the rights of persons and human rights. the aim of the recommendation seems to be quite clear: to take all necessary steps to achieve the broadest possible consensus on un action to ensure a stable future for libya in its political, institutional and constitutional structures.

president of the republic of colombia. mr president, mr antonio tajani and honourable members of the european parliament, i am very honoured to address this international legislative body, the representative par excellence of european democracy, to speak about peace and its challenges. last sunday, just three days ago, the first round of elections was held in colombia to choose my successor as president of the republic. we were accompanied by a multi-party committee of the european parliament - eight meps - and a mission of electoral experts from the european union, who were able to verify the vitality, plurality and transparency that today characterize colombian democracy. two candidates received the majority of votes, and between them the colombians will decide on june 17 who will preside over the destinies of the nation until august 7 of the year 2022. this was not an ordinary election, nor were the parliamentary elections last march. these are the first elections, after more than half a century, that we have without the threat and interference of the internal armed conflict with the farc guerrillas, the largest and oldest in the americas. it was also the safest, most transparent, with the greatest guarantees, with the greatest number of observers, and most importantly, with the greatest participation in our history. even my most staunch opponents say so. seeing rodrigo londoño, formerly alias timochenko, former farc commander and now head of his political party, voting for the first time says it all. (applause) that, ladies and gentlemen, makes a big difference, and that is why this time the candidates' discussions focused on issues such as education, health, pensions, public security or taxes, and no longer - as had happened for so many years - on the absurd war we were suffering. i am not here to tell you that colombia has already achieved complete peace, because it has not. the threat of a last guerrilla, much smaller than the farc, the eln, with which we are currently holding peace talks in havana, and also organized crime groups dedicated to the nefarious business of drug trafficking, remains. but the achievement of the demobilization and disarmament of the farc, and its constitution as a political party - without prejudice to its leaders and main responsible parties having to undergo a transitional justice process - has fundamentally changed the landscape and perspective of our country. and whoever my successor is, this advance towards peace is final. it's not reversible. not only because our own constitutional court has so ordered, but because it is the pledge of the colombian state. it is also a commitment to the international community. never in the history of the united nations, for example, has the security council unanimously adopted so many resolutions in favour of a process. because, as secretary-general guterres said at the last assembly, colombia is the only good news the world had today. but it is irreversible, mainly because no one wants to return to the horrors of war. in a world where intolerance and confrontation between societies and nations are still a constant, it is great news that in colombia - a country with more than 50 million inhabitants and all the potential to contribute positively to humanity - an armed conflict has been brought to an end which has left more than 8 million victims and more than 270 000 dead. in a world where some still prefer the option of arms to dialogue and coexistence, it is good to be able to tell you that the weapons that so many colombians used against each other are now being turned into monuments of peace. because without peace no society can achieve true development. a little over two weeks ago, in the convent of assisi, in your country, mr president, in italy, i had the pleasant opportunity of presenting to german chancellor angela merkel the lamp of peace given to her by the franciscan community, which protects saint francis of assisi, the patron of peace of the catholic church. a highly symbolic recognition that i also had the honor of receiving in 2016. and on that day i recalled - as i want to recall here today - the legacy of coexistence that the european union represents for the world. and the norwegian committee summed it up well when it awarded you, the europeans, the nobel peace prize in 2012: it said that its most important achievement - yours - has been the successful struggle for peace and reconciliation, and for democracy and human rights. europe has been an example in this, and that example must continue to illuminate the path of humanity. because only peace and reconciliation, only democracy and respect for human rights can counter the harmful influence of nationalism, fundamentalism, racism, populism and intolerance. (applause) and i can think of no better scenario than this one to thank the european union and the nations that make up it for their determined and ongoing support of our peace process, and this complex phase that we are now facing, which is the post-conflict phase. we feel that the european union is with us in the pursuit of the supreme good of any society, which is peace. and we greatly appreciate the work of your special envoy eamon gilmore, not only during the negotiation process but also now, in the implementation phase of the agreement. a year and a half ago, the european union trust fund was set up in brussels to support post-conflict colombia, with an initial capital of 95 million euro. some 62 million euros have already been committed to various projects, such as the case of the indigenous community of nasa in the south of the country, which has already exported its first container of coffee to europe thanks to this contribution. another project, for example, for small farmers in areas recovered from the conflict, who have been able to achieve the bio-certification of their products, thereby increasing their income by at least 15%. the european union has also offered eur 400 million of repayable cooperation through the european investment bank. and it has committed another 85 million euros to cooperation programmes for humanitarian demining, sustainable development, the fight against climate change, innovation, technology, education, human rights... look at this encouraging fact: thanks to the end of the armed conflict with the farc, and to the international cooperation that you are providing us, colombia went from being the second country with the most victims caused by anti-personnel mines to being the tenth today. and we're going down. we have 673 municipalities planted with anti-personnel mines and we have already been able to declare 225 - a third of them - as suspect mine-free. you can't imagine what this means for the peasants of those alleys, who can now walk their land and work their plots without fear! and we hope to reach the year 2021 as a completely mine-free country. we are thus making progress - with difficulties, of course, but with firm steps and with the help of the european union - in the peace building that follows the signing of the peace agreement. because it's one thing to silence the guns and stop the bloodshed and stop the deaths that come from the conflict. and another, even more far-reaching task is to reconcile hearts and ensure opportunities for progress for millions of families who suffered the consequences of violence. only then can a stable and lasting peace be consolidated. and in this respect, you europeans have been a great ally of colombia. thank you for your company! thank you for your support! our country offers the international community, in return, a successful model of peace process. in a world full of unresolved conflicts, colombia's peace process has become a laboratory that can be useful for trying solutions in other scenarios. ours was a sui generis process because it did not simply set the conditions for the end of the armed conflict - as is the usual - but focused on asserting the rights of the victims, the rights to truth, justice, reparation and non-repetition, and on implementing - and this is very important - development plans in the areas most affected by the conflict. i mean, more than a pact to end the war, it was a pact for humanity and development, a more just, more inclusive development, that focused on the victims of that war. the peace agreement establishes a comprehensive system for the fulfillment of victims' rights that includes a truth commission, a missing persons unit and a transitional justice system that "experts say" is a model for the world, being the first time a peace settlement is made under the umbrella of the rome statute. and in any peace process, one of the most difficult aspects is to reconcile society's demand for justice - that is, sanction - with society's own desire for an end to the confrontation. the eternal dilemma between justice and peace! our challenge was to achieve a transitional justice system that guaranteed maximum justice without sacrificing peace, respecting our constitution, respecting our international treaties, such as the rome statute. and i think we did it. now colombia will see a new dawn, a much better future without the burden of armed conflict. but we know it's just the beginning of a long road. in addition to the implementation of the agreement to end the conflict with the farc - which is itself long and complex - we have another challenge ahead, an immense challenge: to build peace in the minds and hearts of colombians, accustomed for so long to hate and disqualify the adversary. we are saddened by the murders of social leaders, human rights defenders, representatives of the victims, ex-combatants, which have occurred since the signing of the peace agreement, and i want to assure you here that the colombian state is committed to clarifying these cases and to putting a stop to this situation. we have set up - and are running - a national commission for guarantees, which i myself chair, to coordinate between the various institutions the actions to protect the communities and their leaders. we have already clarified 40% of the cases reported to the prosecutor general's office and we are determined to continue to move forward so that those responsible are punished and so that no more murders occur. that is our greatest challenge today as a society: to learn to recognize the other, to learn to live together in the midst of difference, to learn to process disputes without violence, something in which you in europe have made positive progress. i am an optimist because i know that the values of unity, love, tolerance, compassion are more powerful than the counter-values of fear, hatred, revenge, exclusion. this is a universal truth, applicable not only in colombia, but around the world, for example, in the fight against terrorism or the management of the migrant crisis. i said it when i received the nobel peace prize and i want to say it again today in this iconic auditorium of a continent that has given the world a lesson of unity in diversity. human beings have to understand that, beyond all differences, beyond all nuances, in the end we are one people and one race: of all colors, of all beliefs and of all preferences. our people, ladies and gentlemen, are called the world. and our race is called... humanity! member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, thank you very much for this most engaging and important debate. i have taken good note of all your comments. odometer fraud is indeed a major problem, and we clearly need even more effective solutions to fight it in the future, but please acknowledge all that we have done already up to now. i am sure that that will have a very positive effect on the market. please inform all of your voters of the activities that have been done. let me go through the major points again. we now have new roadworthiness rules which oblige inspectors to collect odometer data, and they have been in force for only 10 days. i hope everybody in europe knows that. we will assess the implementation, as required by the legislation, by 2020 and propose additional measures if we find that they are necessary. secondly, we have new type-approval rules that were set and adopted last year with new obligations for manufacturers to address the odometer fraud issue. the commission plans to review their application and then decide on future steps if necessary. thirdly, cross-border data exchange is the next step. as i said before, we will now use the budget allocated by parliament in pilot projects to prepare a proposal going in this direction. beyond legislation, awareness-raising is essential. member states must exchange experience and good practices, and this is what we promote in the commission’s roadworthiness committee, which pays special attention to automotive topics. so as you can see, there were four clear actions that we have taken just in the last few years. we will be very much directly engaged with you to take the next steps, but let’s see how far we get through the implementation of these four elements.
in writing. odometer fraud is a widespread phenomenon that seriously jeopardises road safety, distorts the proper functioning of the internal market and imposes additional undue costs on consumers, insurers, used car dealers, leasing companies and even manufacturers. the economic damage for the union as a whole is estimated at between eur 5.6 and eur 9.6 billion. in addition to the economic effects, there are also serious negative impacts on road safety. the problem of odometer fraud should be addressed by a multi-layered approach. obliging manufacturers to specifically protect odometers from tampering is a first step that will better safeguard all new passenger cars on the market. a solution based on a uniform european database would also be needed, which would collect all eu mileage records during periodic technical inspections and maintenance and inspection in workshops, via the eucaris system and a european blockchain network, allowing for cross-border exchange of information.

member of the commission. – mr president, we are gathered here today to talk about the impact of delocalisation on workers and regions. it is clear that our policies are geared towards the creation of jobs in the european regions. the commission has presented an industrial policy strategy to help our industries to stay, or become, strong on innovation, digitisation and decarbonisation. some regions benefit from globalisation and demographic change but others are struggling with this industrial transition process. the need to strengthen the abilities of local communities to cope with and adapt to social or economic change was also emphasised in our renewed industrial policy strategy. it is at regional level that the effect of the industrial transformation is greatest. that is why our industrial policy aims at empowering regions to benefit from the opportunities of industrial transition. in a single market, companies are free to establish factories anywhere in the european union. freedom of establishment is a basic principle of the treaty and the commission cannot interfere in such investment or disinvestment decisions by private companies. when it comes to location, it is also the role of the regions to provide an attractive environment for investment and growth. however, we are, of course, very vigilant if relocation decisions involve public funds. we are aware of the high political sensitivity of the few cases in which public funds are used to move an economic activity to another member state, causing substantial job losses. that is why in the 2014—2020 period, we have strengthened the rules in the fields where the commission can act: state aid and the european union funds. we react immediately whenever we are alerted. the commission has no power to interfere in companies’ reorganisation plans. nevertheless, we urge companies to follow good practices on the anticipation and socially responsible management of restructuring. the european union state aid rules provide safeguards to prevent member states from using public money to incentivise the relocation of existing jobs from one european union country to another. in addition, the european union has several instruments to support workers’ employability in order to mitigate the adverse social consequences of restructuring, for example the european globalisation adjustment fund. there is a strict regulatory framework that imposes obligations on companies concerning the provision of information to, and consultation of, workers, in particular with regard to the opening of social dialogue in order to mitigate the consequences of reorganisation. even more importantly, cohesion policy support from the european social fund and the european regional development fund is available in all european union regions to mitigate its potential negative effects, and in the context of cohesion policy we have included additional safeguards to avoid those funds being used for delocalisation. i can assure you that, in the proposal for the new post—2020 regulations, we will include prevention of the use of funds to support delocalisation. cohesion policy support can also be used for industrial transition, training and skills development as well as other measures to mitigate negative effects. the commission has also launched pilot actions in order to work with a selected number of interested regions to master the challenges of industrial transition. one of these regions is the piedmont region, the home region of embraco. other examples are hauts-de-france and wallonia. you surely remember the caterpillar and other similar restructuring cases in these regions. we will support these regions with the aim of accelerating innovation uptake, removing investment barriers and facilitating reskilling and preparing for industrial and societal change.

commission proposal is therefore solidly based on stakeholder opinions and evidence. the commission proposes three main areas of action for our future cooperation in the field of youth. they are captured by the words ‘engage’, ‘connect’ and ‘empower’. first, ‘engage’ is about fostering young people’s participation in civic and democratic life. the biggest priority for me will be to reform the dialogue with young people. we want to make sure we make it more open and inclusive, less formal and rigid. the current format has achieved positive results. since 2010, we have reached over 250 000 opportunities. young people who are struggling with disadvantages tend to be less active citizens and to have less trust in institutions. let us try to change that. second, the word ‘connect’ underlines our intention to bring together young people across the european union and beyond. the commission wants to foster volunteering, learning mobility, solidarity and intercultural understanding. for example, we want to build a policy framework for volunteering and solidarity activities, which will underpin the activities funded through the european solidarity corps. the commission also agrees with you on the need to clarify and reinforce the link between european union youth policy and the related european union spending programmes. indeed, we are proud that the commission proposal for the next multiannual financial framework places a strong focus on youth – the commission is proposing to more than double the budget of erasmus and the european solidarity corps. this is a clear sign. we are committed to investing in youth. we must be ambitious in this area: our young people deserve nothing less. we count on you to defend our proposals in the tough negotiations ahead. third, the word ‘empower’ is about supporting young people through a youth work agenda. the focus is on quality, innovation, digitalisation and recognition of youth work and non-formal learning. we must ensure that the youth sector is ready to fulfil its potential in times of change. but this is not all. we want to ensure that young people are heard when decisions are taken across policy areas. we have taken on board your recommendation to better coordinate the different youth-related initiatives in order to make our youth activities more visible and improve their outreach. the commission is therefore proposing to create the position of an eu youth coordinator inside the european commission. this person will be a contact and reference point for young people across the continent. this unique position will be an important signal of the importance we attach to the young generation and help us enhance coordination and coherence. we also want to be much more transparent about what the european union does for young people. to this end, we propose to track how much funding from the european union budget is devoted to youth, looking at a wide range of programmes. finally, we also want to introduce more flexibility. that is why the commission proposal suggests that member states set ‘national action plans’, translating european union-level youth priorities into their own plans. young people face quite different challenges in each member state. national action plans can be most helpful in fitting specific national contexts. these are just some highlights of the commission proposal for the new youth strategy. i am now looking forward to hearing your views and to discussing how we can best make this strategy a reality as of 2019. let us work together to make it as effective as possible, because we owe it to our young people.

in writing. this report analyses quite appropriately the effectiveness of the eu youth strategy in achieving its objectives. the report highlights critical issues such as the heterogeneity of results and the lack of systematic communication and reliable information on the implementation of the strategy, and makes recommendations to the commission and the member states. in particular, it calls for intensified efforts to increase the participation of young people at risk of discrimination, to facilitate the active participation of young people, including through new technology tools, to ensure greater representativeness by youth organisations, to develop and implement policies for functional, media and digital literacy, and to make greater efforts to ensure access to culture and public life for the most disadvantaged or disabled young people. finally, with regard to the youth guarantee, thanks to an amendment of ours, it has been made clear that the member states must have effective monitoring systems in place to combat abuse. it is therefore a report containing good indications which should be implemented promptly in order to respond more effectively to the problems and needs of the new generations.

on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, precarious employment is a scourge which exposes its victims to enormous socioeconomic vulnerability. and that is what this resolution says, which takes shape and substance from the many petitions sent by precarious workers, precarious workers in the schools, the health service, the public administration in general, but also in the private sector. it is an unmistakable fact that the number of unemployed in the european union has increased exponentially, and that this number has been aggravated by the obvious impact of austerity policies. it is also clear that there is a direct link between precarious working conditions and the absence of effective legislative measures to prevent and punish discrimination and abuse in the field of fixedterm contracts, as in the case of italy. the european commission bears direct responsibility for this because it has wasted time, accumulated delays and has therefore in fact allowed the repeated and abusive use of fixed-term contracts in violation of workers' rights. the european court of justice has for years stated that eu law provides that permanent employment contracts must be the common form of employment relationship and that fixed-term contracts are only applicable to the specific features of certain sectors and for certain occupations and activities. in italy, ladies and gentlemen, we have even reached the limiting point where a worker who has been given a favourable ruling by an employment court, which recognises him as a victim of the repeated and abusive use of fixed-term contracts, is dismissed. this is clearly unacceptable, and we must put stability, dignity and effective social protection measures back at the centre of work.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, our citizens are paying today, and obviously at a very high price, for the last ten years of structural reforms which europe has asked us to carry out, and which have only led to an increase in precariousness, inequality and poverty. in italy, two and a half million workers have a fixed-term contract. in the last three years, the unemployed have grown by 8.5 percent because of the damage done by the jobs act and the good schools act. in the last year alone, one million employment contracts were created, but only 27 000 are permanent. the rest belong to the jungle of non-standard contracts, such as zero-hour contracts, which have even increased by 124.7%. these new forms of employment are also blurring the boundaries between employed and selfemployed, leading to a deterioration in the quality of work and an increase in sham selfemployment. today we have judgments certifying the absence of effective protection for those who are victims of abuse of fixed-term contracts, in violation of european legislation on fixed-term work. today we are in effect declaring the failure of the reforms implemented in our country at the request of europe, because, as we always say, it is really harmful to impose structural reforms without an ex ante assessment.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposal for a regulation under consideration fills a serious gap: the lack, to date, of a system for monitoring, reporting and verifying data on carbon dioxide emissions and fuel consumption of heavy-duty vehicles registered and placed on the market in the european union. a common database containing all member states' monitoring data is missing. these data have not yet been certified, monitored or reported in an objective and comparable way, as is the case for cars and vans. this lack of information has firstly resulted in reduced competition among european heavy-duty vehicle manufacturers, with little incentive to innovate and implement energy-efficient technologies. it also made it impossible for transport operators, which are mainly small and medium-sized enterprises, more than 500 000, to choose the most fuel-efficient vehicles and thus save on fuel costs, which represent one third of operating costs. in addition, this lack of information has been a drag on eu national action to reduce emissions from heavy-duty vehicles, given that 25% of co2 emissions from the road transport sector come from trucks, buses and coaches, which account for 5% of total emissions. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european union agency for fundamental rights. the regulation will make available on the european environment agency's website, within two years, data on carbon dioxide emissions and consumption of all categories of newly built heavy-duty vehicles. the european commission's proposal was already a good starting point and the work of comparison with colleagues from the committee on the environment, public health and food safety and with the bulgarian presidency of the council and the commission itself has enabled us to reach an even more ambitious compromise. in particular, we have improved the quantity and quality of information that will be made public, increasing transparency, for example, on engine performance. the only exceptions will be those justified by the need to protect sensitive private data and to ensure fair competition between manufacturers. we have also included in the compulsory checks the provision for administrative penalties, which was absent from the commission proposal. another of the qualifying points we have insisted on as a parliament is the inclusion of the result of road tests in the annual publication of the data to compare the vector data measured in the laboratory with the emissions under real driving conditions. we can now proceed to the setting of mandatory co2 emission standards, which already exist for cars and vans, including all heavy vehicles. i hope that this will happen in the not too distant future, on the basis of the proposal for a regulation which has already been rejected by the commission. thanks to this regulation, we will have cleaner air in our cities and our mayors will have green school buses. europe is movement. europe is moving towards a more competitive and low-carbon economy than it is today, with 94% of its transport sector still dependent on oil. today we are taking another step towards a new alliance between industry and the environment, an alliance capable of creating new and good jobs. we are taking a step towards a smarter development model that respects people's health and quality of life.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, until yesterday we had no data on emissions and no data on fuel consumption. today, finally, we are introducing monitoring and reporting of co2 emissions and fuel consumption data from new heavy duty vehicles. i welcome this and congratulate the rapporteur on leading parliament in the negotiations. this regulation fills a gap, because finally the comparison of data obtained by the vector simulation software and collected in the public register that is being set up will allow small and mediumsized enterprises and public administrations to make informed purchasing choices, guiding them - hopefully - towards models that generate the greatest fuel savings and not only that, of course we are also talking about emissions. i am also particularly pleased with the agreement reached in the interinstitutional negotiations on the transparency and publicity of the data collected, especially as regards the performance of heavy-duty engines and test cycles. it was one of our amendments, which parliament did not support at first, but fortunately this aspect is covered in the final agreement. but let us not forget that the most important battle will be fought in the coming months, with the setting of co2 reduction targets for these vehicles, which alone are responsible for 30% of total road traffic emissions and are projected to grow by a worrying amount. i conclude by saying that we must listen to the virtuous companies and motorists who are already asking us today to cut emissions by at least 24% by 2025 and to push decisively towards the electrification of heavy vehicles.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, first i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, ms nicolai, and the committee on fisheries for their report on this very important issue. providing a comprehensive overview of the state of play of recreational fisheries in the eu and drawing public attention to this topic is extremely useful and necessary. scientific advice increasingly suggests that recreational fisheries can have an important impact on the state of some stocks. this is, for instance, the case with cod in the baltic, sea bass in the atlantic, and eels. in some of these cases, recreational catches could actually be more important than commercial catches. the commission is monitoring this situation closely and proposes measures for recreational fisheries on a case—by—case basis when science advises that these are needed. to give you some examples: for eels, the eu regulation requires member states to make estimates of recreational fishing licenses and their catches. for western baltic cod and sea bass in the bay of biscay, bag limits currently apply to recreational fisheries. for the northern stock of sea bass, only the catch-and-release practice is allowed. let me mention here the pilot project proposed by parliament to reinforce the control schemes for recreational catches of sea bass in the atlantic. the study will evaluate existing control measures and tools, identify the strengths and weaknesses of available solutions, assess the costs and benefits of different options, explore good practices and propose recommendations or guidelines to improve control schemes. more generally, the control regulation requires member states to monitor recreational catches of stocks, subject to recovery plans, excluding fishing from shore. this implies the establishment of sampling plans and biannual reporting to the commission. this provision is intended to ensure the appropriate monitoring of recreational fisheries of depleted stocks. our proposal for the revision of the control regulation, adopted only two weeks ago, goes even further. it acknowledges that recreational fishing can have a significant impact on certain stocks and provides for specific tools allowing an effective control of recreational fisheries by the member states. for example, we are proposing that member states establish a registration or licensing system to monitor the number of natural and legal persons involved in recreational fisheries and also to collect data on catches from such fisheries through catch reporting or other appropriate data collection mechanisms. furthermore, for stocks where eu conservation measures apply to recreational fisheries, the commission proposes that member states ensure that all persons involved in recreational fisheries record and send catch declarations electronically to the competent authorities on a daily basis or after each fishing trip. to make this happen, we need solid databases, in particular for stock assessment purposes. the ices working group on recreational fisheries surveys highlighted that data from member states are still missing, in particular in the mediterranean. to remedy this, we have now made it compulsory for member states to provide such data and conduct validation pilot projects within two years of the entry into force of the new eu multiannual programme for data collection. this deadline of two years will expire on 31 december 2018. this is a big step forward, as the conservation of some marine biological resources might indeed require measures on recreational fisheries, and these cannot be properly shaped without reliable data. this being said, the one—size—fits—all approach cannot be applied regarding recreational fisheries. this is an issue that we need to look into on a case—by—case basis, stock by stock, also when preparing proposals for multiannual management plans. while the baltic map does not include provisions on recreational fisheries, both the western waters map and the map for demersal fisheries in the western mediterranean cover recreational fisheries for stocks, where these have an important impact. this shows that the commission is actively engaging in the discussion around the impact of recreational fisheries. we are open to your ideas and views to further address this issue with a view to ensuring the sustainability of stocks for future generations and the long—term viability of this segment of the sector. your report provides precious information and guidance in this respect. once again, thank you for your efforts and input.

first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i have been listening very carefully to the debate on migration, and having dealt with this issue over the last four years, i try to formulate for myself why it has been impossible to find a solution so far at the european level. i think the answer lies in the concept of moral hazard. there is a lack of confidence between the member states that the other state will do what they agreed to do to find a solution. indeed, italy and greece for a very long time complained and said ‘you’re leaving us alone; we need to find a solution; dublin doesn’t work; we’re swamped; we’re overwhelmed by the numbers of refugees arriving’. and then for too long they got the answer ‘that’s dublin, deal with it. it’s your task’. and then of course, we arrived at a situation of waving through, and this led to a lot of suspicion in other member states: they’re not doing their job; they’re waving through refugees in large numbers. so there is no state that can claim to be completely innocent in the situation we have found ourselves now. i also believe there is some criticism possible if people in italy keep saying ‘we were left completely alone; we were completely abandoned’. yes, for a long time that was true, but i find it difficult to explain that when i go to germany. look at the numbers of refugees that were taken in in germany. look at the number of refugees that were taken in in sweden. an incredibly vast problem is now the integration of these refugees in many countries. as long as we keep refusing the idea that we have a collective problem that can only be tackled with collective solutions, we will not find a solution. as long as member states just stick to their own solution and say ‘we are the only ones who are right’ and as long as the rest of the union does not do what we do, we will not find a solution. and we will fail collectively. given the size of the migration challenge the world faces, not just europe, given the developments in africa, do you really think that building walls and fences and refusing to accept ships is going to bring a solution? will that stop the pressure? do you really think that if we do not stick together on this, individual member states will be able to reach agreements with the states of origin to take back their migrants if they do not have the right to asylum? do you really think that, individually, we can create a prospect for africa that will allow young africans to see a future in their own countries instead of feeling the need to come to europe? do you really think that if we take away a bit of the humanity of people on ships and say these are just migrants, that we will continue our policy on the basis of our values and human rights? don’t you agree that by denying other people’s humanity, we take away part of our own humanity? doesn’t that kill us morally if we continue like that? i am not saying everyone who wants to come to europe should be welcomed, but i am saying we need to put an end to the dying in the mediterranean. this can only be done if europe collectively devises stronger protection of our external borders; if we finally devise a common european asylum policy; if we finally make headway in having agreements with the countries of origin so that they take back the citizens; if we finally have a realistic plan of investment in africa so that africa develops in a way that makes people want to stay in africa; and if we finally come to terms with the fact that in a time of crisis, and one or two or three of our member states are overwhelmed, they should be able to count on the solidarity of all member states. the only way we will find a sustainable solution for the migration issue – which will not go away, whatever we do – is if we do all these things at the same time. according to your political preferences, you have a preference for one or other of the solutions, but none of you can close your eyes to the fact that you can only deal with it if all these solutions are part of our approach. and if we do not do this as europeans, who else will? member states will not be able to do it on their own, whatever their policies are. let me end on one point. we are at a risk, in this time of turbulence and huge challenges, of falling into the trap of entering into faustian deals. to handle the migration issue, perhaps we should not have as much of the rule of law or the respect for human rights as is good for us. please, please, stay away from that faustian deal, because you will lose on all scores. what is the price of unity of the european union? should the price of unity of the european union be ‘let’s not make a point of the rule of law and human rights just so we can have unity’? i can guarantee you if respect for the rule of law and human rights is no longer a quintessential element of our union, we will lose human rights, the rule of law and the european union. that is a price that is far too high to pay. interests of our citizens.

the agenda includes the debate on the question with request for an oral reply to the commission on the economic and monetary union package, tabled by mr roberto gualtieri, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs (000047/2018 b8-0027/2018) (2018/2724(rsp)).
author. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this debate is taking place at a crucial juncture for the future of europe and the euro area. we acknowledge that the commission has put on the table a wide range of proposals which outline the pillars of a more complete economic and monetary union and which are better able to generate growth, employment, cohesion and resilience to shocks. we note, however, that some of these proposals define more as an embryo of the instruments we need than as a complete implementation and that criticisms remain. the most important proposal is undoubtedly the introduction of a macroeconomic stabilisation instrument, through an investment protection fund, during the adverse phases of the cycle. this is a crucial function because the absorption of asymmetric shocks cannot be effectively carried out by monetary policy or national budgets. if we had had this tool during the crisis, we probably would have avoided the second recession and all its economic, social and political consequences. we would point out to those who speak of moral hazard that, on the contrary, this instrument would provide an incentive for responsible budgetary policies and the correction of macroeconomic imbalances. it is therefore good that there is a proposal, even if it seems insufficient in terms of size, and an unemployment benefit would be a more effective and more transparent automatic stabilizer. the reform support programme is also in line with the recommendations of this parliament. it is important here that the concept of structural reforms be adapted to the real challenges of today's world, which do not require a devaluation of labour and price competitiveness, but a capacity for innovation and development that is also based on a cohesive society. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the european stability mechanism to include the backstop for the bank resolution fund. i would like to express the frustration of this parliament at the apparent intention of the member states not to follow the commission's proposal to integrate the fund into the legal framework of the union. i would like to make it clear once and for all that the justification for this choice, namely that otherwise the control powers of the national parliaments would be lost, is not the truth, it is one. the commission's proposal would not change anything in this respect. as has been said many times, the european parliament would not use its right of consent to alter the institutional balance of a body which uses the resources of the member states. finally, i would advise some member states to avoid formulating mechanisms for the restructuring of sovereign debts which would not only be counterproductive to financial stability but would also deprive the necessary unanimity for the reform of the esm. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european social fund is not a proposal for a regulation on the european social fund. the commission's package also includes the integration of article 3 of the fiscal compact into european legislation. i must say that the commission has missed an opportunity. we need to simplify and improve our budgetary rules and that would require, firstly, a different treatment of investment expenditure and the avoidance of pro-cyclical mechanisms. it is clear that the proposal put forward on the fiscal compact will not go far and that there is a long way to go to bring our budgetary rules up to date. finally, it is good to reiterate to everyone, including this parliament, that without a mechanism to ensure the same level of protection for deposits, not only banking union but monetary union itself is incomplete. mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, parliament will try to improve the commission's proposals and to ensure consistency between them and the mff. we hope that a minimalist approach will not prevail among the member states, which would risk preventing us from making full use of the decisive window of opportunity which this latest glimpse of legislation represents.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, let me thank you for this timely oral question on the deepening of our economic and monetary union. democratic accountability is one of the key principles on which this work is based, and i am happy to be here to respond and to hear your views. a well—functioning emu is at the core of eu integration. our economic and monetary union is more resilient now than it was before the crisis, but the work is not yet complete. a more integrated and performing euro area is needed to bring increased stability and prosperity to all europeans. reconciling very different views on these matters is sometimes difficult, but we are making some progress. the general approach on the 2016 banking package at the may ecofin is a major milestone that lays the basis for further progress on the banking union, including on the risk-sharing side. we hope that at the june summit it will be possible to take the concrete decisions which are expected, notably regarding the completion of the banking union and further development of the european stability mechanism. we would like to see agreement on key principles and clear milestones for future work. coming more specifically to mr gualtieri’s questions on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ): with regard to the integration of the esm into the eu legal framework, regrettably the council has not yet started legislative negotiations on the commission’s proposal, as several member states are not in favour of anchoring the esm in eu law. however, there is general support for the goal of converting the esm into the european monetary fund. discussions on related issues, such as the role of the esm as a backstop for a single resolution fund or the new esm instruments, are taking place in an intergovernmental format. the commission’s position is that integration of the esm into the eu legal framework is important to allow full accountability and democratic and judicial oversight of esm activities, to promote the interests of the whole union and to ensure swift and timely esm actions under the well—defined framework. the commission also considers that any reforms of the esm should not undermine the institutional prerogatives set out in the treaties, in particular when it comes to fiscal and economic surveillance. we also remain convinced that the incorporation of esm into the union framework can be done by means of article 352 of the treaty. we also maintain that article 126(14) is an appropriate legal basis for the directive transposing into union law the key provisions as set out in the fiscal compact. this legal basis has also been used in the past to introduce comparable fiscal rules and obligations. as regards the involvement of the european parliament, let me recall that we put the community method at the centre of the emu package precisely to increase transparency and accountability. the community method would increase the european parliament’s and the national parliaments’ oversight of eu economic governance. the commission attaches great importance to the views of the european parliament. in preparing our proposals we have taken into consideration the recent own—initiative reports on the budgetary capacity of the eurozone; the böge-berès report on the possible evolutions and adjustments of the current institutional set up of the european union; the verhofstadt report; and, on improving the functioning of the european union, building on the potential of the lisbon treaty, the brok-bresso report. we look forward to the input from the european parliament in a formal legislative process and remain fully available to hold regular exchanges of views and debate on these topics. a first exchange of views took place in the econ committee on 27 march with commissioner moscovici and myself. finally, let me say a few words on the two emu-related proposals, which we adopted on 31 may in the context of the next multiannual financial framework. the european investment stabilisation function will help member states to absorb large asymmetric shocks by helping to protect public investment levels. it will work through a provision of loans of up to eur 30 billion, guaranteed by the eu budget, and grants to cover the related interest costs. to receive this support, member states will have to comply with strict eligibility criteria based on sound fiscal and macroeconomic policies. the reform support programme will provide financial and technical support to the structural reforms. a budget of eur 25 billion will be divided among three instruments: a reform delivery tool providing financial support for agreed reform packages (eur 22 billion), a technical support instrument continuing the successful experience with the current structural reform support programme (eur 840 million), and a convergence facility to offer dedicated financial and technical support to those non-euro-area member states that take demonstrable steps towards adopting the euro (eur 2.16 billion). the package will complement other eu programmes and funds in support of jobs and growth, notably the structural and cohesion funds and the new invest eu fund. an important theme of our mff proposal is a stronger link between the eu budget and the european semester, which is a framework for economic policy coordination. it is now time to decide and to live up to our commitments to reform the emu. our end goal is to achieve better living and social standards for all europeans. that is what matters in the end. i count on your support in this process.
