i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr schwab, and the other shadow rapporteurs for the long and difficult work we have done together. the goal we set for ourselves was an ambitious one. it was a matter of substantially changing the text which had been handed to us by the commission. so finding balance and convergence on new formulations was not a small task, we succeeded and that is very important. we had this objective and together we wanted to find solutions which would not restrict the autonomy of the member states. it was our job to support the member states in maintaining their autonomy in regulating professional activities and in pursuing public interest objectives through this regulation, as was already said in the debate. we have now amended that proposal and reached a conclusion, of which i would like to stress some aspects. we have ensured that the test arrangements are flexible and proportionate to the changes under consideration. it wasn't like that at first. we have explicitly reiterated the competence of the member states to regulate the professions. the different approaches are not to be regarded as wrong or negative before they are even proposed, but they must be synergistic with the overall solution we are considering here. we rejected - yes, because there are not only the positive things we added, there are also the things we removed - the commission's proposal to create independent monitoring bodies that could disrupt future work, ensuring that the list of criteria to be assessed is proportionate and less burdensome for the member states, including by eliminating the economic impact assessment that was in the original text. we have strengthened the measures for transparency and consultation of stakeholders, starting with the social partners, and we have finally maintained the explicit recognition in the text of the directive of the specific nature of the regulation of health professions, which has been the subject of much discussion but which has created a great deal of sensitivity in all the countries of the union. we have therefore the autonomy of the member states, which avoids deregulation, and at the same time we have increased transparency and the involvement of the social partners. it was a necessary balance, but not a simple one. i'm very glad we did it.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, very few thoughts. freedom to pursue professions, including healthcare, and freedom to conduct a business are fundamental prerequisites for the development of human capital in a europe of growth, while protecting the rights of consumers, workers and professionals as well as the business system. to achieve this, it is necessary to avoid imposing disproportionate and sometimes insurmountable obstacles to the achievement of these objectives. while it is true, as it is true, that in the absence of specific provisions aimed at harmonising the requirements for access to and the exercise of regulated professions, the member states are responsible for their regulation, that responsibility cannot but be embedded in the indispensable principles of non-discrimination and proportionality, thus tending towards homogenisation also with regard to the mechanism of mutual evaluation. the ex ante evaluation of existing or new regulations therefore seems to us to be a fair and acceptable option for the proper functioning of the market, which we want to make ever more transparent and ever more consumer-friendly.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i believe that the directive on the proportionality test, thanks to the work of our colleagues, in particular the rapporteur and the shadow rapporteur, should help the national authorities to legislate better, not to prevent legitimate legislative action by the member states. competent professionals who are fully integrated into the new digital dimension will be crucial for europe to remain competitive in the world and to safeguard our social model. to preserve a high quality of professional services we therefore need supportive policies, but above all a common, effective and proportionate regulatory framework. we have corrected a wrong attitude on the part of the commission, which regarded all legislative measures as an obstacle to economic growth. on the contrary, madam president, commissioner, i believe that we must promote rules which support healthy competition, young people's access to the labour market, growth and innovation, but which also protect the quality of the services provided, public interest objectives and final consumers.
member of the commission. – madam president, i want to thank all the speakers who took the floor. of course, i very much welcome the positive remarks. i listened carefully to the negative ones and to some concerns that honourable members have. i would like once again to highlight the importance of this directive for the further improvement of the single market for services. this is one of the most important parts of our services package, and i am glad that, at least for now, we have this part of the package. i want to add that professional mobility is a right of eu citizens and i will echo some of you in saying that the vote tomorrow will be about values and freedoms, not just about professional services. so i hope that, with that vote tomorrow, you will support the compromise that has been reached in the proposal. i think it is a good compromise and i want to thank everyone involved and everyone who cooperated with us and with whom we reached this outcome.
in writing. smart regulation of professions can boost economic growth in the member states and the eu as a whole, provided that this does not come at the expense of professionalism itself as not all member states have the same professional standards. the proportionality tests of the directive in question should therefore not only focus on the economic impact as a criterion in assessing the proportionality of the measures, but should ensure transparency, a high quality of professional services provided and a high level of consumer protection, seeking to ensure a balance between the restrictions imposed on a fundamental freedom and the objective of public interest. member states should be able to impose different requirements on access to certain professions, such as membership of professional organisations, continuing training and others, which may be important for the achievement of the public interest objective. service providers in regulated professions are already required to meet higher quality standards in terms of professional independence, education or lifelong learning. consequently, those professions must be able to rely on proportionate measures by the member states in which they provide services.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the opening of negotiations for the new partnership agreement between the european union and the african, caribbean and pacific states represents a great opportunity to improve the characteristics of the cotonou agreement and to contribute to the achievement of the sustainable development objectives. the eradication of poverty, respect for human rights, economic and social development and the integration of the acp states into the global economy must remain the focal points of the new negotiation. at the same time, the challenges of today embodied in the un 2030 agenda and the african union 2063 agenda need to be highlighted in the new agreement as well: the european union is committed to the development of a sustainable economy, the fight against climate change, the definition of legal pathways for immigration and the promotion of peace. we have also stressed today the role of immigration in the european context. the new agreement between the acp countries and europe cannot deal with immigration in terms of return only. an ambitious, holistic policy must be put in place to work towards eradicating poverty and the root causes of immigration. the future agreement requires a strengthening of the parliamentary dimension. we insist on the strengthening of political dialogue to ensure that our activities are democratically relevant. we therefore welcome the possibility of involving the opposition and civil society in the periodic acp-eu meetings. we must work more and more with the citizens and towards the citizens. implement and strengthen youth and gender policies, build a system that allows monitoring of human rights, taking into account civil society reports. respect for and promotion of fundamental human rights was the cornerstone of the cotonou agreement and must be the basis on which the future agreement is built.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the cotonou agreement has so far been based on three pillars: development cooperation, political and economic cooperation and cooperation in trade. the trade policy has been a total failure. some countries of the union have set up agreements of a neo-colonialist nature, in which only in words were sustainable measures on human rights, new social norms and environmental protection aimed at, but in fact they have fuelled trade liberalization, imposing high prices on our products, such as new medicines, such as processed products or those of advanced technology such as mobile phones. as this was happening, these countries, particularly france, were raiding raw materials, from rare materials in congo to fishery products in senegal, fossil fuels in nigeria, uranium in niger, blood diamonds in sierra leone and cocoa in the ivory coast. political cooperation should have been one of the cornerstones of the cotonou agreement, but it has so far not led anywhere near the stability we all wanted. it seems to us that insecurity is being fuelled and even encouraged in order to finance the arms trade and also the business of migrants. the negotiations should stress that political dialogue is a fundamental aspect of the cotonou agreement and that it must remain a central pillar in the overall legal framework. if we want to do only trade policy without thinking about the rights situation and without meaningful involvement of civil society in the dialogue at all levels, the new agreement will fail as the previous one did. i am not mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the new agreement will have to be firmly rooted in the 2030 agenda, with a mechanism to monitor the progress made by both sides in implementing the new sustainable development goals. particular attention should be paid to those which were the essential elements of cotonou: the european union is committed to the implementation of the un charter and the un convention on the rights of the child. i would add the great theme of combating tax evasion and avoidance, for which the developing countries are already paying the highest price. on immigration, we call on the council and the commission not to continue on the shameful path they have taken in recent times, of making aid conditional on greater border controls. unfortunately, the proposal seems to us to be too unbalanced towards returns and says little or nothing about opening up channels of legal immigration. let us work to ensure that the new partnership does not abandon its commitment to the fight against poverty and is a tool for addressing needs and protecting rights and for sustainable development that truly leaves no one behind.

president-in-office of the council. – mr president, at the gothenburg summit in november 2017 the eu heads of state and government chose education and culture as the first subject to be addressed under the new leaders’ agenda, underlining their willingness to do more in these areas. the results of the gothenburg discussions were formalised in the conclusions of the european council meeting on 14 december last year, which emphasised that education and culture are key to building inclusive and cohesive societies. but the european council didn’t limit itself to such general statements: it also set out a number of specific areas for work to be taken forward. i would like to mention two such areas, which are specifically relevant to the question posed today. the first is language learning, where the heads of state and government called for action so that more young people will speak at least two european languages in addition to their mother tongue. the second area is the mutual recognition of higher education and school leaving diplomas, and here member states’ cooperation is key. the benefits of multilingual competences impact upon all aspects of life. they contribute to mutual understanding and mobility within the union. they increase our productivity, competitiveness and economic resilience. the lack of multilingual competences hampers the mobility of our citizens within the european union and beyond and limits access to education, training and the labour market. at a time when europe is looking to the future and seeking to re—engage, especially with young people, around an agenda of shared values, we believe multilingual and multicultural competences are crucial to creating a sense of belonging among europeans. here, i would like to remind you that multilingualism was one of the core elements of the modernised key competence framework adopted by the council in may and the council recommendation on promoting common values. the council recommendation on key competences for lifelong learning is particularly relevant because multilingual competence is identified as one of the eight key competences which should be developed by the member states’ education systems. this update was not just a single act by the council to address the common challenge in the european union of the modernisation of educational institutions, but also part of the member states’ overall ambition to keep working on the new skills agenda for europe. the council’s recent extensive work on that matter, including the provision of a quality framework for language learning and recognition, started with the revision of the european qualifications framework. the revised european qualifications framework recommendation provided better understanding of qualifications and enabled better use of the skills available on the european labour market. the new europass framework, agreed recently, builds on the successful formula with easy—to—use tools to help people identify and communicate their skills and qualifications in all eu languages, which is a major boost for the recognition of all eu languages. in addition, many other initiatives in europe have supported the definition and development of language competences. the council supports in a sustainable manner the use of the common european framework of reference for languages and recognises the impact of the european language label award for excellence and innovation in language teaching. allow me to remind you that the council held an education ministerial debate in february this year, when it called for a stronger erasmus+ programme building on current successful instruments and further boosting participation. the call for an inclusive erasmus+ programme, providing more and new participants with mobility opportunities, will increase the opportunities for young people both to learn more languages and to promote their own mother tongue with the european union and beyond. in may the council adopted important strategic conclusions on moving towards the vision a european education area, which recognised multilingual competence as an important building block of such an area. in the meantime, the commission has issued a package of three further proposals for council recommendations, including a proposal on the mutual recognition of higher education and school leaving diplomas and the proposal on improving language learning. the two proposed recommendations are particularly relevant to today’s discussion. the recommendation on improving language learning focuses on language teaching and learning in compulsory education, covering both general and vocational schools, as well as multilingual competences in a lifelong perspective. both recommendations will be examined in detail by the council. this process has only just begun and it is therefore too early at this point to comment on the substance. however, there is already broad consensus that these are the key areas to be addressed in seeking to build a european education area and it is my understanding that the ambition of the forthcoming austrian presidency is to seek agreement at least on the first proposal, on mutual recognition of diplomas, before the end of this year. therefore, on the issue of language learning, as well as mutual recognition of diplomas, it is clear that the work is progressing quite quickly. these issues are a priority for the council, and parliament can expect quality results during the upcoming presidencies.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, the number of elephants poached is alarming. it is estimated that some 30,000 african elephants are killed each year to meet the world's demand for ivory. this makes certain african landmasses a veritable elephant graveyard. of course, poaching is not limited to elephants but involves a whole range of animals. in the face of such a disaster, we recognise that the european union's action plan against wildlife trafficking, which came into force last year, is a first step towards containing the scourge of ivory trafficking. however, the more restrictive measures adopted by the united states, china and hong kong are much more effective. the european union should raise the level of vigilance by adopting equally severe measures. the cycle of death that involves not only the elephants but also the forest rangers who dedicate their lives to their protection must be broken. we have received a call from africa and from the citizens of europe, and we must respond to it. the fight to safeguard biodiversity and wildlife conservation also requires a firm stance against the illegal ivory market.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the illegal trade in ivory threatens the existence of wild elephants and rhinos and inevitably fuels the demand for ivory products obtained illegally, which undermines any attempt to control and reduce trade. we have already addressed the commission on this subject, most recently with a letter on 3 may, and we are here again to ask you - and i ask my colleagues - how you assess this problem and this particular aspect of the problem, that is, legal trade and its impact on illegal trade. the scientific community is unanimous in recognizing that the illegal killing of elephants by poachers for ivory is the primary cause of their decline, and in africa they are being killed at a staggering rate of 30,000 a year. the sad reality, commissioner, is that as long as there is an ivory market, there will be poaching and illegal trafficking. for this reason, i agree with what my colleagues are asking: imports into the union should be prohibited completely. there is no more time to lose. the time is ripe and we must act.
member of the commission. – madam president, the 2014 eu anti-corruption report provided a useful overview of the situation in each member state: measures in place, outstanding issues, policies that are working and areas that could be improved. the report showed that the nature and scope of corruption varies from one member state to another and that the effectiveness of anti-corruption policies is quite different. it also showed that corruption deserved attention in all eu member states. in the past years the commission has increasingly prioritised integrity and anti—corruption, also in the european semester of economic governance. corruption is still a key issue in a number of states, hampering investment, efficient resource allocation, economic performance and growth. the situation calls for continued, persistent and coherent action. it is against this background, in line with the general approach of this commission to streamline processes and focus on key issues in the relevant fora, that we considered that the european semester, which is the main economic policy dialogue with member states, is the most appropriate policy instrument for systematically engaging with the member states in this area of major common interest. in march 2018, the issue of corruption was included in 14 country reports. for several member states, the commission underlined the need to strengthen the effective investigation and prosecution of corruption and enhance prevention. other areas requiring improvement are whistle—blower protection, lobbying legislation, assets and interest disclosure and verifications, adequate resourcing for anti-corruption bodies, as well as transparency and public access to information. in the country—specific recommendations published on 23 may 2018, recommendations focusing on these aspects were proposed for six countries. facilitating experience-sharing among member states in the fight against corruption is a key aspect of anti-corruption efforts at eu level. in 2015 the commission launched the eu anti—corruption experience-sharing programme. it offers anti—corruption practitioners from member states a forum for exchanging views on topics of common interest and on legislative and institutional reforms and policy initiatives in other member states. these workshops cover topics such as corruption in the private sector, political immunities, public procurement at local level, asset disclosure, whistle—blower protection, corruption in health care, conflicts of interest, and measuring corruption and its economic and social impact. more than 300 experts have participated in the programme since 2015. these efforts go hand in hand with our legislative activity. the commission has taken action to ensure that anti-corruption provisions are an integral part of all relevant legislative instruments. such is the case for the recent initiative on the protection of whistle—blowers. adequate whistle—blowing mechanisms that codify processes within public administration to allow officials channels for reporting what they may perceive as irregularities or even illegal acts can help overcome detection problems inherent to corruption. the commission has also recently proposed a package of measures enabling the national competent authorities to access and exchange financial and other information in a timely manner. the measures aim to grant law enforcement authorities, asset recovery offices and anti-corruption authorities direct access to the information contained in the centralised bank account registers. the measures also aim at improving cooperation between law enforcement authorities and financial intelligence units (fius), as well as between fius. these recent initiatives complement other measures in areas ranging from public procurement and the protection of eu financial interests to asset recovery and anti-money laundering. the commission also provides financial support for a wide range of projects in the field of anti-corruption under a variety of financial instruments, for example in the internal security fund for police, european social and investment funds, horizon 2020 and hercule ii and iii programmes, to promote activities designed to boost eu action to prevent and combat fraud undermining the eu’s financial interests. the european institutions have put in place a comprehensive framework of rules on ethics and mechanisms to deter, investigate and punish misconduct, including corruption and associated wrongdoings. these rules are fully integrated inter alia in the staff regulations and the rules on financial management and internal control. they include enforcement mechanisms and proportionate, effective and dissuasive sanctions for possible breaches. transparency and accountability are key principles of the commission’s decision—making process. president juncker has established greater transparency as a top priority since the beginning of his mandate. as part of the commission’s commitment to transparency, the commissioners, their cabinet members and directors—general publish information on meetings held with organisations and self-employed individuals on the eu transparency register. furthermore, on 1 february 2018, a new code of conduct for commissioners entered into force, significantly enhancing the ethics framework at the political level. the modernised rules set new standards for ethics rules in europe, for example by extending the cooling—off period from 18 months to two years for former commissioners and to three years for the president of the commission. as regards the potential participation of the eu in the implementation review mechanism to the un convention against corruption (uncac), to which the eu is a party, the commission is now in the process of assessing the extent of the modifications of the union’s competence with regard to all the matters governed by the uncac after the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, as well as the legal and institutional implications of this modification of competences. it is to be recalled that the eu is a unique regional economic integration organisation and, as such, this raises specific and complex legal and institutional questions.
the question we are discussing today deals with the fight against corruption, which is a real obstacle to economic growth in the european union. the commission shall be empowered to adopt delegated acts in accordance with article 264 concerning the establishment of a european data protection supervisor. corruption is not only an offence against public administration but also an attack on the public and private economy, as it distorts free competition between businesses, degrades the quality of public services and unduly withdraws funds from the tax base. at european level, despite the recent adoption of important legislative measures such as the pif directive or the european public prosecutor's regulation, not enough has been done, even in terms of prevention, by de facto delegating the repression of the phenomenon to the criminal systems of the member states alone. the commission's failure to publish the second report on corruption has raised concern, particularly in view of the need to develop new measures in this area. among the most urgent measures, given that it has been established that there are some 3 600 criminal organisations operating in the union and that their illegal interference is seriously damaging to the economy, i would mention the development of a common definition of organised crime at european level, as well as the introduction of common rules for the protection of witnesses, informants and judicial assistants at european level. the union, in conclusion, must take a firm and authoritative stance in the fight against corruption to ensure that all member states have more effective anti-corruption policies, but also to make a careful assessment of the compliance of its institutions with the provisions of the un convention against corruption, which have not yet been fully implemented.

in writing. the protracted political, social and economic crisis in venezuela has triggered the largest mass migration in latin american history since the continent's discovery. according to recent estimates, some two million venezuelans have left the country to escape food and medicine shortages, unemployment, rampant crime, and repression by an increasingly authoritarian government. the scale of the phenomenon is such as to produce destabilising effects and strong social tensions even in neighbouring countries; i am thinking particularly of colombia, but also of brazil, guyana and ecuador. in the face of this unprecedented humanitarian crisis, it is imperative that the european union intervene by providing additional aid to support neighbouring countries in coping with the enormous humanitarian effort needed to ensure the reception of all refugees. but to tackle the root causes of the phenomenon, the european union will need to step up its international mediation efforts with the venezuelan government to end the violation of human rights and restore democracy, which is an essential prerequisite for stopping the escalation of the crisis and for holding new presidential elections in accordance with the internationally recognised principles enshrined in the venezuelan constitutional charter.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have worked very hard and actively on this proposal for a reform of european road transport put forward by the commission. we have done this in order to solve the problems of the thousands of drivers who travel every day throughout europe, very often in inhuman conditions and without respect for basic conditions of human dignity. we have done this to eliminate the problem of social dumping, which very often also results in a distortion of competition to the detriment of firms, especially italian ones, which are forced to close down because they cannot compete with eastern european firms under completely different tax and social conditions. we have put forward our proposals on all three reports under discussion, which have in fact become the position of the empl committee, which has accepted them and made them its own. we therefore felt it was right and necessary to support these proposals to the end, also because the tran committee had the bad idea of twisting them and ignoring them. in particular, we asked for the problem of social dumping to be solved by maintaining the status quo for weekly rest periods and ensuring that vehicles and drivers return home every two weeks, thus allowing drivers to see their families and loved ones again. we have asked for a ban on cabin rest, thus eliminating the problem of so many drivers being forced to sleep for hours and days on board, on the road. we have asked for the posting to apply to all hauliers engaged in cabotage and international transport operations. we have also advocated limiting the phenomenon of irregular cabotage, including through better control instruments. with today's vote parliament has lost a great opportunity to solve the problems of road hauliers, demonstrating a complete lack of common sense and confirming once again to the citizens of europe that the interests of the lobbies take precedence over those of honest workers and decent people.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the proposals we made and which the empl committee adopted were aimed at creating a greater balance of wages at european level and at applying the principle of 'same place, same pay'. the absence of common rules for posted drivers is a serious problem in terms of social dumping and disparities between workers in the european union. that is why we have strongly supported the application of posting, also in the case of cabotage operations and international transport, taking into account the high mobility of this category of workers. today's vote on the posting of workers is a clear failure of this europe, which pays a great deal of attention to markets and to the business of trade in goods but very little attention to the social rights of workers.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, our position on this report was to prohibit rest in the driver's cab, to guarantee return within two weeks and to maintain the status quo on weekly rests. the tran committee tried to water down this position and for that reason we opposed it, backing again in the house the positions adopted by the empl committee. it is vital for us to guarantee the dignity and rights of all road hauliers and to put an end to what is a veritable slavery, where drivers are not able to see their families for weeks at a time and are forced to live in deeply uncomfortable conditions. the report also shows that parliament has missed a historic opportunity to improve the conditions of workers in strenuous jobs which seriously undermine human rights.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, irregular cabotage is one of the main problems affecting italian road haulage companies. unconcerned eastern european companies are abusing the existing rules, practicing unfair competition with our entrepreneurs, in effect destroying an entire national market. we have therefore proposed that the vehicle of the vehicle be taxed in the member state of origin, that the days available for cabotage be reduced, which should be understood as a mere occasional phenomenon linked to the return of vehicles, and that the monitoring instruments be improved, also by means of the gnss technology available today. we therefore express our disappointment with the fact that we have not included proposals to solve the problem, and that we have once again protected certain realities rather than others and penalized our country once again.

over 450 policy actions across a vast array of areas. of course, implementation takes time, and we need to be resilient. patience, though often in short supply, is critical but reforms are indeed paying off. economic growth has been back in positive territory. since last year, the economy grew by 1.4% in 2017, and is expected to increase 1.9% this year. the outlook – according to the latest forecasts – is bright and in line with the euro area average. the results have been particularly impressive on the fiscal side. today, greece’s budget is running a solid primary surplus, above 4% for two consecutive years, and has been made more sustainable through ambitious taxation and patient reforms. importantly, the social safety net is being revamped to better protect vulnerable groups. the country’s competitiveness has been improving, with a positive effect on the labour market. that means faster job creation and falling unemployment. greece’s business cycle is now more aligned with the euro area economy and this is great news. against this positive backdrop, the financial sector is more and more resilient. all these are encouraging signs that will help greece to regain investor confidence. it has already successfully raised funds from bond markets on several occasions. the income—passing agreement of euro area finance ministers of 22 june will improve market sentiment even further, as already seen on the secondary market. the recent agreement on debt relief is the last of several improvements in greece’s lending terms since 2012. thanks to these favourable landing conditions, greece saves money every year. in 2017 alone, it saved eur 12 billion in debt service payments, or 6.7% of the country’s gdp, according to the european civility mechanism estimates. these benefits represent no cost for the european tax payer; on the contrary, we all gain from a stable and growing economy across our common currency area. back in 2012, private creditors did agree to take a hit to the tune of 53% on their holdings of greek debt. this was a unique feature of the second assistance programme. already in the esm programme, we had agreed short term debt measures that reduced the debt to gdp ratio by 25% in 2016. in the last eurogroup, we agreed to an even more substantial package of measures to make greece’s debt sustainable. this includes an extension of the bulk of the loans by the european financial stability facility (efsf) and a deferral of interest by an additional ten years. in other words, until 2033, greece will have less interest and have the motivation to burden its budget and this means more fiscal leeway to support its economy and its citizens. in addition to that reprofiling, the eurogroup last month agreed to resume transferring to greece the profits made by the euro system on its holdings of greek government bonds. this will take the form of semi—annual payments in december and in june until 2022. these payments give a positive incentive for greece to continue implementing reforms in the coming years. it is time to continue the process of reforms that is now fully owned by greece. this process must prove resilient over forthcoming political and economic cycles, and we must never forget that. the final tranche of the european stability mechanism to greece was another element of this package. we agreed that eur 15 billion will be disbursed after the national parliaments in a number of member states have had their say, and this can happen as soon as next week. out of this amount of eur 15 billion, eur 9.5 billion will be dedicated to a cash buffer, which should also reassure investors as it will act as greece’s fiscal backstop. the remaining eur 5.5 billion will be disbursed in 2020 to a segregated account and should be used to cover greece’s debt servicing needs. at the end of the programme, the overall size of the cash buffer in greece will be eur 24.1 billion, which is a very large amount that covers greece’s financing needs for around 22 months after the exit from the programme on 20 august. this is a longer safety net than in any other country’s programme so far. so, it is now up to greece to build on the programme’s success and to consolidate its achievements. greece should continue implementing responsible fiscal policies and growth—enacting reforms to improve the living conditions and the chances and prospects of its citizens. this is what greece’s post—programme framework will be about. we all agree that for the next couple of years, the so—called enhanced surveillance by the european commission will help greece stay the course. commissioner moscovici will be able to tell you more about that in a minute. but let me be clear, being out of the programme means greece being out of the programme. greece should commit to the requirements to participate in the euro just like any other country in the euro, but in this safe framework the government has an obligation to provide policy options to its citizens and to debate them internally. that is indeed a good thing for democracy. i am confident that greece will look at its policy options and be able to improve on existing reforms to promote stability and political compromise – stability to spur investment, compromise in the name of future generations. this will require action on several fronts: prudent fiscal policy based on primary surpluses and sound management of public finance, financial sector governance and handling of non—performing loans, an efficient and effective social safety net, flexible and open labour and product markets and – also very importantly – modern public administration, just to name a few. for this purpose the greek government presented a growth model which is based on the continuation of reforms. these will help greece to continuously lift its productivity capacity and offer a solid anchor for confidence amongst foreign investors and greek citizens. market volatility some weeks ago has shown that greece remains vulnerable to risks. new policy options should take this into account. it is very important that greece continues to take ownership and implement its ambitious long—term growth strategy. i am encouraged to find that the greek authorities see it that way too, and i welcome the policy commitments they have announced to the eurogroup. confidence in greece’s future is the key message i wanted to convey to you. i would now very much like to hear your views on this matter.

reduce the level of public debt considerably. we expect a fall below the symbolic 100% of gdp mark at the end of the process. the arrangements provided for in the agreement will provide up to eur 1.2 europe of solidarity, the idea of politicians whom we unfortunately also know in my country, such as minister salvini. it is precisely on these contrasting human and cultural values that the european solidarity corps is based, and it now requires the involvement of all european, national, social and institutional actors to maximise its impact. from the very beginning of the discussion i have fought to ensure that the programme remains as inclusive as possible, allowing all young europeans to take part, regardless of their country of origin, their personal needs, their family economic situation, with particular attention to young people with disabilities. it was essential to guarantee equal opportunities, compliance with quality criteria for the offers made, the possibility of combining a volunteering pathway central to the programme with a series of measures for work, with adequate remuneration and guaranteed contractual conditions. this so-called employment strand of the programme will make it possible to create partnerships with different socioeconomic actors, such as small and medium-sized enterprises, chambers of commerce, social enterprises and cooperatives, while broadening the spectrum of possible actions within it. it was necessary to separate voluntary activities from work more closely than in the commission's initial proposal, and i believe that work vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, structural reforms are crucial to modernise our economies, strengthen their performance and resilience and foster real convergence within and across member states. the crisis has shown that given the high level of integration of eu economies, reform efforts are a matter of common concern. your vote tomorrow will be a signal that we stand by member states in these efforts, and it will be an important step in finalising the package of proposals for deepening economic and monetary union. structural reforms not only create an environment that is conducive to investment growth and job creation, they can also help eu economies withstand shocks and contribute to economic and social cohesion. this is why structural reforms are important building blocks for a more resilient economic and monetary union. since may 2017 we have been supporting the design and implementation of structural reforms in member states through the structural reforms support programme (srsp). this has proven its usefulness, judging from the number of requests from member states which significantly exceeded the current budget possibilities. this year 24 member states applied for an amount that was five times the available budget. to respond to the growing demand from member states we need to increase the funding. at the same time, to strengthen the euro it will be beneficial to provide targeted support to those member states wishing to adopt the euro, in order to help them to prepare better and facilitate their smooth participation in economic and monetary union. this is why on 6 december 2017 we proposed to increase the budget of srsp by eur 80 million. throughout the legislative process both the parliament and the council have shown a clear commitment to eu support for structural reforms in the member states. the compromise that we found is a good one. half of the increase of eur 80 million will be funded by the global margin for commitments, the other half will be funded through redeployment available from heading 2, not affecting the rural and development programmes, nor technical assistance. this means that we are fully respecting the commitment from the original srsp regulation not to provide further financing for the programme at the expense of cohesion policy. i want to thank the european parliament, the rapporteur ms tomašić, the shadow rapporteurs, and the committee chair, ms mihaylova, for the hard work and constructive efforts during the trilogue negotiations. honourable members, by endorsing the political agreement tomorrow you will move europe one step closer to a more integrated, more resilient and more cohesive economic and monetary union. the swift adoption of this file will also enable us to increase our support for reforms in member states already as of next year.
i would like to thank mrs tomašić for her report. we support the report and we also support the programme, which has been a success, but we also support the demand that this reform does not damage the social rights of european citizens in the first place and that it leads to structural reforms which are socially responsible. we need structural reforms that promote sustainable growth, in addition to the social issues i have already mentioned, and for this we must combine national efforts with the support, where necessary, of the european institutions as well. structural reforms must be made because they serve to make the economy stronger, but they cannot be a tool to undermine the rights of citizens. they must be done as quickly as possible, but always in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, and they must be coordinated with the specific programmes and objectives of the structural funds and therefore with the specific policies of the various countries on the basis, as i said, of the principle of subsidiarity. it is also essential that this programme should remain voluntary, that is to say, available to the states which request it. of course, at the end of this mandate we will be able to take a further look at it and assess its effectiveness for the next programming period as well.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, last year the delegation of the five star movement opposed the establishment of this programme of support for structural reforms, both in committee and in plenary. on this specific text, which proposes adjustment of the objective and increase of the budget, we cannot support it completely, even if the 80 million proposed does not come from cohesion policy. but let 's be clear . the commission's proposal for a regulation on the introduction of a system of national social security contributions for the benefit of the handicapped is a very good one. we disagree on these and we will never agree on them. we agree on reforms such as simplifying public procurement rules or fighting money laundering, measures towards social inclusion and the fight against poverty, such as the citizenship income. the european union must therefore pay attention to the political direction of structural reforms and to what it imposes on the member states. it 's true . membership of the programme is optional. but are you sure that all the states, such as the italian government, will implement reforms that are directed solely towards the common good and not towards supporting private individuals and lobbies? we're not sure at all.

the agenda includes the brief presentation of the report by ms jana žitňanská, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on pathways for the reintegration of workers into quality employment after an accident or illness (2017/2277 ((ini)) ((a8-0208/2018).
member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members for these constructive and valuable remarks. the commission has put inclusive growth and social fairness at the core of its political agenda, and we are working hard to make sure that no one is left behind. i therefore welcome ms žitňanská’s report, and the commission agrees that we need effective and concrete measures for workers returning to the labour market after injury and illness. the prerequisite for successful reintegration into the labour market is ensuring the right to a healthy, safe and well-adapted working environment, as clearly recalled in the european pillar of social rights. european union legislation on occupational safety and health focuses on the legal obligation imposed on employers to assess all occupational risks on a case-by-case basis and to adapt work to the special needs of individuals. we have to bear in mind that europe is confronted with an ageing working population with increasing work-related health problems, such as muscular-skeletal disorders and mental health conditions, so we need to face and address this reality. the european union strategic framework on health and safety for the current programming period already proposes a number of measures to address demographic change and the ageing workforce. besides, the 2017 commission communication on ‘safer and healthier work for all’ has put forward specific preventive and protective measures in accordance with the requirements of sensitive workers. now, on the reintegration and rehabilitation of workers more specifically, i agree with you that measures allowing early return to work after an accident or disease are needed in order to avoid permanent exclusion. and, you are right, we should see the reintegration process as a new opportunity to benefit from workers’ skills, competence and experience. that is why we have the european social fund, on which member states can already rely to help injured workers, for instance, to get back to work more quickly. for the next multiannual financial framework (mff) the commission is going further by proposing to include the health programme as a strand of the european social fund plus (esf+) so health aspects are addressed in all social spending, and vice versa. to conclude, let me assure you that the commission will continue, in cooperation with the european agency for safety and health at work, which is based in bilbao, to raise awareness, develop practical guidance and promote the exchange of good practices. once again, i would like to thank the rapporteur for her work. this is an important contribution in defining the steps forward in the effective reintegration of workers recovering from injuries and illness.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, tomorrow we shall be voting on the result of a long process, lasting more than a year, on a directive which is objectively important and which is particularly close to my heart, since it is aimed at combating a hate crime whose social danger is often underestimated: money laundering. money laundering is a global problem, which requires a strong response from the legislator to be tackled effectively. money is the element that allows criminal organizations to run their dirty business. that is why it is crucial to develop rules that affect what is their most valuable resource, the source of funding that fuels their criminal activities. recycling also has a further odious indirect effect: the proceeds of illicit activities are funneled into the legal economy through shell companies. the market is thus narcoticised, with serious damage to the businesses that follow the rules and are destroyed by this illegal and unfair competition. criminal organizations operate like large multinational corporations, diversifying their activities to maximize profits, and they are very good at exploiting loopholes and securing impunity. for example, the proceeds of drug trafficking in italy can be reinvested by buying restaurants in the netherlands or germany, which will remain on the market supported by this financing of illicit origin, regardless of their actual turnover. for this reason, we have been working for a long time on a text which will enable law enforcement authorities throughout europe to investigate and prosecute this crime wherever it occurs. to do this we have ensured that european legislation is aligned with international standards in this area and we have gone further with the warsaw convention on recycling. we have worked hard to complete, as quickly as possible, the institutional process leading to the adoption of this directive tomorrow. i thank all the members present, the commission and the bulgarian presidency of the council for the excellent cooperation throughout the interinstitutional negotiations, which has enabled us to adopt a very comprehensive text, which is an important step forward in the fight against organised crime at european level, and which provides the judicial and law enforcement authorities with effective and decisive instruments. from the outset of our work we have sought to achieve a legislative text which is effective, clear and comprehensive, and which will put an end once and for all to the loopholes in the laws of the member states which are exploited by criminals to escape justice, without forgetting respect for fundamental rights. the directive provides for a common definition and alignment of penalties for the crime of money laundering. we started with the excellent commission proposal and, together with the other shadow rapporteurs, we carried out a lot of preparatory and consultative work involving the leading experts in the field, whose valuable contributions we then translated into amendments to the commission proposal. i should now like to focus briefly on the main results we have achieved with this directive. thanks to our work, we have removed the main potential obstacle to the investigation and ensured that money laundering is punishable. we have in fact eliminated the requirement of double criminality for criminal conduct, which is the source of the proceeds of particularly serious crimes, such as human trafficking, terrorism or corruption. this means that investigators in one member state will be able to prosecute money launderers without having to worry about whether or not their conduct is a criminal offence for the law of other countries that may be involved. as regards penalties, we felt it was essential not to limit ourselves to prison sentences, but to focus on ancillary sanctions which we consider to be particularly effective and dissuasive. (the president asked the speaker to speak more slowly) member states will be required to provide for sanctions such as a permanent ban on contracting with the public administration and accessing public funding, a ban on exercising a commercial activity or a ban on running for elective or public office. those who are guilty of such serious and dangerous crimes should stay away from public administration. this is also our commitment in italy, as we are already demonstrating with the decree "spazzacorrotti". the directive also lays down rules on the confiscation of the proceeds of this offence. we would have liked to see more effort on the part of the other institutions to meet parliament's demands. my report, which was rejected by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, did indeed contain much stricter and more innovative rules, which unfortunately met with strong opposition from the other institutions involved in the negotiations. i hope that the commission will honour the commitments it made during the trilogues and present a short-term revision of the existing directive on the freezing and confiscation of instrumentalities and proceeds of crime, so as to provide for the seizure of assets even for a non-permanent sentence, in the event of the prescription or death of the offender. this directive also contains rules on cooperation between judicial and law enforcement authorities, which, as we have always said, is an essential prerequisite for ensuring the practical effectiveness of the rules. finally, we have sought to strengthen significantly the exchange of information and the obligation to cooperate between the authorities and the member states and, in line with the position of the committee on development, of which i am a member, we have sought to include specific rules to encourage in future ever more effective cooperation with third countries, including developing countries, than with the european union.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, an effective fight against money laundering requires, at european level, an organic framework of common minimum standards to provide national judicial authorities with modern and appropriate criminal instruments and to fill the gaps caused by the diversity of the laws of the member states. i am thinking, for example, of the differences in the definitions of the offence of money laundering, or the legal concept of a presumptive offence, or the absence of rules on money laundering in some national legislation. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european police force. the proposal we are voting on tomorrow is a decisive step forward in the fight against money laundering, terrorism and criminal organisations, and it prepares the way for a wider debate on a fundamental issue, which is now unavoidable, for the development of a genuine european criminal policy: the fight against money laundering, terrorism and criminal organisations. the commission is proposing a common definition of organised crime, taking account of the transnational dimension of the phenomenon and the more advanced strategies developed by some member states to combat it.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. all speakers unanimously stressed the objective that citizens in europe deserve human dignity in old age, a sufficiently good, stable standard of living and also personal independence. we agree on the goal. secondly, the commission believes that, in the light of the historical development of pension systems, the different age structures in the member states and the different labour and social legislation, the responsibility for pension provision should remain primarily with the member states. you're the one who's responsible. i share the view of many speakers on behalf of the commission that the statutory pension scheme financed by contributions must remain the most important, the central pillar, which then receives a supplement in the member states in varying degrees from the national budgets and thus tax-financed . we believe that occupational retirement provision, along the lines of different cultures in the member states, is also a useful second, albeit narrower, pillar. and we believe that adult private pension schemes, often motivated by tax incentives, as a third pillar have a complementary - not a replacement - meaning. the market for private pension products is not sufficiently developed in europe. and in only a few member states is private pension provision of any significance, with up to 15% of total pension provision. and here we want to make an offer no obligation. we want to strengthen the national legislature by offering a suitable solution, by building a european single market of reputable products. the extent to which these products are then used is a matter for national policy, but it is also a matter for our citizens in all member states. it shouldn't be a commitment, it should be an offer. in this context, we have noted your critical and constructive contributions and will take them into account in the further course of the procedure, but believe that the commission's proposal can be a good basis for complementary support for primary national and private pension schemes in the member states.
president-in-office of the council. – madam president, first of all i would like to thank you for this very interesting discussion. it showed that even young people will be concerned in the near future by the pension systems. so it is very important to think about these pension systems. however, the council does not take decisions on specific features of national pension systems. it is up to each member state to take decisions on their own pension systems. the member states retain full responsibility for the organisation of such systems, as was also mentioned by the commissioner. in the context of the european semester in june this year, the council welcomed the fact that in most countries, recent pension reforms have had a positive impact on sustainability by containing public expenditure dynamics. however, on the basis of the economic and budgetary projections for the member states over the period 2016-2070, presented in the 2018 ageing report, the council also noted that the scale of reforms in several countries was still insufficient to curb the increase in public pension expenditures. the council therefore underlined that further steps still need to be taken by member states. the council’s priorities do not refer to the need for private schemes. policy decisions in this area are made by national governments based on whatever action they deem appropriate to tackle their own individual challenges. i think there is also a lot to do for the member states and i hope that every member state will do that. we can only do so much.

tight cages, among their own excrement and often among mice. and these are animals that are intended for human consumption, that can live in these very dense camps only because they're filled with antibiotics, which then affect the resistance that develops in humans. so, in our view, the key is to ensure that the livestock and aquaculture sectors prevent disease through good hygiene and good farming practices, rather than using antibiotics as prophylaxis. in short, we are not saying anything new today, but we are saying it with the awareness that time is running out and that we must speed up the search for new, but above all pragmatic solutions. so we have to make sure: the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on veterinary medicinal products are applied. two, the use of antibiotics in intensive farming as prophylaxis must be prohibited. and three, encourage organic and extensive farming models.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, antimicrobial resistance is a serious threat to human health and economic development. the overuse and misuse of antimicrobials in humans and animals has accelerated the natural evolutionary processes of resistance, to the point that today some infections have even been rendered untreatable by existing antimicrobials. projections indicate that antimicrobial resistance could cause up to 10 million deaths per year by 2050 if no action is taken. the one health action plan will have to play a central role in tackling antimicrobial resistance. diseases in both humans and animals should be addressed with particular regard to the food chain and the environment. the role of the european commission in coordinating and monitoring the national action plans implemented by the member states will be crucial in this respect. the correct use of antibiotics should be ensured by investing more in research, development, training and information, and by providing constant updates for medical staff on the careful use of antibiotics.
member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, thank you very much for this discussion on a single digital gateway. first, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mrs mizzi, the shadow rapporteurs and the chair of the internal market and consumer protection committee for the really excellent cooperation, which enabled us to improve our initial proposals and reach a quick agreement on this file last may. let me begin by saying why this proposal on the single digital gateway is so important. as we all know, the single market is a cornerstone of the european union, but we observe that when crossing borders, many european citizens and companies still experience a jungle of confusing rules, complex procedures and endless paperwork. a survey has shown that more than 80% of businesses see administrative complexity as the number one problem for them in the single market, and this is exactly the problem we want to address with this regulation establishing a single digital gateway. let me go through the three points that i think are the most important. first, we want to inform people better – because most people and businesses are really keen to respect the law, but imagine yourself settling in another country, even for a very short time, and think about how difficult it is to find out which rules you have to comply with, let alone in another language. two in every three small enterprises say that finding out about applicable rules is a huge challenge for them for exporting. as for bigger businesses – this is also very interesting data – bigger businesses dedicate up to 20% of human resources to keeping track of rules applicable to them. even those twelve million people in europe who reside in another member state – if they even find information, they are not certain that they can really rely on it. the regulation will make sure that citizens and small businesses can easily find all the information they need on single market rules and it will be done at both eu and national level via the your europe web portal. they will be guided directly to official national websites that provide the precise clarification that they need. the information must be easy to find, easy to understand, up to date and translated into english. thanks to the gateway quality label, they will know that they can trust this information. but speaking about quality, let me mention one very important thing that you have drawn attention to: the specific needs of persons with disabilities. in this context, i really welcome the introduction of requirements similar to those we have at national level for the commission websites which will be part of the gateway. second, the regulation will ensure that in five years, the most important procedures can be handled entirely online in all eu member states. you are very ambitious on this because this will apply not just to the 13 procedures that we initially proposed but to the more than 20 that were proposed by you. the regulation will also ban any discrimination against cross-border citizens or companies who want to make use of national procedures that are already online. they will no longer be blocked because their phone numbers, postcodes or eid are rejected. the regulation also makes a start with the implementation of the so-called ‘once only’ principle for cross-border data exchange. you rightly insisted that the regulation should ensure full data protection for the european citizens and, again, i want to reassure you that all the necessary data protection safeguards are in place in this regulation. the third point: the commission and the national authorities have already set up numerous assistance services that citizens and companies can contact when facing problems, but still more than 9 out of 10 consumers and businesses – a huge majority – are unaware of their existence. thanks to this regulation, anyone looking for assistance will be guided towards the service that is most suited to help. let me conclude by saying that users are at the centre of our interest. users should not be asked to adapt to public authorities, but the other way round. this is what this regulation will ensure. with this regulation, the eu will deliver on some of the commitments from our digital single market communication and from the tallinn declaration. it will be a big step towards making the single market work better. thank you very much for your valuable help and i am looking forward to this discussion.
the creation of a european digital single market has been one of the political priorities of this legislature. in this context, one of the main challenges is to make the benefits of new technologies directly perceptible to citizens by simplifying their daily lives. the digital single window is a first concrete example. it is a significant step forward in the digitalisation of public administrations and in simplifying procedures for citizens and businesses. the fundamental change introduced by the new regulation concerns the obligation for european public administrations to digitise a number of administrative procedures, so that they can be completed online. it will be easier for citizens and businesses to apply for a birth certificate or recognition of a diploma obtained abroad, to declare ownership of a vehicle, to notify the opening or closing of a business or activity in another country. in addition to encouraging the digitalisation of many services, this regulation establishes the 'once only' principle in the union. this will enable the european authorities to exchange data and documents already provided by the user, thus minimising the administrative burden. the s&d group has been working to ensure that the application of this principle is fully in line with the general data protection regulation, in full respect of privacy. the digital single window regulation therefore represents an important step forward in digitalising and simplifying the relationship between public administrations and citizens and businesses, increasing transparency and promoting mobility within the european union.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today we are taking an essential step towards achieving one of the objectives of the european digital single market. the digital single window aims to create a single entry point, namely at union level, by integrating existing european and national portals, websites, networks, services and systems. this is key to helping citizens and businesses to take full advantage of the new digital tools and e-government strategies. parliament has repeatedly called for the needs of citizens and businesses to be met in their crossborder activities in the european internal market, and this proposal, for which i congratulate mrs mizzi, means that for the first time member states will be obliged to make key administrative procedures available online, and that equally important information at national level will be available in another official language of the european union. it is a success which we can claim as genuinely european, given the resistance of the member states, and i only hope that care will be taken that the possible exceptions granted to the states do not become a pretext for not complying with the obligations imposed.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the internet and digital technologies are transforming the way people and businesses live, work, study, do business and travel. benefits for all europeans can be achieved with an open, efficient, inclusive public administration geared towards ambitious e-government projects that provide borderless, personalised and user-friendly end-to-end public digital services. the regulation under discussion aims to simplify contact between citizens and businesses, with problem-solving assistance services by establishing a digital one-stop shop to access information on the rules and requirements to be met under eu or national law. however, the european commission and the member states need to cooperate in synergy to facilitate an effective and gradual implementation of the project and to facilitate the implementation of fully online procedures, fully accessible also for cross-border users in the european union.
member of the commission. – mr president, the transport sector is changing fast. if we act now, we can seize the opportunity of this change and make european mobility sustainable, safe, smart and more accessible; european industry more competitive; and european jobs more secure. if we act now, we can lead in setting new global standards. these concepts are well reflected in the draft resolution prepared by mr ujhelyi, which supports more action – including at eu level – in this field. allow me to specifically address three important topics raised in the report. first, sustainability, transport is a major contributor to eu greenhouse gas emissions, as well as air pollution. we are committed to reducing and ultimately eliminating the negative externalities of our mobility. we can achieve this goal through stricter emissions standards, better consumer information, multimodality, smarter road charging, urban mobility planning, research and innovation, and by smarter use of public procurement to accelerate the transition towards zero— and low-emission vehicles. i would like to thank you for your support for this objective. we have several pending legislative proposals aimed at contributing to achieving exactly this. i therefore count on your active support to examine them as much as possible before the end of your mandate. that brings me to the second point: vision zero. until recently, vision zero – no road fatalities on european roads by 2050 – might have been perceived by some as an ambitious but distant vision. today we can be much more confident. the fresh approach we are taking in road safety, with the so—called safe system approach, and our move towards a connected and autonomous mobility are making vision zero a reality. with the third mobility package, we are proposing a strategy to make the eu an engaging global leader in autonomous mobility systems. we propose a clear, forward—looking and ambitious european agenda that provides a common vision, identifies clear supporting actions for developing and deploying key technology services and infrastructure, and that provides a clear action plan. our strategy is based on three pillars. first, a legal framework that creates a single market for autonomous mobility, covering road safety, cybersecurity, access to data and data protection. second, financial support to establish a new partnership with a consolidated sector—wide approach towards research and deployment throughout the eu, including for the coordination of pilot projects. third, an in-depth assessment of the socioeconomic and ethical aspects of autonomous mobility, making deployment suitable to absorption capacity as well as the maturity of autonomous relations. we also propose to make a number of new vehicle safety technologies mandatory as part of the revision of the general safety regulation, for example, intelligence speed assistance, autonomous emergency braking and detection of pedestrians and cyclists. this will make sure that all road users will be able to benefit from the latest developments in technologies. that brings me to the third topic: one platform for connected and autonomous mobility. citizens’ mobility demands are growing, and their attitude to mobility is indeed changing. they want to shift seamlessly between different transport modes and enjoy easy access to travel information. meanwhile, vehicles are becoming increasingly clean, connected and automated, and ultimately driverless and zero—emissions. this opens the possibility for vehicles to become an integral part of multimodal mobility, providing first and last—mile service and inclusive solutions for the elderly, disabled, and young people. before we get there, we are engaging with stakeholders to address some very important enabling topics such as security, data protection, fair and equal access to data, liability and ethical implications, integration of automated vehicles into existing traffic, public acceptance, global standard settings, and many more. this is why we proposed to bundle all efforts and create a single platform, the connected and automated mobility (cam), where all stakeholders come together to push our ambitious agenda further. under the next mff, this platform should evolve towards a fully—fledged partnership for connected and autonomous mobility, combining public and private efforts to escalate the development and deployment of innovative mobility solutions.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, europe is on the move, europe is moving towards a new model of development: a low carbon economy. that's a long way to go. the transport sector is currently 94% dependent on oil and is responsible for over 25% of greenhouse gas emissions. in addition, passenger and freight transport activities in europe will increase by 60% and 40% respectively in 2050. the central point of the communication, which i share, is the respect of the paris agreement on climate change and the 2030 agenda for sustainable development of the united nations. but how can these ambitious goals be achieved? here 's the answer: promoting low- and zero-emission mobility, intermodality, shared mobility, the development of automated vehicles through the interconnections of transport infrastructure networks, digital energy networks, digital technologies that will allow the implementation of the fundamental polluter-pays principle, for example with a toll system based on the environmental performance of vehicles.

member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank all the authors of the question for their outstanding work. the european union’s lgbti human rights guidelines from 2013 help address the human rights issues confronting lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (lgbti) persons, in particular by setting out measures which can be used in the eu’s relations with third countries. the european union’s diplomatic efforts worldwide on lgbti human rights focus on the following: firstly, combating discriminatory laws and policies and ensuring decriminalisation; secondly, promoting equality and non-discrimination; thirdly, combating state or individual violence against lgbti persons; and, last but not least, supporting and protecting human rights defenders. depending on the country situation, the european union is able to address the issue through a variety of means including high-level advocacy, quiet diplomacy, public statements, political and human rights dialogues with third countries, and financial support to civil society via the european instrument for democracy and human rights. in april last year, the russian media reported on the persecution, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as always, the council promises moments of truth - these are tusk's words - and strong decisions, but then it lives on procrastination. the most striking story is that of the dublin reform, as my colleague kyenge called it, which could have been done already and is now in danger of dying. the council is thus not exposing the lies of the eurosceptics, which we hear all the time in this house, it is not exposing their deceit against the people - as mr corbett said - the council is above all covering up its own contradictions, the contradictions of its members, mr minister, and it is also playing a double game in order to protect itself. how else can i describe it if i am not duplicating what is being done, when it is said that on the one hand we are ensuring a policy of solidarity for immigration and then we are enshrining the voluntary basis. my government has a very great responsibility here, and in this chapter too, as it were, if it is not a double game what your president kurz, who is also president of the council, is doing at this stage, which is speaking of solidarity on the one hand and then doing it, strengthening national borders. it is double-crossing to condemn orban for violations of the rule of law and then accept his nationalist approach to immigration. parliament is very much alone, sometimes with the commission, but it will nevertheless continue to do its part in the knowledge that it is directly elected by the european citizens.
