first vice-president of the commission. – madam president, i have listened very carefully to the debate and on that basis i would like to react to two issues: migration and brexit. to start with migration, it should be obvious to all of us that we can only find a sustainable solution to the challenge of migration if it is a comprehensive solution. yes, we are working hard to strengthen our external border protection, but those who believe that we will solve this issue just by strengthening the external borders are delusional. we can only solve this issue in a european way – and i believe by now every member state understands that this cannot be done just individually by member states – but we can only find a comprehensive and sustainable solution if it comprises all elements linked to migration. not just a stronger protection of our external borders, but also agreements with countries of origin for the return of people who do not have the right to asylum, as well as forms of internal solidarity in the european union and the revision of the dublin agreement. why? because frankly it boils down to a very simple truth: either we find a solution internally for that challenge that effectively shows the understanding that we cannot leave countries alone simply because of reasons of geography, because they are closest to where the migration flows come from. either we understand that, or we condemn ourselves to reintroduce internal borders in the european union. it is as simple as that. that is why the commission strongly believes that we need to revise the dublin regulation, but we need to do it in a way that expresses the new realities, which were not known when dublin came into being, and expresses the future reality that we will only solve this issue on the basis of european-wide solidarity. just imagine what would have happened in 2015 and 2016 if all nations in europe had said we just close our borders and we will not let in anyone. what would have happened to greece and italy if everybody had taken that attitude, as some nations have? it would have been a tragedy of incredible proportions, a human tragedy. so leaders at that time took their responsibility, sometimes at incredible political cost, but on the basis of the values i hope we continue to share. let me end on one issue about migration. our sister continent, africa, is at the core of the problem and will have to be at the core of the solution. no other parts of the world will have to take a greater responsibility for the future of africa than europe. only if we understand that the future of africa is the future of europe, will we be able to solve the issue. in that sense, i honestly believe the challenge we are facing – to bridge the mediterranean – is of the same magnitude as the challenge our grandparents faced to bridge the rhine after the second world war, and the challenge we faced when we were younger, to bridge the elbe after the fall of the berlin wall. that is the magnitude of the challenge, and the sooner we wake up to that challenge, the sooner we will find a comprehensive solution to an issue, migration, that will not go away simply by refusing entry, simply by building walls, simply by protecting better our external borders. on the issue of brexit, the british people have voted, and that means that for now, we are all under the obligation to do as little harm as possible. that is in the interest of all europeans, whether they are in the united kingdom or on the continent. and i believe this means trying to find solutions for the problem we face. but let me be very clear: carving out parts of the four liberties is not going to bring a solution. let me also be very clear. if somebody says ‘i want to leave your house but i’ll take the key, and i’ll come back in whenever i like, and take whatever i like from that house’, that doesn’t work. we have to make sure that we come to terms with the fact that the united kingdom has expressed a wish to leave the european union and that we negotiate in good faith to make this happen in a way that respects the integrity of the european union, including its four freedoms, and respects the wish of the british people as it stands. i want to make add two remarks. first of all, on the good friday agreement. how is it possible that people coming from the united kingdom maintain that there is no link between the european union and the good friday agreement? the european union is an integral part of the success of the good friday agreement. it would not have been possible without the european union. and you cannot just brush away that responsibility, which is a collective responsibility. the good friday agreement was one of the most historic achievements of the united kingdom, ireland and the european union, and we are all responsible for maintaining that legacy and for preventing the island of ireland from going back to a past that i knew as a young man, and i hope i will never see again. this agreement was concluded 20 years ago, one month before i was elected to the dutch parliament for the first time. and yes, mr farage, i was elected six times to a national parliament. i would like to see you try that in the united kingdom at some stage – we’ll see. but again, the issue of ireland – i want to stress what jean-claude juncker said – is central to our responsibility to do as little harm as possible in these negotiations, and just to brush us aside in london is completely irresponsible; the commission will never take the responsibility to do the same thing, and that is why michel barnier is doing what he is doing. finally, of course, at this stage emotions run high on all sides. i have some understanding for that, and you have to sort of forget some of the things that are being said with all these emotions. but, i represent a college of commissioners, where more than one third of its members have personal experience with dictatorship, with oppression and with dictatorial communist rule inspired by the soviet union. they have all fought to liberate themselves from this. one of my colleagues, vytenis andriukaitis, was born in siberia. why? because his parents, lithuanians, were deported by the soviet regime to the gulag. vytenis did not know sunlight, what it meant. he did not know what the length of a day was. he had never seen an orange as a child. all these things that he has told me over the years show clearly what the soviet union was. and any comparison to the eu is not just misleading. it is insulting to what the union is, to what we have become. (applause)
president-in-office of the council. – madam president, honorable members, thank you for your remarks and for your comments. i will convey them, of course, also to president tusk. in our endeavours, whether on migration or on security, we should be clear that there is no silver bullet. we can only achieve results through a comprehensive approach and cooperation at the european level. one of your main criticisms was on dublin. you are for sure aware of the fact that mandatory allocation, which is at the heart of parliament’s mandate, continues to be the main stumbling block in the negotiations in the council and divides not only the member states, but also the electorates which you represent. to make progress in finding a compromise, the presidency, in particular chancellor kurz, has conducted bilateral talks with all member states over the summer, in order to find a possible middle—ground. the issue was discussed at the informal meeting in salzburg and we will have a discussion at the justice and home affairs council on 12 october. we aim to present the outcome of our efforts to heads of state and government at the european council later this month. we are also working on the other files to find a solution to the whole package. for example, i would like to inform you about the africa—europe high—level forum on taking cooperation to the digital age, which will take place on 18 december in vienna. chancellor kurz and the president of the republic of rwanda, mr kagame, will host this high level forum, which will bring together european and african heads of state will continue to strive for the best possible deal.
mr president, welcome to strasbourg and to the plenary session of the european parliament. i am particularly pleased to have you here, because you are the first head of state from a balkan country to address this parliament. i am pleased to welcome you for the fourth time in just over a year, and the regularity of our meetings confirms a reality that has become established: montenegro is part of europe, not only geographically but also because we share the cultural heritage, history and values that have shaped our european identity. and as an italian, i cannot help but remember how the history of montenegro and that of italy have intertwined several times. these meetings are an opportunity to anchor montenegro and the balkans more generally to the european union. it's important to give your country a clear perspective. it must be emphasized that your accession to the union is irreversible. your leadership is essential in this process because it is a political path and not a bureaucratic one. you can count on my support and that of the european parliament. we need to step up our cooperation to address security challenges and the threat of terrorism. it is our responsibility to work together, including to manage migration flows. the union must also stand by your side to oppose together the influence of those who want to destabilise us. the agendas of the extremists and the fanatics, the islamic radicals, are contrary to our values. your stability is our stability. we are also at your disposal to help you make the necessary reforms of the administration and the judiciary. they are valuable tools for consolidating a healthy business climate and for attracting even more european investment to your country. now, mr president, i ask you to take the floor to speak to our european members, informally about the situation in your country, but also to give us a picture of what is happening in the balkans. mr president, i give you the floor.
president of montenegro. – (the following is a transcript of the interpretation of the original speech from montenegrin into english) mr president, esteemed meps, ladies and gentlemen, you have bestowed a great honour upon me by inviting me to address this highest house in european politics in my capacity as the president of montenegro – one of the youngest and smallest european states. thank you for giving me this opportunity to inform you of the achievements and plans for montenegro, the country that is the frontrunner in the negotiating process with the eu, and the country that, since its independence referendum in 2006, has been approaching its strategic national goal in a determined, stable and dynamic way. that goal is full membership in contemporary europe’s system of values. i would also like to present our views on the future of the western balkans and the european union. i would like to understand your invitation as yet another confirmation of the european parliament’s commitment and support, not only to the eu prospects of montenegro, but also to the eu accession of the region and the eu’s enlargement policy. so the question is: where is montenegro today, 12 years on, as a country whose renewed independence was met by scepticism by many in the country and neighbourhood, but also in europe and the world? i would like to draw your attention to two of our key achievements. we have strengthened our internal stability and ensured dynamic economic, institutional and democratic development. internationally, we have been achieving – and over-achieving – our very ambitious goals. we have been a nato member for a year and a half; we are a candidate country for eu membership, and there are only two remaining chapters to open. we are a responsible neighbour and an important contributor to regional stability and cooperation. and as a result of all of this, we are a destination for investments and an inspiration for many renowned foreign partners. with the moral and political capital of an ex-yugoslav republic that did not see a war on its territory in the 1990s, we are now developing a civic society of multi-ethnic and multi-religious harmony, without outstanding issues with our neighbours, which is confirmed by our border agreements with bosnia and herzegovina and kosovo, the first such agreement among ex-yugoslav countries. despite being one of the least developed ex-yugoslav republics, our economy is the leading one in the balkans today. last year, we registered real growth in gdp of 4.7%, which is one of the highest rates in europe. throughout the period since the independence referendum, we have had average annual rate of real growth of the economy of over 3%, and the living standards of our population are now among the highest in the region. twelve years ago, we were at 34% of the eu average, and last year it was 46%. all the other balkan countries are below 40% and some, unfortunately, are even below 30%. from 2006 to the end of last year, our gdp grew nominally by 100%. consequently, gdp per capita in current prices in 2017 was close to eur 7 000, compared to close to eur 3 500 in 2006. in august this year, the average rate was eur 511, which is nominally around 80% higher than the previous year. the average wages in montenegro are the highest in the region, but still, unfortunately, three times lower than the eu average. this is a consequence of the historical lagging behind of this part of europe in terms of economic development. an important impetus to economic growth has been given by foreign direct investment in this period, with net inflows of over eur six billion, or close to 18% of annual average gdp. we have also been registering very good results in tourism, which accounts for 20% of gdp. we have a population of over 600 000, and last year we had around two million tourists in hotel and private accommodation. of course, we should recall that throughout a good part of this period, we had a devastating financial and economic crisis in europe and the world, which has logically adversely affected our economy as well. insufficient employment, especially of young people, is still the biggest challenge in terms of social development in montenegro for the period to come. it is necessary to strengthen macroeconomic stability and improve our competitiveness internationally through further structural reforms. we have made a major step forward in the euro-atlantic accession processes. last year we became a fully-fledged member of nato and, as such, we participated in the nato summit in brussels and confirmed our readiness to contribute to the policies of the alliance as a responsible and credible ally. nato membership for us is the greatest recognition of our enormous efforts in implementing comprehensive reforms and our contribution to regional and global stability through developing cooperation among partners. our nato membership has produced positive effects, not only in terms of security and political stability, but also in other areas. we have more direct investments from nato countries, and the share of tourists from nato countries this year grew by 25%. our nato accession testifies to an important reform-based step forward for our entire society, economically and politically speaking, and of the results of the continuous efforts we are investing in building rule of law.as a candidate country, montenegro has made much progress in the process of eu negotiations. in the six years of negotiations, we have opened 31 negotiating chapters and provisionally closed three. montenegro has fulfilled all the opening benchmarks, in total 22 of them that were set for 13 areas, thus completing this demanding phase. we have also submitted 32 negotiating positions and we are preparing for chapter viii – competition. we hope that the remaining two chapters will be opened in the near future. apart from competition, there is chapter 27 – environment. at the same time we are committed to fulfilling the closing benchmarks in all the areas in which these parameters have been defined. one should not forget that the negotiating process with montenegro started with the new approach in which chapters 23 and 24 are opened at the beginning, and the whole process depends on the progress of these two chapters, which is the greatest challenge for the region. already today, montenegro behaves as a member of the european union when it comes to the eu common foreign and security policy. we unequivocally adhere to the common eu positions, despite the frequent pressures we are subjected to because of this. furthermore, montenegro is continuously contributing to peace and security through the participation of the army of montenegro in nato, eu and un operations and missions. when it comes to the issue of resolving the migrant crisis, montenegro is in line with the principles of solidarity and humanity, expressing the wish to receive migrants from african countries within the limits of its capacities. that is an expression of our dedication to humanitarian goals forged in the time of wars in the former yugoslavia, when refugees of all ethnic origins at times made up a fourth of our population. economic and social progress is directly linked to the results in the field of the rule of law. during the negotiations in this field, we have passed approximately 70 reform laws, strengthened the strategic framework and created institutions such as the special public prosecutor’s office and the agency for the prevention of corruption. we have made progress in the fight against high-level corruption and organised crime. we know the importance of the rule of law for society as a whole, not only for the negotiations. we are working hard on fulfilling the provisional benchmarks, and we hope they will be recognised in the positive report and the closing benchmarks. we are committed to enhancing justice, creating conditions for a full guarantee of the freedom of expression in the media, and cooperation with civil society; we are supported in this by the european commission, the council of europe and the osce. we appreciate the financial, technical and any other form of assistance from the eu and its member states. we also share our experiences with other candidate countries. we believe that the success of any western balkan country on the european path is the success of all, and we are convinced that the ‘regatta approach’, reconfirmed in the recent enlargement strategy, is a mechanism that represents a true incentive for the whole western balkans. integration of the countries of the region is a good strategy for the stability of the european continent. the enlargement process is important not only for the balkans, but also for the stability and competitiveness of europe. i underline this because it seems that the strong euro-enthusiasm, which was characteristic of central and eastern europe and also of the western balkans, is losing momentum. there are two strong causes for this. it is the dissonant tones coming from different parts of europe regarding the pace of the european enlargement, and also the unresolved problems and issues that have remained open in the regions since the yugoslav crisis, such as the problems in the relations between serbia and kosovo, in macedonia and in bosnia and herzegovina. these two causes are interdependent. the confusion and uncertainty in europe feed the illusions of the proponents of regressive politics in our region, who still dream of reshuffling the region and seek support for these ideas from some important international actors. they are counting on the short memory of the international community. that is why sometimes one has the impression that the destructive tones are louder today than in the 1990s. that is why i believe that the european prospects of the region in the certain and foreseeable future – which were implicitly announced at the sofia summit and in the last speech of president juncker – will be wind in the sails of the pro-european elites. unfortunately, the results of the referendum in macedonia are the best illustration of the problems i am referring to. decades of neglecting the problem could not be overcome through the intensified western support in the last few months. also, the referendum was organised too soon and without enough preparation. perhaps the domestic public should have been given more time to fully grasp the importance of such a decision. however, one should not lose hope that, through a two-thirds majority vote in the parliament or through new elections, this outcome can be achieved. i hope that, in brussels and in other capitals, this result will be understood as an alarm bell and a sign that it is necessary to take more decisive strategic policy steps. what remains is the hope that this will not reflect negatively on the dialogue between serbia and kosovo, which is already very complicated even without this. additional efforts are necessary to ensure that the result is achieved, even more so when knowing that there is enthusiasm, both in pristina and in belgrade. the most important thing is that the dialogue has been established and that it lasts, regardless of occasional incidents and the political temperature that has been raised on both sides. i sincerely hope that all those involved in this process will take into account the traditionally fragile stability of the western balkans and strive for a solution that will be in favour of overcoming this historically burdensome gap between belgrade and pristina and, at the same time, not jeopardise broader regional security interests unfortunately, there also remains the unresolved issue of the functioning of bosnia and herzegovina. there is a strong feeling of dissatisfaction with the results of political players – both domestic and international – in the 25 years of implementation of the dayton agreement. bosnia and herzegovina will go to the polls soon, but regardless of the individual composition of the future three-member presidency, i do not expect either consensus to be reached or greater commitment of leading political structure and individuals to reforms that would take the country in the direction of adoption of the european system of values and integration. it will take a new, broader international action to achieve that goal, with emphasis on the constructive consensus of all keen neighbouring countries and the most relevant international community players, who have a special role in that part of the country. we understand very well the need of the eu to eliminate the causes of the crisis it is going through and to carry out the process of internal consolidation, but we do not think the answer to those problems is to stop or seriously slow down the missionary project of unifying europe. on the contrary, i believe that full unification is the most important part of the answer to all problems that the eu is going through. of course, we are not trying to overlook the numerous weaknesses in the eu’s architecture, but we do not want to fall into the despondency that suggests giving up on this vision. therefore, i think it is necessary to consolidate the vision and fix the architecture. that is the road that will bring the best guarantees that europe keeps its global competition. everything else would lead to its weakening, and despite the differences in our views, primarily due to current differences in the level of development, it would lead to loss for all of us, the citizens of europe. in addition, if the european union misses another opportunity to integrate the western balkans, this would bring a big threat of political involvement of other countries, third countries, which do not share the same strategic goals as the european union. this would hold our region back within the zone of conflict and would make the european continent insufficiently stable and disunited. the process of enlargement and full unification of the eu is therefore an optimal path for montenegro, for the region and for europe as a whole. however, whether this will happen certainly does not decisively depend on us. we will do what we can do, with or without enlargement policy. whether it moves quickly or slowly, we will pursue the europeanisation of montenegrin society with even greater commitment. besides, we are already well-advanced on the track that resembles a one-way street. we simply cannot go in the opposite direction. montenegro does not want to have any other option. when we speak critically of the european union, it is because we believe that, as europeans, we have the right to think and speak about a topic that is our common interest and responsibility, thus we also observe the deficiencies of european policy. we will certainly continue doing so in the future, because i believe that is how we contribute to the growth in support of the regional public for the european future of our states, not the stagnation or decline as is the case now. we do not accept that we must speak of the eu uncritically, as if it were a new religion, but rather we see it as our joint home – the current one or the future one. in the worst case scenario, as the most important neighbour of all of us but without us being members. i am sometimes misunderstood myself, at home and in some european contexts, because of these statements that are tendentious or that are seen, due to lack of understanding, as euro-sceptical. this is not euroscepticism. on the contrary, i consider the idea of a united europe to be absolutely superior, and i see the european path for the development of the balkans as a path without an alternative, but we expect everybody to accept that we in the balkans are partners in the negotiation process with the european union, and not an experimental laboratory of its administration. we in the region can complete this process of further unification with europe much quicker and better if the vision is crystal clear and if the partnership is honest and in line with mutual respect. everything that modern montenegro has gone through is based on, and is fully in line with, the essential values that the european union was founded on and continues to preserve, from preserving peace and multi-ethnic harmony in the 1990s, to the referendum on independence held in line with the highest european standards, and finally to the decisive and successful resistance to the brutal aggression in 2016, which aimed to take freedom away from montenegro and divert it from the european and euro-atlantic path of development. therefore, we are right to emphasis montenegro took a ground-breaking step forward after roaming the wastelands outside europe, together with the region, throughout history. we have finally taken our ship of state into the direction of its natural european harbour, and we shall not give up on this intention of ours. the western balkans region is at a turning point too: it will complete its political and economic transition and join the club of european union states, or it will continue to struggle with its interethnic and interreligious conflicts, complicated open issues, underdevelopment and low standard of living. like a time bomb that can still jeopardise european security. i believe i share the opinion of all of you when i say that all institutions and official authorities, as well as all individuals who are politically involved in any way at the national level or within the european framework, today have the responsibility to contemplate a better and safer future for a united europe throughout the entire continent that is based on traditional values and embroidered with the spirit of the new times we live in. it is very important that the forthcoming elections for the european parliament are prepared and held in this positive atmosphere. the balance of power in parliament will, to a great extent, define europe’s path and determine the future of european nations. i want to believe that this path will be a joint path for us from the western balkans too. with this, i would like to thank you all once again. i want to assure you that you will always have a reliable partner in the small country of montenegro, which sees the eu as a lighthouse we are getting closer to. (loud and sustained applause)

author. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, respect for human rights in the business world is a crucial issue for us, particularly as many companies operate in developing countries. yet a global approach to regulating respect for human rights in transnational societies is still lacking. the united nations in 2014 with a resolution of the human rights council specifically established an intergovernmental working group, in order to create a legally binding instrument on transnational corporations and above all to fill a gap between respect for human rights and commercial interests. although the protection of human rights is one of the main objectives of the european union in its external action, in line with the treaty on european union, the european union itself has been very reluctant to accept the binding treaty. it should be recalled that several member states voted against the resolution on the establishment of the working group in 2014. the european union and the member states must commit themselves to playing a key role in this process, maintaining a single clear position and a common negotiating mandate which are currently lacking. i am pleased to note that after much internal debate we were able to put to the vote on thursday the resolution containing the european parliament's position on this matter. four years after the creation of the working party, i would like the council, the eeas and the commission to provide some justification for the absence of a negotiating mandate, allowing the european union to participate effectively in the process. given the differences of opinion between member states on the need for a binding instrument at international level, we ask here today, commissioner, what are the main issues that the member states of the european union consider problematic in this field, in a debate which must be very clear and transparent to all.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is unacceptable that in 2018 the international community continues to witness the systematic violation of human rights by certain multinational companies in developing countries. and worse still, the victims are not guaranteed any real judicial protection: human rights, the environment, the rights of indigenous peoples, the working conditions of men, women and children, all of these things are constantly being put on the back burner by the god of money. this complex issue and all its corollaries were addressed extensively in the report on 'corporate liability for serious human rights abuses in third countries', which i was rapporteur for and which was approved by a very slim majority in this house in 2016. but then the commission, which was repeatedly asked to do so, did not follow up on anything parliament had asked for. now that the united nations has promoted an international treaty on this subject, with a universal purpose, containing binding rules on corporate responsibility, we expect the commission to follow up parliament's repeated requests and actively support this initiative.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in a world so interconnected and ravaged by global inequalities, there are enormous challenges that we must face at international level. we therefore call on the eu and its member states to support the un process to establish a binding instrument for transnational corporations to respect human rights. voluntary instruments are not enough, the activities of companies, especially in developing countries, can lead to serious violations of human rights, not to mention the possible negative effects on the environment, for which there is often no provision for compensation for the affected populations. if we are to achieve the 2030 sustainable development goals, corporations must also align themselves. some of the multinationals that are humiliating work are the same ones that are opposed to the ecological transition and that are evading taxes by hundreds of billions of euros a year stealing our future. it is not just an industrial strategy, but an attempt to impose a model of society which crushes rights and people, and for this reason we must establish common standards and effective remedies which are accessible to all people who see their rights violated.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, four years after the establishment of the un intergovernmental working group on transnational corporations, a first draft of the text has been presented. the commission is laying the foundations for a genuine approach to the victims of human rights violations and responding to the requests of the countries of the global south, but substantial work is still needed. i would like to emphasize that this question is not just a question of answers, but of the importance of the union's contribution to the development of this binding instrument. every day, in our institutions, we work to combat violations of workers' rights, land grabbing, pollution and environmental damage, protection of the rights of communities; we are working to reduce disparities, to fight against corruption and against all forms of exploitation. we hope that the daily efforts of the union will be put to the service of the intergovernmental working group by actively participating in the work on the final text.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, on 5 july 2016 this house adopted the report i was rapporteur for, which dealt specifically with human rights and corporate social responsibility. the text called for the human rights clauses to be binding and for the commission to be more active in the united nations in support of the treaty. i can therefore only be a firm supporter of the resolution already adopted in the deve committee and i too strongly urge that there be a greater commitment by the community and the member states to a binding treaty and a binding treaty for corporate social responsibility and the responsibility of multinationals. finally, the glyphosate case, which, as you know, we have discussed a lot and are discussing a lot in the pest committee, reminds us of how urgent it is.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members of the european parliament, i want to thank all of you for this debate which shows the high interest and need for deep reform of the european vat system. there is significant progress that we have already made, because, since 2015, new rules for sales of e—services online came into force which allows member states to collect vat where the consumer is based, through a one—stop shop. member states have also now agreed to extend this new system to services and goods online, delivering another boost for vat collection in the european union. as i mentioned in the introduction, the european union has also recently agreed on a ground—breaking new framework to exchange more information and boost cooperation between national tax authorities and law enforcement authorities. however, after all the fundamental reform, a european union vat definitive system is still to be adopted by the council. in his state of the union speech, president juncker called for an end of unanimity in taxation policy. unanimity can block proposals that are in the interests of the majority and thus prevent companies and citizens from benefiting from a full single market. the commission will play its role in the reflection towards a chain of rules by presenting a communication in the coming months on qualified majority voting in the field of taxation. with your support, i am confident that the two proposals you will vote on will benefit from broad support and that progress can be achieved on all vat proposals in the coming months. finally, in reply to the question from mr arthuis, yes, the horse sector can benefit from vat reduced rates if the member state so decides. commission statement(in writing) the commission and the council are aware of a certain divergence in the vat treatment of independent groups of persons that pool their services and share costs between their members. the council and the commission recognize the need to clarify such vat rules on independent groups of persons. the commission will analyse this matter in detail in a study to be launched shortly with a view, subject to its right of initiative, to a possible proposal.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, thank you for the invitation and the opportunity to contribute to your debate on minimum income. our joint commitments to the european people are to protect those most vulnerable, to create adequate jobs and to lift up those who have fallen behind. less than a year ago, we reaffirmed the basic principles – the european pillar of social rights, principle 14 states that everyone lacking sufficient resources has the right to adequate minimum income benefits, ensuring a life with dignity at all stages of life. in 2008, the banking crisis and the ensuing sovereign debt crisis tested our economies, shocked our labour markets and put a strain on our social protection system. unemployment rates and at-risk-of-poverty rates soared throughout the eu. in the past decade, we have had to tackle manifold emergency situations. however, with determination and hard work and by taking difficult decisions, we have managed to restore our economies. in 2017, the eu average unemployment rate stood at 7.3% and employment exceeded its pre-crisis peak. albeit with some delay, youth unemployment and long-term unemployment also continue to decline. today, thanks to our combined efforts, the europe 2020 strategy target of 75% employment rate for men and women seems again to be within reach. while the picture looks positive from certain angles, there is no place for complacency. the total number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion remains very high. in 2016, 118 million european citizens, 23.5% of the total population, were at risk of poverty, even after social transfers. it is clear we still have a long way to go before we reach the europe 2020 target of lifting at least 20 million people out of poverty. ladies and gentlemen, we are all increasingly aware that economic growth must be to the benefit of all and must be socially sustainable. this is clearly demonstrated by the fact that almost all member states have made a real effort and have established schemes for minimum income or benefit in one form or another. furthermore, member states are making good use of the open method of coordination (omc), to cooperate and to exchange best practices. the european semester equally has provided an excellent platform for cooperation in this area. however, minimum income schemes do not exist in a vacuum. the real challenge is to establish inclusive labour markets to make sure that people don’t fall through the social net and, at the same time, to ensure that national social security systems remain sustainable. balancing these elements is not an easy task, especially if we look at the wider context of an ageing population and increased digitalisation and robotisation. again, i am grateful for your invitation to contribute to this debate. it was with great interest that we took note of parliament’s latest resolution on minimum income policies as a tool for fighting poverty. i’m looking forward to hearing your input on this important matter.
member of the commission. – madam president, i am very glad that this house keeps social issues high on its agenda and debates them regularly. as president juncker said in his state of the union address, europe has largely turned a page on the economic and financial crisis, and this is well reflected in the employment and social situation in europe. employment has indeed been growing for more than five years in a row and there are now 239 million people at work in the european union. this is more than ever before. the unemployment rate has dropped to 6.8%. these are the figures from eurostat for august 2018. in 2016, there were 5.6 million fewer people at risk of poverty or social exclusion than at the peak of 2012, and there are clear signs that the situation has further improved since. for instance, severe material deprivation declined in almost all member states, falling to an all—time low of 33.4 million in 2017. this is a reduction of 16 million people since 2012. having said this, we should not be complacent. thirty—three million materially deprived people is still too many, and we know that income inequality has stabilised in the last few years, but at higher levels in the european union than before the crisis. moreover, the overall number of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, albeit reduced relative to 2012, is still higher now in 2018. this is, as we all know, far from the europe 2020 target of taking 20 million people out of risk of poverty and social exclusion, and that is why the commission has proposed to act. a year ago we all proclaimed the european pillar of social rights, which recognises that everyone lacking sufficient resources has the right to adequate minimum income benefits ensuring a life in dignity at all stages of life, and effective access to enabling goods and services. for those who can work, minimum income benefits should be combined with incentives to integrate or reintegrate into the labour market. that is what the pillar says. in other words, the provision of adequate minimum income schemes is non—discriminatory and should go hand—in—hand with access to services, with employment in line with the active inclusion approach. however, i would like to recall that the setting—up of minimum income benefits is the responsibility of member states. since the introduction of minimum income schemes in greece and italy in the last two years, now all member states have some form of minimum income scheme. however, their design and implementation vary greatly. for this reason, the commission and member states have decided to deepen the analysis. a benchmarking framework has been agreed with member states for minimum income schemes supporting a thorough across—country comparison of national practices. it looks in particular at adequacy, coverage and activation and it will feed into the country—specific analysis in the 2019 european semester. the european semester has proved to be an effective framework to monitor and provide guidance to member states. it is now the main instrument for monitoring the implementation of the pillar. in 2018, some member states received country—specific recommendations addressing minimum income. and, of course, the european semester framework allows us to have a comprehensive view, including the availability of fiscal space to expand social provision. in addition, the commission has already put forward proposals and initiatives that want to make sure no one is left behind. to ensure the rights for the most vulnerable workers we presented the proposal for a directive on transparent and predictable working conditions to tackle women’s under—representation in employment and to create a more balanced distribution of caring responsibilities between women and men we put forward the work—life balance for parents and carers initiative. so this is just to mention a few of our initiatives on the table. they now need to be adopted and implemented and, honourable members, i count on your support to make sure that they will be adopted within the current mandate of this parliament.
the socialist group, on behalf of the s&d group, has strongly supported the european pillar of social rights, which includes income support measures for people in difficulty and at risk of poverty, because we believe that no one should be left behind and that all citizens have the right to decent social and economic living conditions. we have supported, in particular, proposals for the most vulnerable such as the youth guarantee for our young people, the child guarantee for our children, and we have promoted concrete aid to families, in particular single-parent families headed by a woman, who are those who are almost 50% at risk of falling into poverty. we believe, however, that the first right of a person is to work, to work in a dignified, safe, stable and protected way, to work which enables everyone to be an active part of society and to contribute to its growth. we believe in fair pay and fair work. that is why our group was the first to put forward the proposal for a minimum wage at european level. and we're talking about a guaranteed minimum wage, not just an income. we believe that a minimum wage for all workers allows for a peaceful life with real work for all, and that is our main objective. all this, of course, in the context of investments that can grow the economy and stimulate people's participation in society, especially with strong active policies on employment, training and continuing support. but protections and rights must not become forms of welfare-ism that look backwards, but must ensure that everyone has the opportunity to contribute to the growth of society and not be excluded from it. the debate under way is, however, closely linked to an internal italian political debate which is preparing a measure which seems to us to be discriminatory and punitive, since, for example, it would be reserved only for italian citizens, contrary to european rules which say that it should be reserved for all people at risk of poverty living in the countries.

on behalf of the ppe group. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i too join in the congratulations to mrs griesbeck for her work as rapporteur and i, as the shadow rapporteur, the successor to my colleague from apulia, whose post i have taken over, would point out that the 98.9% of proceeds from unconfiscated criminal activities is an exaggerated percentage. the confiscation of proceeds of crime and the freezing of such assets is a fundamental measure in the fight against organised crime and terrorist activity. to date, member states have implemented only weakly or rarely the minimum measures in force in the member states. on 21 december 2016, the commission adopted a proposal for a regulation on the mutual recognition by member states of confiscation and freezing of assets resulting from criminal activities. from now on, a decision issued by an authority in one member state can be recognised and enforced swiftly in all the other member states. the scope of this regulation extends to new types of confiscation, in line with but going beyond directive 2014/42/eu, in particular where it provides for less limited forms of non-conviction-based confiscation. the implementation of this regulation makes it possible to use resources for compensation to the families of victims, for activities to combat organised crime and for initiatives with a social purpose, by providing for the establishment of competent offices for each member state. the council and parliament have agreed on a text which provides for 45 days for the execution of confiscation orders and 96 hours for the execution of freezing orders. the regulation makes the mutual recognition of freezing orders more efficient, faster and more uniform.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i thank mr griesbeck and the shadow rapporteurs for the excellent work they have done on a proposal for a regulation which is another essential element in the fight against transnational crime. to hit the criminal organizations where it hurts the most, namely in the economic interests: the freezing and confiscation of assets are the main means of depriving organised criminal groups of the profits and resources necessary for their illegal activities. the regulation complements and strengthens the european regulatory framework, will ensure more effective and faster recognition of freezing and confiscation orders between member states, allowing for the targeting of such criminal proceeds across the entire territory of the union, and it is particularly important to provide for the mutual recognition of so-called confiscation orders without conviction, which with the right safeguards and respect for fundamental rights, represent a significant step forward in the fight against criminal organisations. it is also important to provide for the reuse of confiscated property for social purposes, which is a measure that promotes value and, i would say, a sense of legality.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the mafia is doing business with ease across national borders and exploiting the legislative weaknesses of the various countries and their lack of cooperation, so it makes sense, if we are a union, to try to take the good practices developed in one country and make them part of the common european heritage. it is therefore essential to provide for strong measures such as the one we are discussing today, the mutual recognition of confiscation orders even in the absence of a conviction, because this aspect has proved to be crucial in the italian context for the fight against mafia organizations. it is also a tool that can be very dissuasive. the union is therefore taking a very important step towards harmonizing the rules for fighting the mafia, by choosing to attack the strong to protect the weak. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the financial interests of the union. so we're very happy that this tool is finally coming into port.
in writing. the regulation on the mutual recognition of freezing and confiscation orders is part of the package of three legislative proposals (together with the money transfer control regulation and the anti-money laundering directive) presented by the commission in december 2016 to strengthen the eu's capacity to counter the financing of organised crime and terrorism. as the italian experience also shows, attacking the financial aspects of the activities of criminal organisations is one of the most effective methods of countering them, and given the intrinsically cross-border nature of criminal and terrorist actions, cooperation at eu level in these areas is absolutely necessary.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank the rapporteur for her excellent work and the speed with which she has carried it out. after the regulation on the protection of personal data, the regulation on the free flow of non-personal data is another important step towards completing a european data market, with data that is increasingly transparent, accessible and at the same time better protected. today, companies cannot choose the cheapest places to store or process their data. the numerous administrative obstacles present make it difficult to change service providers or to transfer data back to one's own computer systems. this legislation will help companies avoid duplication of data in multiple locations, enter new markets and expand their business. data will flow freely throughout the european union and barriers to archiving services will be removed, which are the starting point for the development of an increasingly open and digital public administration, where services and documents are available to citizens with a single click. to appreciate the importance of this, it is enough to remember that in ten years the scope of the data economy will grow almost twentyfold and so beyond people, goods, services and capital, the doors are opening to the fifth freedom in the digital single market, that of data, which will favor sectors such as the internet of things, blockchain, healthcare, remote surgery and smart mobility solutions, such as self-driving cars. this will not, however, weaken the control of national authorities who will be able to exercise their right of access to data throughout europe. this control will be crucial because an increasingly digitised world is a more vulnerable world and it is our duty to work to protect the most exposed parties, namely citizens, individuals and businesses.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs maria corazza bildt, and our shadow rapporteur, mrs christel schaldemose, for the work they have done. we know that data management, the rules by which data is processed, transferred, traded and stored, is one of the most important challenges of the digital economy. the creation of a single space of non-personal data within the union creates new opportunities in terms of employment, in particular for start-ups and small businesses, while increasing competition in the sector, increasing the final offer for the benefit of consumers. in addition, mr president, a common legal framework will make it easier for public authorities to exercise supervisory controls to protect citizens and will strengthen the overall data protection framework, alongside the general data protection regulation, which is already in force. i believe that the adoption of this regulation is a further step towards the creation of a european digital single market, which is necessary to compete globally.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner vella, first of all i would like to thank mrs dantin for her valuable work in following up the european citizens' initiative right2water, which called on the commission to ensure that a basic good like water could flow from the tap and be of a quality that is acceptable to all consumers and all european citizens. we want to build consumer confidence and encourage the use of water from our taps, but in setting the parameters that increase water quality we must be careful not to overdo it and not to make it impossible to consume water in certain areas of europe. this is something that is likely to happen in the territory of my region, under the etna volcano, where the volcanic soils are rich in boron and the boron parameter of one milligram per litre proposed by the commission is a very low parameter. efsa itself recommends a higher parameter for the most susceptible categories of consumers; the world health organization has a parameter that's 2.4 times higher. that is why we have tabled an amendment which would allow water to be used in our regions too, and that is why i would ask you to vote for amendment no 180. i agree with the idea of tightening up controls, of guaranteeing consumers, but we must not go beyond what the precautionary principle also requires.
in writing. the drinking water directive is one of the pillars of european water legislation. introduced in the late 1980s, it needs - after more than 20 years - to be revised to bring drinking water quality standards in line with the latest scientific evidence and to adapt the legislative framework to better respond to new challenges such as climate change and the transition to a circular economy. this is the first time that european legislation has taken on board the demands of a european citizens' initiative, which actually went beyond the position reached in the envi committee. for this reason, i have supported the introduction of certain amendments to support the objective of providing universal access to water. the member states must take all the necessary measures to ensure universal access to water, which i consider to be a fundamental right. the revision of the drinking water directive is a great opportunity to finally incorporate this right into legislation and to show that the european union is able to influence concrete issues in the daily lives of european citizens. i agree with all the amendments to reduce or eliminate pfas levels in drinking water.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, europe must also move with great ambition on plastics. our courage and our determination were key to reaching the paris agreement, and they can be key to single-use plastics. in recent days japan, which did not sign the ocean plastics charter at the g7 in july, announced bold first steps to reduce consumption. that is why we in the envi committee did well to make the directive more ambitious, we did so in a sustainable and reasonable way. the vote in the chamber in strasbourg will take us five important steps forward: taking measures that are beneficial for our oceans; take an important step towards curbing an unsustainable throwaway and disposable culture; support innovation and scientific research to create new jobs by developing environmentally sustainable production; strengthen extended producer responsibility in accordance with the 'polluter pays' principle; give our citizens more information; recycle more.

author. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ten years have now passed since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon and it is therefore necessary to take stock of the current situation in the eu. the economic and social data do not lie and tell us that we are worse off today than we were ten years ago, with rising unemployment, diminishing wealth and a debt-to-gdp ratio that has increased by more than 20 percentage points in ten years. this is the reality of the figures, but beyond these clear macro-indicators there is the reality of daily life, which shows how citizens are increasingly in difficulty and how sharp the differences and mistrust between the countries of the union are, reawakening and reinforcing feelings of fear and mutual distrust that we thought had been buried for some time. it is clear that the treaty and the eu have failed to achieve the objectives they set themselves: there is no welfare, no economic cohesion, no social or territorial cohesion, and no much-vaunted solidarity between countries. it is not surprising that one of the objectives of the treaty is to have a highly competitive social market economy. how, i ask, has this principle been translated into practice? it has resulted in the sacrifice of young people, workers and pensioners to harmful neoliberal policies. we have therefore had youth unemployment, wage cuts and pension cuts - the only prescriptions that brussels has been able to impose on the member states. in the last decade, the treaty and the eu have not been able to give a concrete answer to the three major problems facing european citizens today: the european union is also taking action to combat the illegal immigration of refugees. not only has nothing been done, but the european recipes have actually made the situation worse. i wonder how the european union can improve the situation if a democratically elected government cannot even set its own economic measures but must always be blackmailed by this or that eu commissioner, who after failing at home now wants to decide at home. i wonder what power junker, dombrovskis or moscovici have to decide the future and the hopes of millions of young people, workers, pensioners and the unemployed in italy and elsewhere. the arrogance with which you want to pursue a vision of a centralised union, with ever more powers and competences being taken away from national governments, is leading europe to collapse. perhaps we should forget the mantra of 'more europe' or 'there is no alternative', which you think is the solution to all problems but which in reality has been nothing but the sublimation of an undemocratic system at the expense of the freedoms of the citizens and peoples of europe. i ask you if you have ever wondered why, when european citizens have been allowed to speak directly on eu matters, the outcome has often been quite different from what you expected. the latest eurobarometer says that less than half of italians see advantages in the eu but 60% support this government that you oppose. what are you doing? respect for democracy and the freedoms of the people or take them away? for you, the hand of history is now inexorably moving. those who have supported this failed idea of europe will be swept away by the popular vote. for many years in these halls you have ostracized us, mocked us, silenced us. we'll have our revenge in may. the political shock that will wipe you out will allow the real europe to rise from the abyss into which your misguided choices have brought it.

member of the commission. mr president, mr president of the court of auditors, ladies and gentlemen, i have listened attentively to your communications. we shall evaluate them and come back to them in the course of the further discharge procedure. i am grateful for the recognition given by many members to my staff in the commission services for their proper implementation of the budget. i can also accept and take up the expectations of many members here, and i think some critical remarks are worth considering. thank you for your factual comment. if we still see that some programmes have been delayed in 2018, what are the reasons and what should we learn from this for the next budgetary framework? firstly, as the current budgetary framework was only adopted by the council and parliament in mid-december with all the implementing rules, the first year and also the second year of the budgetary framework were lost time, so 2014 and much of 2015 were lost time. it was only in 2017 that all the programs started to run at full speed. this can be particularly noted for 2018 and the implementation of the budget this year. secondly, n+3 does not put a lot of pressure on us to produce invoices quickly and to ask for reimbursement. only a few months ago we virtually completed the 2007-2013 budgetary framework. it is only now that the authorities have some latitude to apply for and receive funds from the current budgetary framework. that's why n+2 instead of n+3. and our joint recommendation - that of parliament and the commission - to the council is to do everything possible to ensure that the next budgetary framework can be adopted before the next elections. this will allow preparations to take advantage of the programmes from 1 january 2021. this lesson must be drawn from the consultation processes of the current budgetary framework, from 2011, 2012 and 2013. thirdly, simplification of the rules governing our programmes. we have clearly associated simplification with our proposal for the next mff. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in some cases, it was only at the beginning of last year that some member states and regions designated the authorities responsible for implementation and programme execution. the lessons to be drawn from the present budgetary framework are these. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the establishment of a european agency for the evaluation of medicinal products for human use (aema) is a very good one. thank you for your advice.
president of the court of auditors. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. i would like to begin by thanking all of you for your words of support for our work. mr lazarou, who as the main rapporteur in the house did the essential work in drawing up the annual report, and i will be happy to pass this on to all the other members and staff of the house. mr czarnecki mentioned that for 24 years now, since the entry into force of the maastricht treaty, we have had to submit the so-called statement of insurance as a court of auditors. we have been giving a negative judgment for 22 years and now for two years we have given a limited positive judgment. i think that's a really positive development. i want to emphasize this again: this is not due to miscalculation or down-counting of the error rate, but it is simply due to the fact that the data actually got better. we have made considerable progress on compliance within the european union, although i do not want to rule out the possibility that next year the picture may not look so good. this is also linked to the fact that we have of course had a relatively small share of cohesion expenditure this year and cohesion expenditure tends to have a slightly higher error rate anyway. so it is not excluded that perhaps the picture next year will not look quite as good as it did this year. i would like to make one further comment on the error rate. this is -- and this is often misunderstood, unfortunately -- not an exact calculation, this is a mathematical-statistical method that you as politicians all know from opinion polls, where you take a sample, and then on that basis you calculate what the likely error rate is. but this always has a variation of about +/- 1% on average, and therefore it must be made very clear that if you make concrete statements about concrete percentages above a certain threshold, namely below the materiality threshold, then they have a relatively low actual statistical value. we are therefore increasingly considering as a court - we will think about this again next year - whether we should not completely spare ourselves all statements that are below the materiality threshold and delete them altogether. this is a question we shall discuss further, simply to avoid any further misunderstanding in this context. the ral, the rest à liquider, has of course played a major role in the debate. i would like to say again very explicitly - to avoid any misunderstanding here too - that rals are normal, as commissioner oettinger has quite rightly said. what concerns us is the sheer scale of the fact that we have ral at the moment on the order of twice the nominal annual budget. of course, this is also a consequence of the n+3 rule. the n+3 rule was introduced in 2008 or after 2008 in the context of the financial crisis, as member states experienced problems in co-financing or financing the planning, implementation and execution of projects. but the financial crisis was ten years ago. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think that mr flanagan, mr van nistelrooij and mr hayes have already made the reference to the mff. you can expect that in the next few days we will be deciding on individual opinions, opinions on agricultural policy, cohesion policy. because the request is for your home, we're happy to do the same for horizon and other topics that are important to you. i want to speak about the error rate because mr kohn has rightly raised the subject, and i am very grateful for that. if we find an estimated error rate of 2.4%, this does not mean that €3.3 billion of eu funds have been wasted. it doesn't mean that. it simply means that we have found errors in the way these funds have been spent, either legal, or in most cases legal, or accounting errors. this is not a question of the usefulness of the expenditure. these funds, even if they were flawed, could have been spent in a very sensible way. it is equally conceivable that funds which have been spent lawfully have been spent in a completely pointless way. this is a compliance check. so all we do is check that things are right legally and mathematically. the other aspect of usefulness is examined in the performance, i.e. in the audit reports, which we are already producing in large numbers - up to 50 per year - at the moment as the european court of auditors. the performance ratio also plays a role in the annual report. we're working on ways to improve this internally, to give you better information about this in detail. the value for money issue has also been raised here; european added value is also a topic that is primarily relevant to the question of performance and only very limited to the question of compliance. mr ashworth rightly pointed out that a large part of the responsibility also lies with the member states. i think that is correct and that should not be forgotten. the commission is not to blame for everything. but it has to stop and monitor the member states to make sure they are doing things right. so far, it's always in business as far as data reliability is concerned. i would also like to say something about that, because it is also raised again and again. rest assured that we only use data from member states and the commission for our audits that we are personally convinced are reliable. all other data which we have doubts about are not included, but are collected by us. i can tell mr marias that the report on the ngos is in the final stages and will be coming soon. i hope you can learn something from this. mrs maletić has quite rightly raised the issue of the frequent lack or insufficiency of technical support. we have already made a report on the jaspers programmes some time ago and we have made some critical remarks on how this can be improved. you see, the court of auditors is trying to keep you all up to date so that we can improve our work as a whole. our criticism is not meant to bring something down, but to improve the situation, to put a finger in the wound, but in the sense of healing, not in the sense of breaking it.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after long negotiations we are finally discussing today the adoption of the regulation on the import of cultural goods. first of all, i would like to thank all my colleagues for the hard work they have put in over the past few months. some studies indicate that illicit trade in works of art is second only to that in weapons and drugs. the images of the destruction of the palmyra site by isis are still vivid in our eyes, but to speak of destruction is inaccurate. it was a real dismantling: the most valuable artifacts were stolen and sold in the european marketplace. after depriving the syrian people of their history and culture, european buyers have helped directly fund a terrorist organization. the illegal trafficking of works of art is a crime against humanity because it robs us of our common artistic heritage and our history, but it also threatens the security of european citizens by helping to finance terrorist activities. not only that: the illegal trade in art, by encouraging tax evasion and money laundering, threatens our social model. the new regulation will therefore contribute to this triple battle by imposing transparency and greater controls. it was not an easy task. while we all share the urgency of action, we have had difficulty in striking the right balance between the need to curb this illicit trade and the objective of avoiding unnecessary red tape for private operators and customs. we have therefore introduced facilities for small and mediumsized enterprises, an electronic registration system which can facilitate procedures and value thresholds which will allow for more targeted application, imposing controls only on the most valuable goods. moreover, starting with the 1970 unesco convention, the text we are proposing will be more consistent with international conventions and union regulations. applying the same annex to the export regulation and drawing on the experience of customs officials and art markets will make implementation easier. the final text is balanced and the very large majority who supported it proves this. the european union will have a state-of-the-art instrument to combat illegal trafficking without hampering legitimate trade, a source of jobs and growth. after approval we will have to ensure that the application is as uniform as possible. we cannot allow internal competition between european ports to create free zones. we must fight internal fraud, such as that perpetrated by the uk authorities on the eu budget since 2011: that is why we are going to introduce a system of due diligence, i.e. a list of documents which are the same for everyone and which the customs authorities will be obliged to require. i would remind our british friends who are worried about the effects of the regulation on the london art market after brexit that you cannot enjoy the benefits of a community without being part of it and if you want to avoid double checks you have to be part of the single market. once again, european trade policy is presented as an alternative to both protectionism and unbridled liberalism. a strategy based on our values: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. with tomorrow's vote we will add to european trade policy another element of sustainability, another brick to make our common home more worthy of the men and women who live in it, another effort to make globalisation a more equitable and humane process. this is the europe we want, a europe which protects without being closed in on itself.
i am speaking as the shadow rapporteur for the gue/ngl group on behalf of the inta committee. already at the joint work stage of the two inta/imco committees i welcomed the european commission's proposal to regulate the importation of cultural goods by the union, with the aim of preventing and blocking the illicit trade in works of art. i would also like to stress the need for such regulation when we vote in plenary. i think the text has been improved by the work of the two committees: the commission has also taken the initiative of introducing a new system of taxation, which is to be applied to all the goods and services produced by the community. we also agreed to simplify the procedures, moving from the dual licence procedure to a single licence procedure. a website will be set up if the commission, as i hope, wishes to incorporate parliament's position so that information searches can be made easily accessible. i would just like to add a political and cultural assessment. access to works of art is one of the forms of citizenship construction. it is the duty of these institutions, and of the european institutions, to make this access available to all and to prevent the arts from becoming contraband goods, especially in those countries which are suffering from conflict situations.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the importation of artefacts and works of art into europe is a very delicate process because without controls, counterfeit goods, stolen goods or even items sold to finance terrorist organisations can be imported. while each country used to apply different rules, this regulation will establish a standardised system of identification, give customs authorities the appropriate tools to detect and stop fraud and illegal products, and require the same checks and training throughout the union. we also want to ensure that the small businesses operating in the art market are given adequate assistance so that they can continue their honest work without being burdened by bureaucracy. with this regulation we hope to put an end to the black market in art. i thank the rapporteurs for this and assure them of my support and that of my delegation.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, you know that the illicit trade in cultural goods has been a feature of the history of all conflicts. today more than ever, this trade is a source of funding for criminal organizations, terrorism and armed groups, as the war in syria has unfortunately shown. this measure is a further part of a strategy that the commission and this parliament have put into place in this parliament on the traceability of goods entering the european union, starting with the measure we have taken on minerals from conflict zones. only through specific customs procedures, harmonized at european level, and effective coordination between the competent authorities will we be able to prevent the entry of illicit cultural goods into our single market and, not least, to protect the cultural heritage of the third countries from which they come. finally, i should like to thank the rapporteur, mrs alessia mosca, and the rapporteur for my committee and my group, mr kohn, for their work.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the cultural heritage of a country, in particular its archaeological findings, its works of art and its oldest objects, represents the roots, the historical memory and the identity of a people. the european parliament, by adopting the regulation on the importation of cultural goods into the eu, is giving substance to these words, adopting the line taken by the cult committee. the european union has a duty to combat the illegal import of cultural property and to establish harmonised rules to protect and safeguard not only its own cultural property but also cultural property from third countries, particularly those in conflict. moreover, cultural property is often stolen and smuggled to finance terrorism, but also for the purpose of recycling and circumvention. by substantially amending the commission proposal, which proposed a minimum age of 250 years to define a cultural object falling within the scope of this regulation, we have lowered the age limit to 100 years, thus aligning ourselves with the main international conventions (unidroit, unesco, hague convention) and our existing regulation on the export of cultural objects. it is precisely because cultural goods are not just any commodity that we have introduced the need to establish a simplified electronic procedure and a set of rules and documents to prove the legality of their importation into europe.
